div.head: POULTRY YARD IN APRIL.
div.p: THE POULTRY YARD IN APRIL.

April is a very important mouth in the poultry yard. Upon the work done or neglected during the next few weeks depends in a large measure the satisfactory or the unsatisfactory state of the balance-sheet at the end of the year. There are several things that must be done at latest during this month; if the opportunity lips by it will not occur again until next spring. It is possible, moreover, to make up in some measure for omissions in March, and espe- cially is this the case during the earlier part of the month.

div.head: Adult Birds.
div.p: The Adult Birds.

Many of the hens which commenced laying last autumn, and have continued to do their duty during the last three or four months, are beginning to show signs of reduced prolificacy, and during the next few weeks those that were later in commencing to lay will have to be de- pended upon mainly for the egg supply. Pro- yided mild weather prevails during April eggs are generally very plentiful indeed, and, as prices have by no means reached their lowest limit, it-ia generally an extremely profitable month for those who specialise in egg produc- tion. Laying hens at this time should be gener- ously fed, for, unless the material for the forma- tion of eggs is placed within their bodies, as it were, the supply will be very small. The foods should be strong in albuminoids and carbohy- drates; they should not receive enough to make them fat and lazy, but yet sufficient to main- tain their strength and vigour. A useful mix- ture for morning use is two parts barley meal, one middlings, one bea4 or pea meal, and half a part lean meat. In the afternoon a mixture of barley, wheat and a little maize is beneficial. It is often found at this time of year that hens lay on flesh too quickly, but this must be avoided, for fat hens rarely prove profitable. Not only do fat hens produce fewer eggs, but a large percentage of them are unfertile. If the weather is fine during April, as many of the laying hens as possible should be removed to movable houses, scattered far and wide about the fields, and allowed full freedom to wander about all day long.
The Young Stock,

If the weather is as changeable during April as it has been during March, poultry-keepers will have to look forward to a pretty trying time, particularly as hatching operations should now be in full swing.; and every few days should see a batch of newly-hatched chickens. Great Care must be -,exercised when removing the youngsters from the incubator or from under the hen to the brooder or coop,, and they should be carried in a felt-lined basket or box, as a chill at this age may have the ,niost serious .conse- quences, the ill-effects of which may remain with them throughout their lives. In the case iof artificially hatched , chickens no coddling must take place, and the heat within the inner compartment sheuld never be allowed; even dur- ing the first week, to rise above 90 degrees; dur- ing the second week 85 degrees is sufficient, dur- ing the third 80 degrees, gradually reducing the temperature as the birds; become older, till they are able to dispense with artificial heat altogether. Just when this can take place must depend upon the weather and Upon the health of the chickens. If the weather is warm and the chickens have developed well, they can often do without artificial heat when they are six weeks old. As a rule, however, eight weeks early in the season is nearer the mark,'

Keeping Chickens Clean. The imp9rtance of cleanliness among all classes of poultry, especially among young chickens, cannot be too greatly nor too often emphasised. If they are carelessly looked after and are allowed to become infested with in- sects, &c., their growth is seriously retarded, and they are very liable to be unhealthy. With newly-hatched chickens it is a good plan to anoint their head S as soon as they arecdry with a preparation composed of the following: loz. mercurial ointment. loz. lard, -?toz. sulphur, and sufficient paraffin oil to make semi-fluid. This process should be repeated when the chickens are about three weeks or a month old, for there is no more effective way of keeping down vermin. When they are older, they must be dusted with a disinfectant powder. particular attention being paid to the-feathers under the wings and on the back, for it is on these parts that the vermin mostly congregate.—E. T. Brown in "Farm and Home."

div.head: WAR REDUCES EGG SUPPLY.
div.p: WAR REDUCES EGG SUPPLY.

Belgium. and France are both great poultryj countries. Another in, which the industry, has been highly developed of late years is Galicia., which is also being ~war-swept. Vast quantities of eggs are exported every year, of 'which.Ger- many has taken the larger portion, although some have come to the United' Kingdom. What the conditions are there we know to a very limited extent ;'hut, with the huge armies tra- yersing that seetion of Europe and . the wide range of conflict, it may reasonably be supposed that production will be greatly reduced, due to destruction of the stock, and it is not im- probable that the Same will take place in other parts of Austria-Hungary. What has previ- ously been pointed out—namely the need for enhancement of home production, not alone to meet present-day requirements, but in view of the futtfie—is,,, says "Expert" in "Farm and ome," becoming increasingly evident.

div.head: GROSSLY OVERFED.
div.p: GROSSLY OVERFED.
Mr. G. F. Case Morris, writing in the Feathered World," says:— .

I think e may safely say that the majority of poultry in confinement are grossly over-fed, hence the egg yield is not 'what it should be. Some people have an idea that the more you feed a hen the greater number of eggs she will lay. This is a fallacy, of course, tt,, will soon become apparent to those who have charge of the feeding.

The golden rule is to give only as much as the fowls will eat at a meal. How is °nett° arrive at the precise amount that they will con- sume and no more at a given meal unless one stands over them to watch? Well, I admit it is a difficult ti,uestion to anwer, 11(“vever, per- haps the bet scheme is to experiment by givin "a small'quantity- at first, and gradually increas- ing the amount if the fowls do not seem to be putting on flesh, . and the laying is unsatis- factory. ' --j .
-.Once '.a laying hen gets really grossly,fat it generally all up with her, for liVet disemPe 'sets in, and there is no certain cure for it. •

In feeding a small number of hens it is an easy matter to count the number of handfuls given at each meal, beginning with half a hand- ful, to Milt hen, and increasing to a full ful if they seem to require it, but only if they seem to. - - - _

_ Now a dozen or more hens for the househola supply or eggs need only cost a very little, to feel if properly Managed. There should alwap; be a poultry tub in'which all pieces are thrown (not refuse), and the whole ,should be boiled up every evening andmleft in the pan to simmer over-night. if tie birds are fed.on.barley meal or Indian meal, which se many people seem to cling to as the staple food diet, one must not be surprised if liver disease soon begins to show itself. Barley in any shape or. form is a mistaken

div.head: POULTRY PEN.
div.p: POULTRY PEN.
WAR STORIES:
TERRITORIAL OFFICER Speaks Of The Increasing Battalion
Casualties.
A 'Warrington Territorial officer writes:— Thursday, April Ist. _ _ _

I am still in the same trench, -w:hich we have occupied since Friday night last. The weather has been exceptionally dry—no rain fox a whole week. The sun has been very bright, but a biting wind, has been blowing. Fortu- nately this ceased to-day, and, as I sit here in the bottom of the trench writing this•note, the sun is almost baking hot and it feels like a foretaste of summer.

The trenches are a curious sight, especially on a warm day like this; you see men lying fast asleep in all attitudes. You would con- sider some of the poses impossible to allow of sleep, but, none the less, although sleep is so intermittent, a man is sound asleep during the first few minutes of his relief. This is in the daytime. At night it is like a _hive of bees, ration parties coming in, working parties im- proving the sand-bag walls.

div.head: Harassing Question of the Wounded.
div.p: Harassing Question of the Wounded.

Thrown in with all this you get the cOn- tinuous whistling of bullets flying over the trench and the thud of those striking the bags in front, and then possibly some casualties. [I havekjust stopped ,writing to look at one of our aeroplanes passing overhead.] First-aid men attend to these whilst the stretcher-bearers are telephoned for from headquarters, which( is some way back behind the firing-line, housed in any shelter available. This question of the wounded is a harassing and unfortunate one, for it is impossible • to move them in daylight from our trenches It must be done at night; so if a man is -wounded at daybreak the poor chap has to remain here till dusk before we can get him to the doctor. Of course, certain men are trained in first-aid and bandage the wounds as best they can with the 'field dressings with which we are all pro- vided. The Germans are a little better off in this respect, as in most cases the positions they settled down in are on the crest lines, and we have had to work our way as close to them as possible, and in nearly all cases they can cover the ground in rear of our trenches with their rifle fire. They can bring up their reliefs and supports without our seeing them, anil so it gives them better opportunity to remove their casualties. The selection of their position is accounted for by their positions being defensive and ours originally offensive, although you might term both at present defensive. Early on the Saturday morning one poor chap, Bridgen—a splendid ifellow—was fatally wounded by a long-range sniper. How Lieutenant Seymour-Jones Was Killed. Seymour-Jones had been to the Major for a chat. About three o'clock they had to go round a traverse wall, very close to the position where 'Bridgen was hit in the morning. The sniper appears to have changed his mark, and when they showed themselves round this wall he fired the bullet, hitting Seymour-Jones, the bullet passing clean through his head. He was unconscious from the time of being hit. Poor chap! We all lament his loss—he was one of our keenest officers and one popular with everybody. He was buried the same evening close by; I believe in the Military cemetery which has sprung up, and, unfortunately, too rapidly being filled. Saturday evening and all. night I spent with a party building up another wall, and since then no mark has been possible for this sniper, although we can hear his bullets pass .to an- other point farther along the line, at which he evidently sees movement. We have been unlucky during this ,turn in the trenches—in, this one. we have had four fatal cases and one wounded, and, I under- stand, there are losses in the others We - are occupying. .
There is little- sickness mono-4 the men., . n- and, generally speaking, it -might be said the battalion is in good fettle and the casualties may round the fifty mark.

div.head: Men Want to Dash for the Germans.
div.p: Men Want to Dash for the Germans.

Au officer • says that his men have actually, and seriously asked him if they would not be, allowed to have a dash at the German trenches. They meant it in all seriousness, but, of course, an isolated attack like this would be futile.

div.head: Germans Flew Away.
div.p: The Germans Flew Away.

This morning we had a German aeroplane over, no sooner he appeared than two of ours seemed to . come from nowhere. The Hun im- mediately turned round and flew home. The sky is perfectly clear, not a cloud in sight, and ideal for flying and observation. Easter Sunday afternoon, 3.15. _ _ .

Well! we got out of the trenches last ,Thurs- day night and returned to our original rest billets. It seemed awfully sad, next morning when we awoke, that .poor Seymour-Jones was not with us. Ever since coming out our -com- pany officers have been very jolly and happy together.

div.head: Sixty Killed and Wounded
div.p: Sixty Killed and Wounded

Our casualty list has been rather heavy this time, 27 killed and wounded. Four killed and, one wounded in my trench. The battalion casualty list up-to-date is 83 killed, wounded and sick, about.6o of the two formed. how they do mount up! -What an. Easter Sunday and the contrast of previous ones, living here in a war-ridden country, housed in the roof of a little cottage, which up to the present is untouched, although within range of tjae German artillery. Of course if this was all we had to put up with we would not mind. It is the strain and -un- certainty of- the whole affair that palls.

div.head: The. Enjoyment of a Bath.
div.p: The. Enjoyment of a Bath.

I have had to break in this letter and turn out to take the men for a hot bath. We are using an old brewery, using the .vats and wash- tubs. Of course, brewing is . suspended, and is in the hands of the military, our Engineers working the machinery, pumps,. &c. You 'must be fixed as .we are to realise the enjoyment of a bath. We try to keep .the vermin down, but are not altogether successful. The places We have to doss in, shippon Stalls, or any kind of cover procurable, is all against it, and we all have to go as long as ten days without a chance of changing clothes. The unpleasantness of this must increase as the hot weather comes. How unsanitary the whole country will become! Even now the land reeks with smells at times. It is easily understood when it has been occupied so long by so many men. You have only to stick your spade anywhere near the trenches, to get the most unpleasant of odours. When we were at the brewery we had several Germans shells ekploding with a few yards of us, but an inch is as good :as a mile where bullets and shells are concerned, and we pay little heed to the noise of shells in the distance. It, is those which are not heard which give the trouble.
I fancy we return to the trenches on Wednes- day evening.

div.head: THIGH GRAZED BY WARMAN BULLET. w
div.p: THIGH GRAZED BY WARMAN BULLET. w

Private H. J. Lawless, a despatch rider in the 4th South Lancashire Regiment, who was formerly employed in the office at Messrs. Rylands' Bros., Ltd., .has sent the following letter to Mr. Knott, with whom he formerly worked:— . •

" Life.outhere" is -Very different from the life we lead in England. I had my baptism, of 'fire about five weeks ago-, both by shells and bullets, and the experience was hair-raising. I have now settled down to my work as signaller„ and consider myself quite an old soldier. Aeroplqne duels are very common, while the shell fire is treated very lightly. Although I have been, in the first line of trenches for several days, I haven't seen, a live German yet, although their bullets have come unpleasantly near.' "'One bullet grazed my thigh and broke the skin, the first night I went to the treoches. These occurrences, however, are very Oommon, and nothing to talk about. Soldiers have different opinions as regards the duration of the war; the majority, however, think it will end suddenly. With the advent .of .warm :weather our greatest. enemy will be fever, owing to the number of dead men and horses lying about, or buried just underneath the 'soil." Writing later. Private Lawless says: "I am just awaiting my turn to go into the trenches."

div.head: By LETTER. AND INTERVIEW. THE LIVERPOOLS' WILD CHARGE. Warringtonian Who Was In It Writes To A Friend.
div.p: By LETTER. AND INTERVIEW. THE LIVERPOOLS' WILD CHARGE. Warringtonian Who Was In It Writes To A Friend.
".A TIME OF SACRIFICE."
Rifleman Who Is Grateful To The Women Workers.

Rifleman E. Morris, one of the Cable Company's employes, who is serving in the Ist Battalion of the Rifle Brigade, writes to Mr. Watson in acknowledgment of a parcel recently forwarded him in the name of the women em- ployed at the works. "It must be a big sacri- fice to them," he said, "to get these things together; but, then, this is a time of sacrifice." He goes on to write of the cold in the trenches and says how welcome gifts of socks and other articles of warm clothing are to the men, who often have to sit through the night in one particular spot, for if they moved they would run an awful risk of being "sniped." In the morning tots of rum are served out to the men for the purpose of restoring the circula- tion of the blood.

div.head: Welcome Change.
div.p: A Welcome Change.

The Brigade, he says, spend -several days at a time in the trenches and then they "go into billet" for a day or two, when they get the luxury of a bath—a much-appreciated luxury, by the way—and have a change of clothes. The rest does them good and they go back to the trenches feeling quite smart and _
fit onoe more, and "ready for the Germans whenever they like to come."

div.head: GAME GERMANS WILL SOON PLAY! –
div.p: GAME GERMANS WILL SOON PLAY! -
"The Running Game," Says Rifleman
Barnes.

Rifleman Fred. Barnes, yet another of the Cable Company's -contingent with the -Tifle Brigade, writes to. Mr. Watson from the Alder Hay Hospital; West Derby, Liverpool, .where he is at present recovering from a wound re- ceived on March 10th.

"It is agony for me to write," the gallant soldier says, "but I feel that I must do so. The doctor tells me that it will be some time before I can leave my bed, as the wound is a very nasty one. I was standing in the trench at the time I was hit.

div.head: Dum-dum Bullet in the Neck.
div.p: A Dum-dum Bullet in the Neck.

"I thought I was hidden from the enemy's snipers, but one of them got me, and the bullet that ` plugged ' me was a dum-dum; so you will see that they are not playing the game. But they will play the game in a little while, only it will be the running game. I think they have about shot their bolt. lam a lucky chap to be here to tell the tale. The bullet entered one side of my neck and simply ploughed its way °through and came out at the other side. I must have turned away from the German lines when I Was hit. You can guess where I would have got it had I been fully turned towards them. It would have been through the mouth!" Rifleman Barnes concludes with the hope that "the good old firm is keeping busy." "Shrapnel for Dinner."

In an earlier letter, written before he was wounded, Rifleman Barnes describes how, as he wrote under cover of the trench, "our boys were giving the Germars shrapnel for dinner," Whilst the enemy were retaliating with "Little Willies," which, however, were " nuth in'," save make a big noise when they bursted.

"One of our airmen." the Rifleman added, "has been over the German lineg:laking ob- servations this morning, and they had about fifty 'pots' at him, but it was a waste of ammunition. He circled about their position like a snake, and this is an every-day occur- rence with him.. He does lead the Germans a dance!

div.head: HIS SLEEPING MATE.
div.p: HIS SLEEPING MATE.
Warrington " Terrier " Describes His Parting AVM.' AVounded "Pal."
Private John Byrne, of "BZ.treoruipany of the 4th South Lancashire:,'it s Sollittks on March 13th, to Mrs. Humphreys, of SO, rorster- street:— ,

"I write, hoPing to :find you zn good health, as I am at present. I have got _through my baptism in the trenches and came out safely. It is a very nerve-trying experience getting in and out of the trenches.: Bullets are flying all round you and we lose many men, almost going into the trenches as we do 'once we a-re inside them. It was awful cold in the trenches at first and I thought my feet were frost-bitten, 'but it has kept fine the last few days. We were out trench-digging the other 'night and it was very dark. We had to walk one behind the other; in fact one had to stick to the coat of the man in ,front of him for fear of getting lost. "

div.head: Man Ahead Fatally Wounded.
div.p: Man Ahead Fatally Wounded.

"The 'one in front of Me was knocked over. I stopped with him and asked him where he Was hit and he told me. When the 'first-aid' man came I left him, thinking he was not so bad, but when I got back a few hours later I was astonished to hear he had been buried. He died as soon as I left him. -1 was upset, as he used rO. sleep with me., We lost a few more besides him that night; but, of course,. we can- not all get through. Some of us are bound to fall. We never know whose turn it will be next, but we trust to God to. pull .us through.

. . . . There are lots of dead, which our Men cannot •get at to • bury. There was a dead Frenchman just behind the trench that I was in. .. . We have seen nothing yet as com- pared to the things seen by those who have been out all along.
Victory Must Be Ours—And The Fruits Thereof!

"I shalr not care when it is all over, pro- vided things are not left in the same condition as when we started. I want victory for our ants and we are sure to get it, sooner, orrlater, because even:now we-a,re- w:nn:ng all along the line. .., . . in, wooden huts. Private :Cattell is in the sanie -hut as -me. He 'getting-on all right.and so is-lteggie. Your Harry is still going on With his police-duties.. He has 'got shut.' of his Cold and .is -looking like ,himself again. He has not been in .the trenches and may not go in as he has plenty to do elsewhere."

div.head: "THE LUCKIEST COMPANY OUT
div.p: "THE LUCKIEST COMPANY OUT
HERE!
Sapper Tells of Trench-bigging Experiences,

' Mrs. A. Deeley, who lives at 83, Longford- street, Warrington, has this week received the following letter from her , son, Sapper A. Deeley, of the West -Lancashire Division (Territorial) Engineers : "We had rather an exciting experience the other day. We had been working on a. farm where some 'artillerymen are billeted. We were putting a barbed wire entanglement around the place, and were loopholing the walls:

div.head: Spotted from An Observation Balloon.
div.p: Spotted from An Observation Balloon.
"We also put a barricade of sandbags up, with two places for Maxim guns, with which to command the road. The Germans had an

. , observation balloon up They must have seen us from this balloon, for they started shelling us. . . . We all got under cover, and it was a good job we did. Some Of our chaps were going to get behind the sandbags, but they thought better of it.

div.head: Narrow Escape.
div.p: A Narrow Escape.

" One shell hit the barricade, and blew the sandbags about ten feet away„ and then burst near the wall. I have a piece of the shell. It is about five-eighths of an inch thick, so you can guess what sort of a wound it would have made had it struck anybody. There were some civilians working on some trenches and you fillould have seen them run!
Germans Are "Rotten Shots," Says "Tommy." . .
"One day, the Germans sent about thirty shells over us, but they did no damage. The enemy seem to be 'rotten .shots.' . . .

On one farm, one of our sections was working with some civilians, ,when a shrapnel shell burst and 'killed a civilian. Two of our fellows went to pick him up when another burst, and slightly wounded both of them. We have been the luckiest company .out here,, for, these were the only casualties up to ' the time of writing."

div.head: ITII THE NATIONAL lIESERA E.
div.p: ITII THE NATIONAL lIESERA E.
How The Veterans Arc. I)l)inii "Their
Little Bi

In the course of a brief letter to Mr. F. Leach, of Hatton Cottage, Mayfield-road, Grappenhall, Private J. J. McHugh—who is now serving as a National Reservist, accredited to the Cheshire Regiment, and who has a son —Private McHugh—at the Front—describes his work in North Wales, where he is at present stationed.

"We are kloing fairly well," he writes, "and are having fine weather, although it is cold. I am employed in doing guard duty on the sea-front, having four hours on and four hours off. We have to see that persons do not sus- piciously loiter about and to keep an eye on the shipping; also we must not allow any per- sons to land without challenging them, and we have to keep our eyes open for suspicions lights and the like. We are billeted at farm houses."

div.head: AVIIAT PRISONERS WANT.
div.p: AVIIAT PRISONERS WANT.
Captured Warringtonian's Brief Message To His Brother.

British captives now in the hands of the 'Germans, are, it is stated, no longer permitted to send letters to their relatives and friends, but are allowed to forward their brief messages on postcards, provided they are not written with ink or indelible pencil. Among the members of the South Lancashire Regiment who are at present captives of the Huns is Private David Balmer, who was wounded at Mons some months ago, and fell into the hands of the enemy.

Writing to his brother, Mr. E. Balmer, of 11, Elaine-street, Warrington, Private Balmer asks him to send supplies of cocoa, sugar, tea, tooth-powder, cake and "tinned-stuff," "as we can't expect to get that sort of thing here." He adds that he is "still in good health, having got all right from the wound trouble."

div.head: " TERRIER'S " CLOSE CALL.
div.p: " TERRIER'S " CLOSE CALL.
Bullet Struck The Stock Of Ills Rifle.

Writing to his mother, Mrs. R. Barton, of 7, Bostock-street, Private Williath Lindsay, one of Warrington's gallant Territorials, who serves in "A T' Company, notified that up to -March 22nd, the date of his letter, he was in the best.of health.

"We have just come back for a rest again," he adds, "having had another spell in the trenches. We only did three days this time. The weather: is getting a lot better and the trenches are becoming quite dry, with the result that cold feet was not so serious a trouble to us this time as they were last. Nor did the Germans shell us quite so much, as.our guns gave them 'a bit to go on with,' which quietened them considerably. An Unforgettable .Artillery Duel. "We have a gun near us that is about threv times as good as their 'Jack Johnsons',' and every time it is fired out boys shout 'Go on England!' And we call it Little Willie! There was a big artillery duel last Sunday night, and it was something I shall never for- get—just like a heavy thunderstorm! The flashes from the guns resembled lightning, and the booming was like thunder, whilst the shrieking of a high wind is nothing as .con\- pared with the screech of the shells. . . . It is surprising how one gets used to bullets buzzing about. As we were coming out of the trenches one night a bullet struck my rifle and smashed part of the stock. It was a lucky escape, for, had not my rifle been in the position it was, the bullet must have gone through my thigh. However, they say that a miss is as good as a mile. I have got the bullet and I hope to bring it home."

div.head: TERRITORIALS AND WARFARE.
div.p: TERRITORIALS AND WARFARE.
"Taking To It Like Ducks," Writes
One Of Them.

The following letter has this week been re- ceived by Councillor E. Osborne, of Bold-street, 'President of the Warrington P.C., from Cor- poral R. P. Anderton, of the 4th (Territorial) Battalion- of. the South Lancashire Regiment. "At the time of writing our half of the Battalion are doing their setond turn—since Friday last—of forty-eight hours in the. actual firing line, and I. think we will have earned a little rest on going.out. .Our boys are taking to this trench warfare like ducks going into water, and they are up to all kinds of pranks.

div.head: "The Cheekiest. Lot of Chaps."
div.p: "The Cheekiest. Lot of Chaps."

"In fact, one of the Engineers remarked that we were about the cheekiest lot of chaps he had come across. Only this morning I. saw a chap lathering himself 'whilst having a look over the parapet, to. see if the Germans were moving at all. We are now teaching a new Battalion the tricks of the trade, it being their first time to visit the 'trenches. As I write, the - enemy's artillery are trying :to locate a 'position just behind us, and shells are. flying over, but from what I have seen of their marks- manship they cannot bold a candle to the Eng- lishmen, who continually drop shells into the German trenches, which are only one hundred .yards from us. German Gunners Pastmasters at Hitting - Churches.

"There is no question whatever, but our oppo- nents are pastznasters at hitting churches. tic., and the destruction in this line is something awful. Last week they tried to range on the trench we occupied. but the result was a 'wash-out.' One 'thing that weuldkamuse our friends in Warrington is lo see US' -moving off ~from -headquarters to- - the trenches.- We re- :Beni hie .ft walking ',stores,' - some ' carrying eat- ables, such as bacon, bully.biscuits. jam, cheese, tea and sugar, while others struggle -along With, coke, wood, braziers,, ,half-gallon bottles' of water, and numerous other things, which help to make the trenches a little like home.
Make Themselves "Perfectly Happy" in the
Trenches. .;

"On arrival there, we make ourselves per- fectly happy, and just to show there is no ill- feeling, we break off,' but not with a miss in baulk,' but by sending some lead pills into the lines opposite. The portion of the trench where I . am stationed: we christened the Hotel de UCkhart, and at meal times- our spread' is too funny for .words. In addition to the daily routine of food our boys go in for all kinds of experiments.

div.head: Culinary Experiments
div.p: Culinary Experiments

. . ." One is to soak a mess -tin full of biscuits and boil same, with a quantity of jam mixed in it. This is called 'plum-duff,' and it makes a tasty bit. One of my luxuries is to fry a biscuit in bacon fat; it is great ! The other night I fell over some barbed wire into a hole full of water. winch had been made by a 'Jack Johnson' shell. Naturally, our Battalion have had a number of casualties, but considering the work we have done I think we have been lucky in this respect.
"Terriers' " Tribute to Lieut. Seymour-Jones.

"We all deplore the loss of any of our com- rades, and .perhaps the one that has 'touched .us Most was that of Lieut. Seymour-Jones. ' He was a man we all respected, and he had proved himself a very fine soldier. His bravery was an example to us all; and Warringtonians have lost an officer of whom they .have every reason to he proud. As, Shakespeare said . His life was gentle; and the elements So mixed in him that Nature might stand up And say to all the world: This was a man."

div.head: " Boys" Keeping Remarkably Fit
div.p: " Boys" Keeping Remarkably Fit

"Taking- everything into consideration, the boys' are keeping remarkably fit, and. are adapting themselves very well to this rough life. One of our greatest disappointments was to hear of,the football team's downfall to Sal- ford. We 'expected to read of them holding their own, ,quite as 'easily as the English are holding the, Huns out here." Corporal Anderton concludes with goodi wishes to the President. committee, and mem- bers of the Warrington Football Club: • -

Priyate M. Melia, of "D" Company, Ist Battalion, King's (Liverpool) Regiment, writing from "somewhere in France," to an old friend, Mr. M. Burke, of the Mersey Hotel, Warring- ton, .says that he is doing as well as can be expected; seeing the terrible severity of the wintry months that he and his comrades had had to fight. through. "I suppose," he adds, "that you are getting rather tired of reading about the grand charge that our boys made on March 10th. I was in it and am glad to say that I pulled through all right. I have just been reading the 'Examiner' and I notice in it two good letters from privates in the King's. One of them writes about twelve men occupy- ing a trench. Well, I happen to have been one of that twelve, and I can assure you that we were very fortunate in not being hit."

div.head: Public-house Hours In France.
div.p: Public-house Hours In France.

Incidentally the writer refers to the earlier closing of the public-houses in Warrington and mentions that the licensed premises in France Are only opened from 12 to 2, mid-day, and 6 to 8 in the evenings.

div.head: NEWS OF "TERRIERS."
div.p: NEWS OF "TERRIERS."
Gave The Germans Something To Go
On With.

Private William Smith, writing to friends at Warrington on April 2nd, says "Just a few lines to let you know that I am well, hoping this will find you the same. You must excuse, me for not writing sooner, for we only came out of the trenches last night. An- other thing, the officers are, grumbling abofit us writing too Many letters. We have had a rough time of it in the trenches. It was terribly cold -at,nights: I cannot tell you how 'long we were in them. I am sorry to say we lost more men again. Of course, that is only to be expected. When we got here last night we were dead-beat.- It is .a long time to be without proper rest, and the strain soon tells. I am anxiously waiting for your parcel, and I must thank you for sending it. Please tell Mrs. Done that Dick is all right [since wounded]. I looked for him last night, but it is hard to recognise- one another in the dark. I saw him last week.- She won't know him when he comes home. Your parcel has just come._

div.head: Thanks for Parcels.
div.p: Thanks for Parcels.

"Please thank Mrs. Done for me for the tobacco. I have had a good smoke, for we Only get .shag bacca ' here and it burns the mouth. The British Army will now dine off the parcel !" The same day came another letter: "You inquire about E. 'Seed. He is here all right. I may •tell you that the place is in an awful mess—houses and churches blown to pieces and the smell round the trenches. is horrible from the dead that are lying about everywhere. We had it pretty hot one nigh*,--the enemy found three of our chaps—so we gave them something to go on with. We have got to be careful of the people here. . . ."

div.head: OUR TERRITORIAL LOSSES.
div.p: OUR TERRITORIAL LOSSES.
A Private Says "About Fifty killed
And Wounded."

After, six . weeks' silence, Private Robert Henry Chadwick :(41), whose wife and family 'reside at 24, Brick-Street, writes to his wife 'under -date April Ist and received by her on Wednesday morning. He says : " I had written a letter 10 days before, but could not get it through, it having been very awkward. Since I last wrote I have been in the trenches several times. It is a -bit warm, I can tell you, going in and out, the bullets flying about all over the place, but when you get in it is a. lot gafer. The country round here is nothing but a mass Of ruins. It is a

shame to see how the houses and places have been knocked about with the shells. When we go into. the trenches we .are sometimes 24 hours and sometimes 48 hours before we are re- lieved, and then we are kept some length of time till the battalion has been relieved by another battalion; then we go for a few days' rest, about three or 'four miles away. No doubt you have seen or heard all about our killed and wounded. Well, I thank God, I have got through so far. Up to the time of writing we have had about 50 killed and wounded, so you see we have been having 'a warm time Of it since we have been _here.- I have seen The Warrington Examiner out here aml it had in it .something about Martin Rooney, who lived with his sister, being killed.

div.head: Danger .of Trench-Digging.
div.p: Danger .of Trench-Digging.

_ "One of the biggest reasons for our killed and wounded is when we go digging trenches. It is a lot worse than whenswe go into the trenches, as sometimes you are three or four hours ,before you have finished your work. We have lost _twice as many in this sort of work than we\ have lost in the trenches. I have received a letter from 'Billy' Stout and am very glad to know that all is well with you. Tell `BillY ' that his- brother 'Jim' is all right and in the pink of condition. It is So warm sometimes that you would think it was hell on earth! Has. Alf. -Cumming gone back yet? 'Billy' Hankey is in the trenches with us and was all right up to last night, for we were all together at fatiguing work.. Joe Per- cival is all right."

div.head: An Old Volunteer.
div.p: An Old Volunteer.

Private IL If.. Chadwick was an old Volunteer of over 15 years' service and was a sergeant. Had he remained six months longer he would have been entitled to a long service medal. lie fought through the Boer War, and his framed photograph and service credentials, along with 'a medal, hangs on the wall. He did not take kindly to the change of name to Territorials, and that was why he did 'not join until the: War broke out and .diaty impelled him to again fight for his country. He en- listed in the Territorials jn_August, and was one of the first to go to Tunbridge Wells, and then to the. firing-line.

div.head: TERRIFIED GERMANS.
div.p: TERRIFIED GERMANS.
Glad They AVere Prisoners And "Safe
At Last."

Rifleman A. Bowden, "D " Company, 2nd - Battalion the Rifle Brigade, writing to Mr. Watson, .St. Helens Cable .and Rubber Co., - March, 29th, says he' is and adds "We have been through some exciting times lately. lidu will have read about our brilliant victory •on the 10th of this month. It was about eleven .o'clock on. the 9th inst. when we set ,off on our six-mile march to be imreadiness for.'the next day:' • At 7.30- next' .-morning the Artillery began to bombard the enemy's trenches. It must have been terrible for them. It was nerve-racking for us with the shells going overhead. At 8.30 we started to advance. It would have .been fine sport, but it was terrible to see the dead- and wounded lying about, both friend and foe. At nine o'clock we started on the village; previous to which the Artillery tried to blow as. much to pieces as possible. We searched all the houses and found numerous prisoners. They all Seemed terrified to death. They were thankful to find themselves in safe .custody;- in fact, one officer was heard to say 'Thank God, I -am safe at lase. , We took. the village and entrenched ourselves: Next morning the Germans made a violent counter-attack' which was' easily re- pulsed. . . The Indian troops did excel- lent work in this great advance. The Gurkas, in fact, are • the most brilliant fighters of modern times. The Germans seem terrified of them. . . .. Hope the war is all over and I am soon back at work again: Peter McDonald wounded."

, • Rifleman Bowden lives- at home with his parents at 21, ,Heaton-street. He has two brothers in the Territorials. He Worked at- St. Helens Cable Works, in the department that makes band tyres; that is, the heavy type of tyre such as are, used on our motor 'buses.

We have already announced that Mr. Mc- Donald, Mentioned above, had been wounded. Air. Watson recently visited him at the 80l- Wigton Red Cross Hospital, and found that he had a serious wound in the thigh, which was- mend i n g.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
PLANTING AND MANURING POTATOES:

. . _ The depth and distance apart at which potatoes should be planted vary according to the soil and :the climate, but generally. speaking potatoes should be planted fairly shallow. Where the soil is light and friable they may be put in at a depth of from five to six inches, and in heavy land about four inches. Early potatoes should be planted at the shallower depth in order that they may get full benefit of the sun's warmth. The standard distance at which each early varieties should be planted from each other is 8 to 12 inches apart in the rows and from 20 to 24 inches between the rows. Mid-season and late varieties may be given 12 to 18 inched between the sets, and 24 to 30 inches between the rows.

div.head: MANURING.
div.p: MANURING.

The potato is a gross feeder, and a liberal supply of soluble plant food is necessary for the production of a large crop. When it can be obtained, perhaps the best source of such food. is farmyard manure, or, failing that,,town 'stable manure. When such is available it should be used at the rate of 15 to 20 tons per acre--sav 2 to 24cwt. per rod. (A large wheel- barrow holds about levrt.) On heavy land it may be useful to apply the dung when digging the ground in autumn or winter, but on very light soils dung, moistened if necessary, may best be applied shortly before planting the tubers.

Alternatively, liewt. of dung per rod may be applied, and at the time of planting lb. to ilb. of sulphate of ammonia, 21b. to 21b. of super- phosphate and I',lb. of sulphate of potash maN\ be added ;as the supply of the ordinary potash' manures will be very limited, ashes from wood or vegetable matter may be used instead, at the rate of 21b. per rod.

„. _„... If no dung is available good results will usually be obtained by the arpijoltion at planting time of lAlb. to 21b, of sulphate of ammonia. and 41b. of superphosphate per rod. in addition to twice the quantity of ashes already mentioned.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

.ROSES. • Prune roses of all kinds: established trees may not be nruned hard if only for garden decoration.. Late-planted trees prune to 2 or :3 eyes so as to get good rods for next season. Give established plants a ton dressing of well- decayed manure (cow or pig for preferenee)•/ and lightly dig in.., .T.4te-planted trees need none, but could have a dressing of bone-nlf, pricked in around each tree. Farmyard Manure being hard to get, a good manure t° give established trees is bone-meal two parts and sulphate of potash one part. well mixed no and evenly scattered all over the bed. Tie climbing roses up and cut all weak and OW " wood entirely out so as to get larger blooms. Use a good' sharp pruning knife so as to give a clean cut and not bruise the Wood or striP • the bark. Kee)) a sham » look-out for suckers and rose-maggots. The latter are found inside - - a leaf that is curled up. Hand-picking is the hest remedy. Suckers are shoots coming from the wild-briar, on which the rose is grafted or budded: Cut these right out with a sharp knife So as to .prevent them coming-

div.head: SEASONABLE HINTS AMONG THE
div.p: SEASONABLE HINTS AMONG THE
VEGETABLES.

Continue to sow broad beans-on rich soil in donble rows 9in. armrt and 2in. to Sin. deeP- Soil. up when 3in. high, and when the flowers .appear -pinch off the tops and Num them, 6() that the , black-fly cannot spread. Bunyard's Long Pod is the best variety to grow. -

Peas may be sown as soon as possible on good, rich soil, the wrinkled varieties being the beit for flavour and cropping. It is a mistake to scatter- the seeds •. broadcast along a drill. because the majority are crowded together too thickly. Peas should be sown 3in. apart and. three rows in a drill and about 21n. deep. Soil up when about 2in. high and insert twigs. • Cover with black cotton- when just coming through the -ground, or the_ sparrow will have - a feast. .Stick them up as soon as pogsible. Cloml varieties to grow for small gardens are Laxtonian, 11,ft.; Little Marvel, lift.; and Daisy, 2ft. For large gardens suitable sorts. - beside the above, are: Gradus, 31ft.: The Glad- stone, 4ft.; Quite Content, 6ft.: Ne Plus Ultra. 61t. Feed with weak liquid manure when the flowers start to fade. •
Sow Radish in any quantity on light, rich soil, French Breakfast, Ne Pins Ultra and Wood's Early rrame being good sorts.
Make sraall sowings of lettuce to plant out later on. •

Plant Early Cabbage out in shallow trenches to keep the wind off them till they get going, then soil up as they grow. Plant out 12in. to 15in. apart, and feed them with Nitrate of soda now and then. Good sorts to grow are: First and Best, Ellam's•Early, and Flower of Spring. • .

Sow Carrots now onwards on light, deep foil, well maniired - last season, because the roots will fork if they come in contact .with manure. Sow thinly in .shallow drills 9in, apart, cover- ing wdith. fine sifted soil. 'Thin out when third leaf 'appears to 6in apart and continually dust the -surface with soot to 'keep off the Carrot-fIY• When the carrots are as thick as your finger pull every other- one and use them for soups' and let the others grow on to maturity. Give no liquid .manure to carrots because- this will cause the.. core to grow too quickly and split the carrot up. Good varieties to grow are Early French Horn for shallow soils, and James' Intermediate and St. Valery for deep soils.

. . Get. groUnd - 'ready• to receive Early Cauli- flowers. These vegetables like good, rich soil and plenty of liquid -manure.. -Early .Snowball and :Early Dwarf Erfurt are very good varieties to grow.

div.head: WARSAW TO-DAY,
div.p: WARSAW TO-DAY,
An Englishman In Poland's War-Pressed Capital.
LESSONS IN PATRIOTISM.
BY HAROLD MAYBURY.

Mr. Harold Maybury, Lovely-lane, who has Previously enlivened the columns of "The Examiner," and other papers, inclueing some Of national repute, with sketches of life in different parts of the world affected and afflicted by the present war, bases the follow- l” article upon the experiences of an Eng- lishman in Warsaw.

Mr. Maybury has a faculty for getting authen- tic information at first hand, and turning it to the best account. Dutch Tulip Farms, A Russian's Impressions of the English, A Japanese Commander's Views on the War, and a vivid description of the Lion's fight in the North Sea, which recently appeared in " The Examiner," are among his most recent _ work.
'He has a music-hall sketch, "The Glove," on tour, and is engaged writing another one.

The house where my destination lay is a little distance from the Saski Gardens, which part of Warsaw in the spring and summer months the Poles of the upper claws make their rendez- vous. I had just passed the spot where in June of 1862 an attempt was made on the life of Count Lambert, and instead of the aristocracy now occupying the benches in this beautiful park there were to be found there for the most part a number of the working classes, namely, the shoemakers, watch-menders, and sand-workers of the Vistula, complacently munching their mid-day meal, although the day was bitterly cold. The gardens in the summer time are a de- lightful spot, but now; instead' of the trees being clothed with their foliage of verdant green, they have their mantle of gleaming snow. In the city itself business is being carried on in much the same manner as before the war began, except that, perhaps, one does not see as many " iisoujiks " with their vehicles standing at the street corners. As I passed out of the large iron gates leading into the principal thoroughfare, I came face to face with one of the leading French jockeys, who is stranded in Warsaw. After the customary salutations, I asked him what he was doing in Poland. "MY friend," said he, "it is this unfortun- ate war. I was engaged last July to ride for Count ---at the spring race meeting here in Vilarsaw, and there will be no racing. I cannot get back to my beloved Paris, and Warsaw in Winter is horrible. It is the cold I feel so much; the grey gloomy atmosphere irritates one, and the people bore me. The feminine heart dearly loves a wedding, and it is no exaggeration to say that the bigger part of a score of hundreds of women assembled in, or in the vicinity of St. Paul's Church, War- rington, on Easter Monday morning, either to catch a glimpse of, or attend, the nuptials of a bride in whom all Warrington is interested, from the fact that she is none other than the niece and an adopted daughter of the popular civic head of the borough, the Mayor (Alder- man Peter Peacock). The bride was Miss Elsie Maud Wilkinson, the second daughter of the late Mr. and Mrs. Peter Wilkinson, of Warrington, and the bride- groom was Mr. Edward Jackson Mee, the youngest son of Mr. and Mrs. Jno. Mee, of 11, Enville-street, Latchford. The bride is a, well- known member of the local Musical Society, and is also an accomplished amateur actress, and, as such, played a leading singing-part in ,ne Operatic Society's uot very distant pr .dic- tion of "Miss Hook of Holland," both her singing and her exposition of the histrionic art winning golden opinions on the occasion of those well-remembered performance. The bride- groom is an assistant master at the St. James' Day School, and is very popular among a wide

THE CEREMONY.

The marriage service, which opened with the singing of the hymn "The voice that breathed o'er Eden," was conducted by the Rev. E. Down- ham, the curate-in-charge of the church, the hymn "0, perfect love" being sung later. Before and after the ceremony the organist (Mr. Ernest Wilkes) played suitable music, which included Mendelssohn's immortal "Wed- ding March." As the wedding party stood at the altar rails after the giving of the sym- bolical ring, the officiating minister delivered a brief exhortation to the newly-married pair, in which he enjoined them never to forget that as Christ had been the great guest at the most important epoch in their careers, so they should see that H were made a holy and ever-welcome guest at all the turning points in their lives, until they at last should come to the great eternal wedding feast when they, and all who had trodden the path of Godliness and upright- ness, should know the real meaning of the saying that blessed were they who loved the Lord

II AIMING-WALSH.

On Tuesday' morning a marriage took place quietly, at St. Paul's Church, between Mr. Win, Chorley Harding, •of ~Buttermarket-street, and Miss Alys Mary Walsh, of Folly-lane. The bride was given away by her father; Mr. Gil, heft Harding (brother of • the bridegroom), acted as best man,, and Miss Harding (sister of the bridegroom) was bridesmaid: Numerous handsome ,presents have been. received. Later the 'happy couple proceeded" to• Grange-over-, Sands for the honeymoon. FAULKS—MANER.

An interesting wedding took place on Satur- day afternoon at Christ Church, Padgate, the contracting parties being Miss Catherine W. Faulks, second daughter of ex-Quartermaster- Sergeant and Mrs. Faulks, of Padgate-lane, and Mr. J. A. Mayer, of Warrington.. The Rev. E. E. Chamberlain officiated; The bride wore a Prussian blue dress, trimmed with Paisley silk and cream silk net, her hat .being Of white silk with blue silk ruche and orange blossom. She carried a bouquet of white uancies, tulips and smilax. The bridesmaids'were Miss Mabel Faulks and Miss Fanny Mayer. They wore dresses of white embroidered voile, with blue silk sashes and blue silk hats, trimmed with pale pink roses, and carried bouquets of white tulips and pink carnations, the gifts of the bridegroom. Mr,. Albert Mayer acted as best man and Mr. Geoffrey Faulks as grobinsman. The bride was given away by her father. The wedding .breakfast was afterwards served in the Church House, when the Rev. E. E. Chamberlain proP9sed the. health- of the bride and bridegroom. Many handsome presents were received.

div.head: DRESSES.
div.p: THE DRESSES.

The bride, who was given away by her uncle, wore a lovely gown of charmeuse satin, the princess overdress being handsomely embroid- ered in pearls and edged with dainty rosebuds, whilst the sleeves,, vest and underdress were of the filmiest 'chiffon, edged with seed pearls. A silVer-tissue sash was looped over the skirt knee- deep in front. The Court train was of ivory- brocaded satin, lined with ruchings of shell pink chiffon and hung from the shoulders by ropes of pearls, and was finished by a bow of silver-tissue and orange-blossom. Her beautiful veil of Brussels lace was arranged to form a cap, being held in place by a wreath of orange blossom, heather and myrtle, whilst she carried a sheaf of Madonna lilies. She was accom- panied by two small train-bearers, Master Jack Langley and Miss Dora Peacock • (her cousins). Little Miss Peacock looked very pretty in a dainty frock of Irish lace and a pretty French cap to match. The quartet of s bridesmaids —Miss Inez Wilkinson (sister .of the bride), and the Misses Annie, Ada and Gladys Peacock (cousins of the bride)—wore white chiffon- taffeta frocks with tunic and sleeves of pink chiffon, an effective contrast to their dresses being.a chieved by the hats with underbrims of black crinoline straw and streamers of black velvet. They carried bouquets of pink car- nations and wore single-pearl gold bar-brooches, the gifts of the bridegroom. The best man was Mr. W. H. Minards, and the groomsmen were Messrs. Sim Bailey and George Bebbington. • The Mayoress was charmingly. attired in a smart costume of petunia trimmed with navy- taffeta and wore a hat of navy-taffeta and ospreys to harmonise. She carried a bouquet of pale pink carnations. Mrs. Mee, the mother of the bridegroom, wore a charming gown of mole charmeuse and a mole hat with plumes to match. • She also carried a bouquet of pinl;•. carnations.

div.head: BEAUTIFUL BRIDE.
div.p: A BEAUTIFUL BRIDE.
At the reception Councillor Osborne had the privilege of proposing the toast of the Bride and Bridegroom. He refgrred to the bride us "like unto a picture of gold set in a silver frame."

After the reception, which waS held at Atkin- son's Cafe, the bride and bridegroom left for London and the South, the newly-made Mrs. Edward Jackson Mee travelling in a lime-green garbadine costume with ninon blouse to match and a close fitting hat of white taffetas with tete de negre mounts.

div.head: SHE iItER-MAY.
div.p: SHE iItER-MAY.

The Rev. E. Downham officiated at a quiet, but pretty weddinc, at St. Paul's Church, War- rington, on Saturday morning, when Miss Alice Isabel , Shearer, third daughter of Mr. Basil Shearer, 26, Crosfield-street, Warrington, be- came the wife of Mr. Albert Carveth May, eldest son of Captain and Mrs. May, of Port Isaac, Cornwall. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a cream-faced cloth costume and shell-piiik picture hat. '• She -carried a shear- of arum lilies, and lilies of the valley. The. briggroom's,,present to the bride was a handsome set of furs. The bridesmaid, Miss Dorothy Shearer (sister o(the bride); looked charming in a vieux rose- faced -cloth- -costume and tete-de-negre hat, and carried a shower bouquet of pink carnations. She also wore a gold curb bracelet, the gift of the bridegroom. Mr. George Newburn was the best man.

The reception waS held at the bride's parents' residence. The honeymoon is being spent on the South Coat. The bride's travelling dress was a tailor-made costume of fawn covert-coating, and she wore a heliotrope Condor hat. Numerous presents were received.

div.head: PERMANENT PEACE PROBLEMS.
div.p: PERMANENT PEACE PROBLEMS.
Mr. A. H. Crosfield and the Basis (;f Nationality.

div.head: MR. W. PETER RYLANDS'S CRITICISMS.
div.p: MR. W. PETER RYLANDS'S CRITICISMS.
Baseless Remarks That Astonished Mr. Crosfield.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield, in the course of the long and able reply which he delivered to the vote of thanks accorded him for his fine discourse upon War Topics at.. the Junior Liberal Club recently, said that In listening to the various speeches of the evening, he must say the first thing that had impressed him was the fact that they had such ability in their midst. (Hear, hear.) He knew very well it was often said of some clubs that they, were given up too much to the merely, recreative side—for instance, clubs which were also intended to have political significance— and he had heard one or two people in War- rington say they feared a Junior Liberal Club might fail in that respect. He told them candidly that he never believed it for a moment. Their Junior Liberal Club would 'LK recruited from the middle-class of W arrington—men who thought and read and utudied for themselves; and he must say that wh at they had listened to that night was as go( d an example of the political talent a club of that kind would bring to the front in the future as they could possibly desire. (Cheers.)

Greece: As a matter of fact it was also re- marked that instead of England taking Smyrna she might, if Russia occupied Constantinople, take Gallipoli." The Tzar of Russia's promise of autonomy for Poland was a hopeful indication, and although in the matter of self-government Russia was considerably less advanced than some of the Western nations, still it might be hoped ,that she would be influenced by her alliance with France and Britain, and struck by the truly remarkable manifestation of 'power which had been witnessed kom end to end of the British Empire, thanks' to the principle of self-govern- ment we had so widely adopted. (Cheers.)

div.head: SITTING ON THE FENCE.
div.p: SITTING ON THE FENCE.

The Chairman (Mr. Toulmin) had spoken of the evil effects of autocratic power, and of the danger to Europe. where one individual had such enormous unchecked authority as that possessed by the Kaiser of Germany or the Tzar of Russia—whose ipse dixit alone was sufficient to decide the issues for peace and war. So he (the speaker) would just throw in one word about a queen for a change. (Laugh- ter.) They, were all,aware at the present time there was a good deal of natural hesitation—or what, cynically-minded observers 'were accus- tomed to describe as the," policy of the jumping cat "—(laughter)—Shown by some of the smaller nationalities a Europe—and by another nation which was by no means a small one. Well now, Greece happened to possess one of the most gifted statesmen who had ever lived in Europe: . Monsieur Venizelos was a man of extraordinary talent and genius, and one of the most remarkably many-sided, tactful, gifted and courageous men who had ever played a part in European politics. Greece had indeed been most fortunate, in having such a statesman, who had, of 'recent years led her to such a position as she had not occupied since the times of the Byzantine Empire.

GREEK QUEEN'S SINISTER INFLUENCE. For some time past Venizelos had urged that Greece should take a decisive step in support of the Allies, and he had brought to bear all his persuasive power, and his energy to carry his point, knowing full well that the people of Greece were just as anxious to follow his lead as he was to lead them. So far unfortunately, owing to the opposition of the Court, all his efforts had been unavailing, and only the pre- vious week the King of Greece finally put his foot down and Said " No, it is not time." there they had an important example of the danger of 'autocratic power and the mis- chief for which it was often responsible. The iKing's.. deeision . was wrong: from. the. Point of view - of Greece; unfortunate ,for the Allies; .deplorable + inasmuch .as •it was. inevitably calculated to prolong the war. . That decision had an immensely important bearing- on the whole situatioa to-day, because if Greece came in, Roumania would come in, and there was a strong possibility that sooner or later Italy would conie in as well. (Hear, hear.) Then why had not Greece seized her opportunity, backing up: France and Britain with her: troops In the :Dartkinelles, and so helping to complete the final overthrow of her old historic enemy, the Turk, at whose hands the sufferings of Greece had been unspeakable? We could understand how keen the men of Greece had been to take up arms, and could understand what it would have meant to the Allies in shortening the duration of the war. Why had nothing been done? Because of the King of Greece? Certainly his was the chief .responsibility, but still—well—there were times when husbands had been known to play second fiddle—(laughter)—and the present attitude of Greece was largely due to the influence of the Queen of. Greece. Her Majesty was a sister of the Kaiser. The Emperor William had brought his influence to bear and the Queen of Greece had , made it clear that if the Central Powers were attacked she would shake the historic dust of ' Greece off her feet. Well, there might be some people who devoutly wished she would do it and take herself .off to Germany for a time. (Hear, hear.) The other day he chanced to be discuss- ing the influence of the Queen of Greece and her threat in the presence of one of the authori- ties at the Admiralty, who at once intervened and said, "Oh, do let us place a Cruiser at her Majesty's disposal, and if the German sub- marines will only keep clear of it we wills guarantee her a safe conduct back to her own country." (Laughter, and applause.)

div.head: BASIS OF SETTLEMENT.
div.p: BASIS OF SETTLEMENT.

A striking part of Mr. Toulmin's speech was his reference to the partition of Poland, and he was quite sure that nationality would in the main, and to a very great extent form the basis of .the settlement they all looked forward to—for the very good reason that after what Europe was passing -through there would be a great effort made to effect a permanent settle- ment. In the course of his. address he had touched , Upon tbat; and beyond question -a powerful ooncert of Europe was wanted to guarantee the permanence of the settlement by making. it far too .dtCngerous.'for any power• in the future to attempt to upset it. (Hear, hear.) It could not be very long now before the whole question of the terms of settlement was upon them. Indeed some of the greatest factors in the case were already in the public eye. He would only refer to one that evening. They knew how the question of Constantinople was being anxiously considered. If Venizelos, and the then Premier of Bulgaria had had their way at the conclusion of the Arst Balkan War he did not believe there would have been a second war. In all .probability a confederation of the Balkan States would have been brought about, and then there would have been no ques- tion of Constantinople arising to-day, and very possibly no European War either. wing Ferdinand of Bulgaria was the man who destroyed the fair proinise of a 'peaceful settle.

div.head: RUSSIA'S STUPENDOUS SACRIFICES.
div.p: RUSSIA'S STUPENDOUS SACRIFICES.

But that was in the past. They had to deal with many formidable problems that would soon. be confronting them. Now Britain and Prance had already made enormous sacrifices in this war; and further sacrifices would yet be demanded from them before victory was theirs. (Hear, hear.) But while their efforts and sacri- fices in the West were so great he thought as rule we rather, failed to realise the stupendous scale of the awful slaughter in the East. Only in some of the wars of the Dark Ages that followed the fall of the Roman Empire would they find a parallel to this terrible bloodshed. They could not be surprised that Russia was asking for concessions at the conclusion of such a war. Mr. Griffiths, in the course of his very interesting speech had, like the Chairman, referred to the claims of nationality as a basis for any settlement. Well, he feared that here and there there would be an exception, though he trusted only as an exception to the general rule. Constantinople might be such an ex- ception. Certainly On the ba4s of nationality Russia had not the slightest claim to it because, besides the large Turkish population there was an enormous Greek population and but a mere handful of Slays.

Again, if it turned out that Constantinople was conceded to Russia it was quite possible that by way of maintaining a balance of power in that quarter of the world, Smyrna might be ceded to England. Well that would be another exception because, so far 'as the people of' that great seaport were concerned, unquestionably it ought to go th Greece, and if we took it he (Mr. Crosfield) thought it would be a fair thing if, while taking, Smyrna we ceded Cyprus to

div.head: WHAT IS WRONG WITH DIPLOMACY?
div.p: WHAT IS WRONG WITH DIPLOMACY?

Passing on to Mr. H. Sherburn's criticism of the whole system of foreign, policy, Mr. Cros- field went on to say that if we are going to have an all round settlement in Europe, with a definite demarcation of boundaries within which each nation should work out its own salvation, striving for supremacy rather in good .government, the welfare, education, enlighten- ment and distinction of its people, than in any attempt to eXtend boundaries at the expense of neighbours—if that was the prospect before them he saw no reason why there should not be something approaching a revolution in diplo- matic custom. Under those changed conditions there would immediately be an overwhelming case for conducting all foreign business to a far greater extent than hitherto with the 'cards on the table." (Hear, •hear, and cheers.) It was well to ponder these things even now when the whole energy, driving power and fight- ing capacity of the nation was splendidly con- centrated on the one great purpose of achieving victory in Europe for the cause of justice, honour,'mercy and progress over the powers of darkness and cruelty. (APplause.) Let us, continued Mr. Crosfield, bear well in mind the magnificent services the Territorials were rendering in helping to accomplish our mighty undertaking. Mr.. Sanders referred to the value of the great services rendered to the nation and the Empire by Lord Haldane-- (cheers)—when he inaugurated our Territorial Forces. Well, during the time when he had the honour to represent the Borough in Parlia- ment he had, not once, but many times, discus- sions with Lord Haldane about the Territorials, urging that in no single respect should they be handicapped, but on the contrary that all pos- sible encouragement should be given them with assistance in the matter of clothing, equipment and so forth, and assuredly as far as the money would go Lord Haldane did all that mortal man could do, and full well did he (Mr. Cros- field) know. how earnestly and whole-heartedly, and with what indefatigable industry the pres- ent Lord Chancellor then worked at his great task. (Cheers.) How any sane man could join in the absolutely idiotic attacks that had been made recently upon Lord Haldane he could not imagine.

div.head: POLITICAL MUD THROWERS.
div.p: POLITICAL MUD THROWERS.

There were, of course, some people always on the look out for an opportunity to throw mud at a. political opponent, and. if there was no reason for doing so -they generally managed . to' invent one. (Laughter.) There was no better British Imperialist than Lord Haldane to be found from John o' Groats to Land's End,, and the attacks upon him .were absolutely preposterous. He noticed ' that his old friend, Mr. Willie Peter Itylands, had been criticising Sir John Brunner, Sir Alfred Mond and himself. So far as he (Mr. Crosfield) was concerned, he hoped Mr. Rylands would not mind,being told that, his criticism was just so much. water on a duck's back because he (Mr. Crosfield) was perfectly content to leave his own record of speeches on the platform in Warrington and votes in the House of Commons to answer and refute Mr. Rylands. It so happened that only a few days previously he had been discussing with Mr. McKenna the memorable events that cul- minated in the debate and vote in the House of Commons on March 16th, 1909. He spoke from memory, but thought that was the correct date. A week or so before that historic occasion he privately saw Mr. McKenna, who was then First Lord of the Admiralty, and in the course of conversation he told Mr. McKenna that while satisfied there was no earthly grounds, neces- sity or justification for a continuance of ani- mosity and antipathy between Britons and Ger- mans, still he was satisfied that Germany had been trying to steal a March upon us in the matter of naval construction, and therefore while he had heard privately that the First Lord had some staggering estimates in store for the House, he intended to vote for every six- pence of them. In face therefore of his record in the Parliaments of 1906 and 1910, and thg policy he had advocated in Warrington, he con- fessed he had read with astonishment Mr. Rylands' criticism. It was really as wide of the mark as his criticism of Sir Alfred Mond or the attacks that had been made upon Lord Haldane, both of them as • good Liberal Imperialists as were to be found in the country. (Hear, hear.)

Mr. Crosfield concluded by assuring the junior Liberals that he looked forward with high hope and entire confidence to the valuable influence on Warrington politics in the future which would be exercised by their club and associa. lion. (Applause.) CORDIAL THANKS.

Fre moved a very hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman for his kindness in presiding, as well as for many other services. This having been carried with acclamation, a return vote of thanks was unanimously accorded to Mr. Crosfield, amidst prolonged applause.

div.head: JUST ESCAPED GERMAN PIRATES.
div.p: JUST ESCAPED GERMAN PIRATES.
Illness That Stopped Musician Sailing On Torpedoed Ship.

Another local musician who should have sailed aboard the ill-fated s.s. Falaba—which was sunk by a German submarine when she was nearing Milford .Haven, over 100 lives being lost—as a member of the ship's orchestra, is Mr. H. Clare, whose home is at Morris Brook Farm, Grawenhall, and who is well-known in Warrington and district, as an artiste of con- siderable ability. Mr. Clare, who was formerly employed at the " Examiner " Office, sailed with the boat on her last .successful trip, and played a no mean part in the programme which was given at the last concert held aboard her on that voyage. That was on February 16th. He was re-engaged as a solo-violinist for the fateful trip, the letter requisitioning his services informing him that the boat would be " pretty well full" and that he should "(10 well." At the last moment, however, illness .prevented Mr. Clare fulfilling the 'engagement, much as he desired to do so, and he was forced to send_a letter "crying off," a doctor's certificate accompanying the missive. The musician who took Mr. Clare!s place in the orchestra at short notice, a Mr. Crane, was among those saved when the vessel was so foully torpedoed by the Hunnish pirates.

div.head: MR. CLARE'S MUSICAL CARER.
div.p: MR. CLARE'S MUSICAL CARER.

_ Mr. Clare commenced his musical career in the -orchestra at the Royal Court, when he was only 16 years of age, leaving the " Examiner " office •in order to devote himself to work that was more congenial to his artistic temperament. Seeking fresh fields and - pastures new he sub- sequently took professional engagements at Morecambe, Blackpool, Stockport, Wigan and Leigh, ultimately coming back to Warrington as leading violinist in the Hippodrome orchestra, in which capacity he did much good work. . Finding himself growing tired of the orchestral work in theatres and music halls—he had had some ten Years of the work—he thought he would like to see something of the world outside the compass of ".the tinsel show dramatic. art can boast," and so he joined the orchestra of the ill-fated liner, which now rests at the bottom of the sea.

div.p: CHESHIRE'S LOSS, LANCA- SHInE'S GAIN. 1

Concerning A Projected Alteration Of Boundary. --- A draft Order issued by the Local Government Board withe reference to a projected alteration of the line of demarcation between the counties 1 of Lancashire and Cheshire, came before the Warrington Board of Guardians and the War- rington Rural District ~Council at their meet- ings on Wednesday. The Local Government Board invited the remarks of the authorities concerned on the matter, and the Guardians decided to refer it for consideration by their Finance Committee before giving an opinion. In reply to the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, the Guardian!s .Clerk . (Mr. A. Bottonaley), told the members of his Board that `the proposed 'alteri- tion of the County boundary, would mean -A slight gain to the-area of. the-Union, the "Size of . Rixton-with:Glazebrool; district being increased. Th Rev. A.• M.. Mitchell : How will it work out financially?. - The Clerk: The other side will have to be compensated. •
The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: And will the com- pensation be more than we are going to gain? The Clerk: I can't tell you that. HOW WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT

COUNCIL IS AFFECTEIi--- --- - The matter was discussed at some length by the Rural District Council, to whom their Sur- veyor (Mr Newcombe) reported that after perusing the proposed Order—it having only been just received—he noted that, so far as the rural district was concerned, the projected transference only applied to the Glazebrook township. In the inquiry at Manchester, which preceded the issue of the Order, it was arranged with Mr. Harcourt Clare (the clerk to the Lancashire County Council) that Glazebrook should be withdrawn from the scope of the application, so that the Rural District Coun- cil's deputation were deprived of representing the ease for their Council to the inspector con- ducting the inquiry, although they were quite prepared to do so. The ,consequence was that the Rural Council had not been heard in the matter and the Order would be made without their view being considered at all unless they put it forward at this stage. The case for the Rural District Council was closely related to that of the Warrington Guardians, though not exactly similar, and he suggested that the Coun- cil should arrange a conference with the Poor Law Authority or their officials. Mr. Mather: Does the Order mean that the Ship Canal is going to be the boundary, from Warrington Bridge to Irlam? ' "GOING TO TAKE THE PLUM FROM OUR

DISTRICT." The Surveyor: It 'means that they are going to take the plum from our district. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: What are we to receive by way of compensation?. The Surveyor replied that that- would be assessed on the basis of a ncw Act of which no authority, ai yet, had had actual experience. The District Council got no land in exchange: Lancashire got a great benefit, but the Councir got: none.

7 Eventually it- was decided to ask the Chair- men, Mr. Mather and the Surveyor to go into the details of the. Order and to report to the Finance Committee the precise -effects the projected alteration of boundary will have upon the Council.

div.head: AMONG THE _SAVED.
div.p: AMONG THE _SAVED.
Glad News Of Two Local Sailors Whose Boats 'Went Down.

It appears that when H.M.S. Ocean was sunk in the Dardanelles, along with H.M.S. Irresistible, that there were two Warrington men on the former boat. The men, who are both naval reservists, are Gunlayer Jonathan Hatton, whose home is at 31, Wakefield-street, and Seaman-Gunner Arthur Jones, who resided at 43, Aitken-street. From au official notice,. to hand this week, it appears that both hav4 been saved, and transferred to. other boats. • -,

Hatton is a Married man, and was formerly employed in the Corporation Sanitary Depart. ment, while- Jones was employed .by Messrs. Bylands Brothers, Ltd. It is interesting to note that two friends of the Men named—Seamen-Gunners Orlando Jones, of 55, Aitken-street, and William Jones, of Wakefield-street—served on the Ocean until November last, when they were transferred to other ships.
