All money spent and received in " bets" is economically unprofitable, but there, is a fur- ther and serious loss of national energy caused by horse racing, which at the present time is of greet importance. What about the thousands of Men who deliberately absent themselves from work on race days? On Wednesday afternoon last 'week, about three o'clock, an early edition of one of the even- ing papers was being eagerly bought in Bridge-street. In walking down from 'Market Gate to the New Bridge one could see at least half a dozen groups of men—mostly young and decently dressed—who eagerly snatched ;the papers' from the 'bOys who sold them. What was the Cause of. this intense desire to buy the paper? War news? Cer- tainly not!, :NO! these Englishmen (?), these noble-minded :patriots, safe and snug in The protection afforded by the British Fleet, not only refrain from offering theniSelv-es for duty in the Army, but are tgiglazy even to do their share of work at home, and prefer, so far as they are concerned, that the Army shall go short of the munition's of war, that more and more of. the very best of England's brave lads shall give their blood. and lives, that the War shall-be unduly and unnecessarily prolonged, in order that they may win or lose a " bit " on a horse. This is sport—save the mark and for this contemptible and degraded minority the vast majority of our country- men mtp-A 'suffer.

The "Chester Chronicle" of last Satur- day says that from two entirely different sources a request had come for the publica- tion of the following letter addressed to the "Morning Post" from "An Operating Sur- geon" in France, apropos of racing and foot- ball, which still go gaily on

Can you not by now imagine our feelings and disgust at still having to explain repeatedly to , our French wounded and friends that England really means to fight, and not only occupies her- self with racing and football? We have to try and explain (word of damnable hypocrisy) that a few " bookies " and jockeys, &c., might sufier a little, a few fine animals (such a " cert," you know) might get fat. So racing must go on. . . . And to explain this to dear old mother, who gently drying a mother's heart-broken tears, brings her one remaining lad crippled for life to me, and I have to. comfort her, telling her to be thankful that she possesses still a living wreck. But racing must go on.

It fills one with grief and indignation, says our Chester contemporary, that after eight months of living agony a section of our People should • still fail utterly to understand the peril in which we stand. Nero fiddling while Rome was burning was not a whit more in- congruous' than racing while the nation is in deadly grips with its terrible foe. Think of it! Ten thousand British casualties in three days at Neuve Chapelle. The Chester Cup may be run amid an even worse holocaust. "But racing as usual" is the decision of the Jockey Club and the Chester Town Council.

Dates of Survoys and Subsequent Changes. The inveAigations were carried out at Reading (in the autumn. of 1912), at North- ampton and .Stanley, a.. mining centre, eight miles from Durham (in July, 1913), and at Warrington (in September, 1913). , It will be seen at onc.e that valuable. as the book will be, it will loSe some of its influence -owing to the fact that great economic changes have already taken place since the figures were obtained. Rents and the cost of living .have advanced and the rates of wages have risen alv,. but the strong probability is that the , main conclusions still remain substan- tially correct.• Practically all pre-war economic conditions have changed, but that -does not lessen the responsibility for facing the. -facts. 'either locally or • nationally. It must be confessed that C. Livelihood- and - .Poverty-" .is not lively or easy reading. It contains more figures than the average, man can masticate. It is, however, of profound '•interest to the student of Aocial welfare,- and .well repays-thoughtful study. • Perhaps the best thing that can he donE is to set forth Some of its conclusions as plainly as possible, for free discussion' in various circles. Chambers of Commerce, Employers' Federations, Trade Unions,, and Study Circles in Churches and Adult Schools should make it their business to get a grip of the economic situation, not merely in the towns specially concerned, but all over the country. For it is clear that one .day when the war cloud has passed, away, one of the most urgent problems to be faced will be that of the living wage. Army allowances are going to Play havoc with the wage system as it existed before the war. In this short review many questions must be passed over which are dealt with incident- ally in the book. Housing. Sanitation, mor- tality, overcrowding, money-lending, and smoke abatement all come in for notice in this volume. , Doubtless -a few of the facts, more strictly about the economic • situation- will interes, Warringtbnians Most. ,
The Condition of the Children. Here is an eKtract about the children :-

Probably one of the most interesting features of Table 11. ig the number of children under 14 who are at work (17 in- stances, out of which 5 are girls). These 17 childrOn in our sample [i.e.. about 1 in 20:1 would probably represent 300 to 400 in the whole town. The regulation of the employ- ment of young children is in The hands of

27 per cent. earn between 30s. and 40s per week. • 11 per cent. earn 408. or more per week. At that time .20s. was about the sfandard rate of wages for general labourers. But after the inquiry took place and well before the outbreak of war the minimum rate among labourers in the ironworks was. raised to 225. Id. This advance is duly noted in the book, but the change does not appreciably alter the classification; . On the other hand, the numerous war bonuses given while the book was in the press to meet the abnormal cost of living would probably lift a, consider- able number above the 255. level.' Still, the two outstanding feattwes of Warrington wages -remain, viz.., that a considerable pro- portion ef men is highly paid, while a larger proportion of unskilled men cannot make both ends meet. • The reader will not require us to empha- sise the enormous part played by low' wages in causing primary poverty. Actually one- half of the households below the poverty line at Warrington and Reading, nearly one- half at York, and one-third in Northampton, were Using in poverty because the wages Of ..the head ,of the household were so low that he could not support a familS, Of three , children or ,less. [This is the statistician's farailY, censisting of man, wife and three ' dependent. children, often spoken of as the average family, for whom an adult wage- earner ought to be able to provide.] It is thus proved that a great part of the poverty revealed by our inquiries is not intermit- tent, but permanent, not accidental or due to exceptional misfortune, but a regular feature of the industries of the towns con- cerned. No doubt it will be asked how far the .con- elusions of 'the statistician may be regarded as accurate. Professor Bowley devotes .a whole chapter to this point, and shows what great pains have been taken to check state- ments in a variety of ways. , Information was first of all obtained from 1 in 20 of the houses in the town taken alpha- betically'. Eight hundred and twenty-six houses were thus markgil off, and then all shops or houses of principal residents were ex- cluded. Finally 640 households of the wage- earning classes were personally visited ,by in- vestigators and statements were recorded on an ,official card. 'Official publications were used to check the accuracy of some state- ments, while employers, assisted by supplying rates of wages, .&c. Now that results are tabulated they are open for criticism on the part of those who have facts in their posses- sion. None of the towns was picked because it was likely to be exceptional. When all the figures are grouped together as if they represented one great town; it is probable that the result is a fair index of economic conditions in urban England, apart from ,the great cities. We shall return to the subject again. Meantime it is a great satisfaction to . have a picture presented that must be so near . the actual truth that it is sufficient for all practical purposes.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
TURDAY, APRIL 10, 191.5

RAGING AND GAMBLING—AS USUAL We are told that "in the interests of sport horse racing is to be carried on "as usual." Even the Cathedial City. of Chester_ has declined to listen to a request not to abandon its races, but to limit them- during this sad and needy year to one day instead .of three. The circumstances are such as forcibly to remind us of -,Esop's Fable of the Frogs., who, being stoned for fun, protested that " what is sport for you is death to us." We wonder if it has ever occurred to English sportsmen to note the close parallel between this fable and their present attitude—to the sportsmen, that is, who stand outside that band of true noblemen, who, in spite of their intense love of horse racing and their heavy expenditure in the upkeep of their racing stables, have protested that this is not the time when-men's minds and efforts should be diverted from one great end.

We have, however, no language isufficiently to coc,demn those " sportsmen," who, in this titne .of their country's travail, when thousands of 'hearts are suffering the agony of 14-•reavement and hundreds of thousands are enduring hourly suspense caused by. the absence of loved ones at the Front; have the shameless audacity to flaunt their indifference and apathy not only before the faces of their own countrymen, but before the eyes of the whole world.

Who is going to benefit by this decision? It is true that there are a certain number of men in bona-fide employment in connection with the breeding, training and running of racehorses, who might, to some extent, suffer if racing was discontinued for this year, but the aggregate number is by no means large. On the other hand there is a perfect "horde" of bookmakers and their satellites who are /4cither more nor less than " parasites," and irho livo and make money out of the ignor- ance and weaknesses of their fellow men. It is for these men in the main, and so that, they' may continue to prey upon the workers Of yinglatd, that racing is to ,be continued.

The Palatial block which the Warrington Guardians have erected at a cost *Df over £13,000 for the purpose of dealing with epileptic and other similar cases, has been offered to and accepted by the War Office as a military hospital, and, will be opened as such on Monday next.,

, The cost of the building including the fur- nishing, is upwards of £15;000, and will com- fortably accommodate from 160 to 200 wounded men. Bathrooms, lavatories, dressing, surgical and operating rooms are provided, as well as other facilities required in an up-to'-date estab- lishment designed to deal with the class of patient for which it. was primarily intended.

div.head: R. W.
div.p: R. W.
MILITARY .HOSPITAL FOR
WARR I NGTON.
RED CaOSS NURSES WANTED.

. What is mot required, in order.to adopt the building to the purposes of a Red. Cross Hospital, is a voluntary staff of Red Cross nurses. The following have already ,offered their services: The Misses Dodds, Murray and Parker, of Penketh; the Misses Hepherd, Tunstall ' and Forshaw, oi Latchford; Miss Nicholson and Miss Groves, of Lymm; the Misses Bainbridge and Colwell, of Lower Walton, and Miss Sloan, of Moore. In addition ten trained nurses have, been already engaged, and are expected to commence their duties on Monday.
• The superintendent nurse will be Miss Emerton

Any ladies possessing lied Cross certificates and willing to offer their services, are invited to comMunicate with Mr. Bottomley. the clerk to the Warrington Vnion, whose offi(..-- are. in Bew,y-street.

div.head: CLARA BUTT COMING.
div.p: CLARA BUTT COMING.
Great Treat For Local Music-Lovers

Madame Clara Butt, the world-famous con- tralto, is engaged on a world-tour„ which in- cludes a visit to the Parr Hall, Warrington, on Monday. evening, April 26th.- when she, will have the 'assistance at Mr. Walter Hyde, the operatic tenor; the -Misses Millie X3lower, and - Essie Faulkner, violin duettists; Mr; W. H. Squire, solo 'cellist; Mr. Harold Craxton," pianist, and Mr. Arthur E. Godfrey, organist. The members of the Warrington Musical Society have generously consented, tO-asSist the distinguished diva of song, by singing the chorus parts in "Land of Hope and Glory" and " The Home Flag," under the conductorship of Mr.. Frank H. Crossley. ; Madame Clara • Butt has been busily engaged in singing for, and in arranging concerts on behalf of, various funds in connec- tion with the war, and through her agency thousands of pounds have been donated to various deserving causes, and she is still con- tinuing her good work and her admirers in War- rington Willbeaskedto help to swell the funds f.sir providing work for artistes out of engagement through the war by buying a small Union Jack and her autographs, which will be offered for sale by lady members of the local Musical Society. Mr. Kennerley Rumford, Madame Butt's singer-husband. it should be added, has- been actively engaged in Red Cross work at the Front since November last. Mr. R. H. Pearson, 75; Bridge-street, Warring- ton, has charge of the plan and ticket arrange- ments.

div.head: "A LIFE OF BEER AND DEGRADA
div.p: "A LIFE OF BEER AND DEGRADA
TION."

At the Borotigh Police Court on Thursday, before Mr. J. Rymer Young and other magis- trates, Annie Mather, . a married woman, of 64, Tanner-street, was summoned for sending her thirteen-year-old son i to the Wheat Sheaf Ina, Orford-lane, for beer, other than in a sealed' vessel.--,-She admitted the offence • The Chief Constable said that at 12.30 p.m. on April Ist a policeman on duty in Orford- lane noticed the boy with a bottle of beer, which had no cork in it. Ile questioned him about it and the boy said that his mother had sent him to the Wheat Sheaf for a javt, tell- ing him to remain outside until somedEe came along,- when be was to ask that person, who- ever it might be, to go in and fetch the beer for him. As it happened' the boy's aunt was passing just about this time and he asked her to go in for the beer, and she did so, handing it over to the boy. , The mother's excusp was that she was "a bit busy getting dinner ready," and wanted her dinner-beer.

The Chief Constable said the woman had been, six times before the Court, the last time being in 1913. She had- been imprisoned for theft. and for neglecting her children. - The Chairman, in imposing a fine of 10s., said that the woman seemed to be living a life of beer and degradation and did not seem to know what decency was.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 10, 1915.

div.head: LIVELIHOOD AND POVERTY
div.p: LIVELIHOOD AND POVERTY
Scientific invesligation of the Economic Conditions
of Warrington.

div.head: FACTS TO STUDY.
div.p: FACTS TO STUDY.

Livelihood and Poverty. Perhaps the two statements above are the most striking conclusions emerging from. !a statistical inquiry held ih.Warrington in 'Sep- tember, 1913. Of course, they need amplifiCa- ! tion. The former -statement, may be more. precisely expressed thus: 111 to 131 per cent. of the working class families in Warrington (in so far s they are dependent on earnings, pensions, &v.), are below the level necessary to keep them in physical health, excepat at the sacrifice of clothing and other necessary intermittent expenditure. This sentence is culled from a book en- titled " Livelihood and Poverty," just pub- lished by Messrs. Bell and Sons at 3s. 6d. net. It is a book which ought' to be inwardly digested by every employer, trade union leader, social student and public man in the town. Undoubtedly it will be widely read. for the investigations concern four towns which may be regarded as fair samples of what is to be found up and down the

country. The volume will take its place on the book- shelves of social reformers, • side by side with the surveys of Rowntree in York, and Booth in London. It has been issued under the auspices Of the Ratan Tata Foundation, which was instituted in order to study conditions of poverty. The inquiry was conducted by Mr. Bnrnett-Hurst (now Professor of Economics at Allahabad), assisted by a number of inves- tigators. Of course; such a survey could not have succeeded without the willing co-opera- tion. of many employers, officials and trade union leaders. In the introduction special' thanks are given to Mr. A. W. Perris and Mr. W. J. Rowland for their assistance. No local people are responsible for any of the conclu- sions, which are based entirely upon the sta- tistical tables worked up at the London School of Economies. The whole work was under the general direction of Prof. Rowley, of London University, the well-known statistician, and was his special method of taking one sample in every 20 working class households, which was adopted in all four towns.
12 per cent. of the Working Class Families below the Poverty Line. 25 per cent. of the Working Class School Children in Poverty. •

the Local Education Authorities, who have the power at present to make their own, by- laws, and to enforce them. . . It is needless to say that 'advantage is taken of these bylaws, especially by the poorer liar- eno, with the result that we find Such a large number of children who are really of school age' in emploYment. Already other industrial centres hair() beeu taking action in the matter by raising the age limit for leaving school., It remains to be seen Warrington will follow their example. It is elsewhere calculated that 25 per cent. of the non-earning school children and 221 per cent. of the children under five years are liv- ing in "primary poverty." Primary poverty is defined thus: That the actual earnings (ineluding, pen- sions) of the family when , pooled together are insufficient to give all Members the food and clothing of the new standard, after_ pay-

ing, for rent, food and household sundries. - The new standard is one based upon .the ROwntree standard, but amended by Professor Rowley. It will be far more convenient to call • it . the. Bowley standard, despite the modesty of the Professor. Particulars of the standard will be dealt with later.

The Earnings of Men. The following facts as to wages of males over 20 years will be worth recording, bearing in mind that the figures belong to the autumn of 1913. The following are approximate per- centages :- 3t per cent. earn less than 20s. per week. 36 per cent. earn between 20s. and 255. per
week. 23 per cent. earn between 255. and 30s. per week.

div.head: CHURCH LADS' BRIGADE, Easter Field Day At Appleton.
div.p: CHURCH LADS' BRIGADE, Easter Field Day At Appleton.

The Warrington Battalion (2nd Liverpool Cadets) Church Lads' Brigade, held their annual Easter lield.day at Appleton on Monday. assembling at the Cannons, Arpley, at 10 a.m. There were on parade some 120 officers and lads, including Major J. A. Brookes; Captain C. Ford, tieutenant F. Bunch and Lieutenant Morris (Quartermaster), also Sergeant-Major Essenhigh Staff-Sergeants Rook and Taylor, Quarter- master-Sergeant Starkey, Colour-Sergeant Appleton and Sergeant Ashton, and the band of St. Paul's Company, -under Corporal-Bugler Monks. Owing to the absence of so many lofficers and senior lads servinf, with the colours, operations .were on a sbuiewhat smaller scale than in previous years.

div.head: SHAM FIGHT.
div.p: SHAM FIGHT.

Arriving at Stockton lleath, an attack and defence scheme WilS at once. opened. Captain Ford, with halt of the battalion, was selected to guard a' Magazine in the lieighbourhood of Appleton Church. The attack, which centred mainly in the Dingle. was led by .Lieutenant Bunch, with St. Paul's Company. The nature' of the ground was all, in favour of the defenders, and their positions were _so firmly held that, despite the *rigorous direct and flank attacks, only small gains were recorded, it being evident that the force was quite too small for the work the attacking party had in hand. .The signallers and :ambulance sections had a busy time during these operations.

div.head: SPORTS.
div.p: SPORTS.

After a. mid-day ration the battalion moved on to Appleton, where a 'field and other require- ments were kindly lent for the , occasion by Mrs. Lambert. The whole of the afternoon was 'devoted to snorts and games, and the following are some of the results -- Puttees (two minutes allowed to put Private J. Monks, St. Elphin's Cu. , Ambulance (skull bandage, two minutes allowed).---1, Private Lilley:St.. Elphin's Co.; 2, Private Mather, St. Paul's. • Half-mile flat race (under 10.-1, Private Sanders, St. Clement'S; 2, Private Mather, St. Paul's. _ _

Three-quarter mile flat race (over 10.-1, Sergeant Appleton, St. Paul's; 2, Staff-Sergeant Taylor, St. Paul's. The football match between St. Paul's and the Rest el the Battalion re-ulted in win for the Rest by two goals to one. Private Meredith (St. Blphin's) scored both goals for his side, and Sergeant Appleton scored for St. Paul's. A little preSent from the officers and three hearty cheers from the lads were given to Mrs. Lambert before leaving for the homeward, march.

div.head: OE HONOUR'S SCROLL.
div.p: OE HONOUR'S SCROLL.
PRIVATE MANUS CAIN KILLED
IN ACTION.

Private Francis Cain, 21 years of age, who be- fore joining the King's Liverpool Regiment, was a labourer, and who resided with his parents at 44, Jockey-street, has been killed in action. The official intimation of the fact came from No. 3 District Station, Preston, was dated March 21th, Riad ,read as follows:—" It is my painful duty to inform you that a report has this day been received from the War Office, notifying the death of No. 1069, Private Francis Cain, King's Liverpool Regiment, which occurred at Givenchy, France, on March 10th. I am to express to you the sympathy and regret of the Army Council at your loss. The cause of death was killed in action.—Thos. E. C. Dins- dale, officer in charge of records."( From Lord Kitchener was received .a message reading as follows: "The King commands me to assure you of the true sympathy of his iMajesty and the Queen in your sorrow." Private Cain formerly worked at the Dallam Forge, and was the eldest son of a family of six, his parents being Mr. and (Mrs. William Cain. , _
A younger brother, Rifleman Wm. Cain, aged 19, is serving in the King's Royal Rifles. William was formerly a labourer in a brick- yard • Private F. Cain had been in France seven months.

div.head: OFFICER'S TRIBUTE TO MEMORY OF PRIVATE ROVtILINSON.
div.p: OFFICER'S TRIBUTE TO MEMORY OF PRIVATE ROVtILINSON.

Reference to the death of Private W. S. Rowlinson, of the Warrington Territorials, is made by an officer of the 4th South Lancs., in the course of a letter to a friend at Warring- ton. "We buried him" the officer says "in a little village churchyard, and a wooden cross marks his grave. He was a good chap, and every 'Jack man in my platoon paid their last tribute of respect to him. The Colonel and the Adjutant were also present.*

div.head: POUND DAY FOR REFUGEES.
div.p: A POUND DAY FOR REFUGEES.

A pound day, when all gifts of butter, fruit, vegetables, &c., will be welcomed, has been arranged for the Belgian refugees in the town, on Wednesday next. Gifts should be ' brought or sent to St. Austizt's, Bold-street.

Wallington, with characteristic generosity, continues to hold out a practically-sympathetic i hand to many of the gallant sons and daughters of the bra velittle Belgian nation, who so pluckily held the breach against the German hordes until the all-conquering Allies were able to get into fighting tilra"and come to her aid. Such of the naives of the country that ha:4. in the words of her King "lost all save honour" as have been made welcome guests of Wdrring- ton, at the Black Bear House, Latchford, are having as good a time as can be reasonably expected. They number thirteen—five men, three women and five children—all they have occupied their present abode -since December 28th. Of the men, two were soldiers. Our representative paid them a call one day this week, and he found it quite unnecessary to ask whether they were happy and comfortable. Their smiling fates and their' Cosy surround- ings told their own tale. A bright little girl of some twelve summers, who was industriously wheeling a somewhat tiresome baby in a. perambulator up, and down the garden; volun- teered her services as interpreter, should our man require them. It was little short of won- derful to notice how she had .picked np our tongue from the children with whom- she had romped and played, for she spoke quite useful English, considering that she only arrived in England last Christmas.

div.head: WESLEYANS AND ,BELGIANS, Warrington Circuit To Support
div.p: WESLEYANS AND ,BELGIANS, Warrington Circuit To Support
An-other Guest House.

. Some time ago the Bible Classes 'connected with the Wesleyan body conceived the idea of providing a home for Belgian refugees. A com- mittee was formed With Mr. C. E. Parker as president, and Messrs. John -Upson and J: C. Holland, vice-presidents, Mr. Appleton acting as treasurer.. There was a rarge working com- mittee of ladies, which included Mrs. jamee Dodd's Women's Class, and Miss Dring acted as secretary. The 'house, No. 9, Palmyra- square, was selected as a suitable place, and steps were taken to furnish it. After arduous labours, particularly on the part of the ladies, the house has been furnished, and a visit on Thursday • revealed a homely-looking state of things, with nothing to be desired that was con- sidered • necessary to add to the comfort of a modern home.. On Thursday, Mrs. Dodds acted las hostess, and received the first half-dozen refugees, .who arrived at Bank .Quay Station .from London. The • home is • calculated .to accommodate at least a -dozen people corn- • fortably. On the ground floor there is a •Iraw- ing;rooni, 'dining-room, two kitchens and a pantry. The home will receive its full complement of guests next week. Two of the women now. there have sons in the Belgian Army. One of them, a-widow, has learnt since she arrived that her son, a lad of eighteen, has been shot in the leg. She was in. a dark cellar with twelve others near one of the Liege forts during the siege. Four of the other women were im- prisoned for tryirg to cross the.. frontier, and everything of any value was taken from them by their captors: For some time." says the editor in the! current issue of "The , Warrington Circuit Wesleyan 'Y,Fethoilist Church Record,'" " it has been felt th,lt Jnoro might he done fot the Belgian Refugees by the various societies con- nected with the _Warrington Circuit. The 'need for bonus is still very great. Between five and six thousand are now in London, while over 15,000 are waiting to •be brought over from Holland. Mr. Parker, president of the. Pen- keth Men's Bible 'Class, got into communica- tion with several of the other leaders of Bible Classes with a view to seeing' 'whether they • might not be associated in maintaining a home. He very generously promised ~e5O, if the class „Would raise another ,C5O. . The sehena has been taken -up with•enthusiasth by Bold-street, Bewsey-road, Penketh, Sankey Bridges, and Stockton Heath, and the money needed for the maintenance of the home has been promised chiefly in small weekly sub- scriptions. A house has been taken in Palmyra- square and is being furnished for the reception at from-ton to twelve Belgian refugees."

div.head: WARRINGTON GUEST HOUSES.
div.p: WARRINGTON GUEST HOUSES.
Hord The Belgian Refugees Are
Faring.
RURAL COUNCIL AS HOSTS.
Search For Another Guest House.

At a meeting of the Way Relief Committee of the Warrington Rural District Count-Al, held on Wednesday afternoon, the Chairman (Mr. W. nirness) said that ,at the last meeting of the. committee a resolution was ,passed in favour. of renting Bruche Hall as a -Home for Belgian refugees. •Before they made an application for the hall he thought it only right thitt he and the Surveyor should pay a visit of inspection to the place to ascertain its condition. He duly paid a vi;iit, along with Mr. NewcoMbe, and, as a result, he formed the opinion that the hall was in such a state that too much money would be required before it could be put into habitable condition. _There were a number of rooms, especially in the lower part of the building, that could not be utilised for sleeping accommoda- tion; indeed., the whole of the heuse would want too Much money spending upon it before it could be made suitable:
It was • suggested that Bank Croft, Sankey. night be !found more suitable..
Where the Money Will Come From.

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell said that the question had been asked: " Where will the mbney 'come from to prepare this refugee home, , when we get it?" The, various Rural and .Urban District Councils in the county had been asked- to assist the Government in the matter of making provision for the Belgian refugees, and had told them that there were 5,000 of these homeless people waiting in London until suit- able places could be .found for them. The majority of the Rural District Councils of the country had been doing something for these hapless people, but so far the Warrington , Rural District Council had, done nothing. At a recent meeting of the Council it was felt that they should fall into line and do their share. As to the question "Where.will the money come from?" they would make a special appeal throughout the area under their jurisdiction. If they were unsuecesful in getting enough they were told that they might expect some assist- ance from the county funds. He should not think they need anticipate that the projected refugee home 'would prove any real burden to the rural district, for he imagined that they could go on the same lines as had other districts, in which. the Councils- had been successful in getting large quantities of furniture lent to them and also in obtaining, voluntary contribu- tions in cash ant kind. Again, the home would only be required, largely, as -a receiving home, for other Councils—and lie anticipated that they could do the same—had succeeded in the majority of cases, in obtaining employment for the refugees, and in many cases in getting them lodgings outside , the refugee; homes. The refugees then became self-supporting, and the homes were only required for such as, from various causes, were unable to earn their own

div.head: House at Sankey Suggested.
div.p: A House at Sankey Suggested.

If was decided that inquiries should be made with regard to Bank Croft House, Sankey, and that, if it be found suitable,. the Chairman and the Surveyor should be empowered to rent the house and get it into order.

div.head: ST. AUSTIN'S HOUSE
div.p: ST. AUSTIN'S HOUSE

Tht% number of Belgian refugees at this home has considerably diminished. There now re- mains only two children, one man and one woman, the man being in employment at bfessrs. R. A. Naylor's Ltd., the timber mer- chants. lip to a month or so ago there were 16 people in the house, but 12, we understand, have been removed to Nottingham.

div.head: THIS WEEK'S ARRIVALS.
div.p: THIS WEEK'S ARRIVALS.

During the week 22 Belgians have arrived in Warrington. Of ,these ten have gone to the home at Latchford provided by Messrs. Tilson, Wheatley, Walker and others. To the home at Palmyra-square eight have been ,admitted, and four, one a. wounded soldier, have been added to the nail 'Nook e6tublizhtheag. •

At the Warrington County Court on Thurs- day, before his Honour Judge Gurner, Coun- cillor John Pemberton, of Stockton Heath, through Mr. Lindon Riley, the well-known barrister, made, application for a re-trial of the recent action brought against him by Messrs. O. and J. Weaver, cabinetmakers, of Bridge- street, to recover the balance of an account for 1:10 15s. ld. for work done, in respect of which account defendant had paid into' Court the sum .of ,t 7 14s. 10d., leaving two items in' dis- pute, the same relating to repairs to a book- ewe and the making of a cushion for an oak settle. ,With regard to the bookcase, it was , stated at the trial that the defendant alleged that the bookcase, which he sent to be mended on December 26th, 1911, had not been returned, another having, been smt in its place; whilst it was contended that the cushion supplied, was too •=.hort. At the trial judgment was given for the plaintiffs for the amount claimed, with costs, his Honour remarking that he did not, believe a single word of the evidence of Mr. Pemberton or his sister, Miss Florence Pem- berton, who also went into the witness-box. His •Honour pointed out that there was no serious Complaint as to the bookcase or the cushion until defendant, and his sister were pressed, three years afterwards, to pay, and then they came forward with thi3 defence. It was a pity they did not consent to judgment instead of going into the witness-box and deliberately perjuring themselves. A Gradually Growing List of Casualties.

div.head: SIXTY KILLED AND WOUNDED.
div.p: SIXTY KILLED AND WOUNDED.

This week we record the fact that two additional Territorials have been killed; and their names have gone to swell the roll of which Warrington will be for ever proud. The latest intimations of men wounded give an addition of ten to those already ;reported. Up to this ,week we have recorded the following - casualties 12; died from wounds, 3; wounded, 18; so that the figure, now

stands:— , Killed - , , Died -of wounds - 3 WOunded , . • 2B Sick . (about) News . comes through slowly, and the above figures do not represent all the casualties that have occurred. In a Private's letter hoine, reproduced in our "War Stories "•'in another column, it is stated ,that up to April - Ist the casualties in the •Battalion numbered ,50 killed and wounded; and an officer, writing last Sun- day, in a letter, also reproduced by. us, says the casualties up to that day numbered 83 .killed, wounded and sick—a bout 60 being killed and
• wounded. It is, however, stated that considering the work title Battalion has done this is not heavy; and the men are " in good fettle." • The casualties notified this weck• are:—
KILLED. Lance-Corporal F. Jarvis. Private James H. Bennett

WOUNDED. Private J. Fillinghanv Private S.. Daniels. Private R. B. Howells. Private W. Hardman. Private J. Laycock. Private Edward Whittaker Private R. G. Done. Private Geo. E. White. Private G. Chadwick. Private John Callon.

div.head: _ANCE-COPPL. F. JARVIS.
div.p: _ANCE-COPPL. F. JARVIS.
One Of Four Soldicr 3rother3.

News that .yet another gallant son :of War- rington has given his life in the . se).vice.of his King and countrY has been .reeeiVed. The brave man in question is:Lance-Corporal Fred Jarvis, who was aged 21i, and, whes:e parents live at 38, Forster-street, off Orford-lane. He was keen on soldiering as a spare-time occu- pation, and that lie was a smart civilian- soldier is attested by the fact that Ile had risen to lion-counui.ek•donctl rank. He ,joined the Territorials about six years ago. He was a single .man, and prior to offering himself for active service—be was • among the first to do so, when the 011 came-7110 worked at the Cnr- Poration Gas Works, at longford, where also his father,•Mz G. L. Jarvis is employed, as a foreman-stoker. The deCeased, Lance-Corporal was keenly in- terested , in manly sportS, and at one time played Rugby football, having figured in several Works Competition fixtures. lie was also in- terested in boxing.

ONE OF THE FIRST '• TERRIERS" TO OFFER. lie took his work, as a Territorial, :,eriOu.sly, and was very proud to be privileged to wear the King's uniform. He left Warrington with the first batch of TerritOrialS, when they went to Tunbridge Wells for their war-training, and he crossed to France, for more Serious work, on February 18th. News of his death first reached Warrington last Sunday morning, thraugh a letter sent to some friends by Private .Johnson, who was serving in the same compilny as the deceased, ' viz., " B " Company, , Following that came confirmation in' the shape of a letter written by Captain Egerton Fair- dough, and Private John Jarvis, a brother of the deceased Lance-Corporal, who •is also serving at the Front with the Territorials, but
LANCE-CORPORAL FRED JARvis. Killed in Action. •
is Nttached to 'another cotiipapy ; viz., "C " Conap
HIS CAPTAIN'S TRIBUTE

• • - - - Captain Fairelough's letter to the parents read as follows :-- I very much regret to have to inform you that No. 1460, F. Jariis, your son, has been killed in action in the trenches. I am very sorry to lose him. as he was always a hard worker, doing his best and, in consequence, being liked and respected by all his comrades. It may ,be some consolation for you to know that he died at his post doing his duty, and alEo that he suffered no pain, being un- conscious from the first. I am sending under separate cover a few personal effects which were found upon him. The Captain's letter was dated .Ipril Rh.

• HOW- A PLUCKY BROTHER HEARD THE 'NEWS. The brother's 'letter read No doubt you will have received the news about our Fred having been killed in action. We were going to the trenches' to relieve the other half-battalion when I.get.the news. There have been a num- ber of casualties whilst We have been occupying the trenches. .Poor Fred, 'he go sitiot in the head and he died almost immediately. It is a comfort to be able to tell :you that he was accorded a very good burial service, with mili- tary honours. I was ,nearly heart-broken when I received the news . . ..but we must keep up our spiritS as .best we can. It is hard to bear. .. . We have had a good .many casualties in bur battalion up to now, so there will be aome more sad homes about as well as ours. . . . I am quite well myself. . . . I don't think the war will last long now."

THREE BROTHERS BEARING ARMS. The dead lance-corporal was educated at St. Ann's School. In addition to his brother John (who; by the way, is about 25 years of age and who also worked at the Gas- Works) the de- ceased has two other • brothers serving King and country—Christopher, aged ,22;. and Wil- liam Henry, aged 18—both of whom are in the Jloyal. Field Artillery ,and are undergoing train- ing •in_this country prior to leaving for the Front. Before "-joining up" Christopher was em- ployed at Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, whilst William wag apprenticed to a - paperhanger and decorator.

div.head: PRIVATE J. H. BENNETT.
div.p: PRIVATE J. H. BENNETT.
Chaplain's Congratulations Upon Heroic Son.

l'rivite James henry Bennett, " A" com- pany, 4th South Lancashire Regiment, was mortally wounded in the trenches on March 31st, and died almost immediately. Tho first sad news came from the Rev. IL Marshall, chaplain of the Bth Field Ambulance British Expeditionary Force,' who, writing on April Ist to .the gallant private's father and mother, Mr. .Albert • and Mrs. Bennett, 139, ballam-lane, said

Dear Mr. Bennett,-1 am sorry to have bad news to break to you or your son. He was brought last night into hospital wounded and unconscious. He passed away before day- break. 1 ' know no othor particulars; but no doubt his regiment will send you word and also will send you his personal belongings. The enclosed letter was in his pocket, and
knowing how you will value his last words, to you I have registered it on. He is to 'be buried to-day noon in a meadow which we

.have set aside as a soldiers' cemetery—a little wooden cross with his name burnt in will be erected. The soldiers will turf the grave and plant flowers, and I have sent a note of the exact spot to the authorities: if will no doubt be communicated to you at the end of the war.
_ May I add my personal syrnPathy in your loss and congratulation in having an heroic
PRIVATE S. DANIELS. Wounded in Action..
from the fire trench to the reserve. lam cer- tain it was done by a sniper, for this spot is
noted for them. We had been in the trenches lour days, and we have had one officer killed and one wounded, and one private killed and _ _
about eight wounded. We have lost more men this time than *e have ever done. I was

wounded on Tuesday, March 30, about 10.30 p.m." - In a postscript to the letter, Private Daniels said he had lauded in England and was on his way to Leeds, a subsequent postcard telling of his safe arrival at the Second Northern General
ctspital. Private Stanley Daniels received his educa,-

tion at the Hamilton-street School, ,Dnd before volunteering for the Front was employed as a range fitter at the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Company's Works. His brother William is also serving with the Territorials. Private Stanley Daniels is well known in local swimming and gymnastic circles.
PRIVATE JOSEPH L VI-COCK.

div.head: Back In The Fighting-Line After A Shot In The Leg.
div.p: Back In The Fighting-Line After A Shot In The Leg.

The name of Private Joseph Laycock has to be added to the list of gallant Warrington Terri- torials who have been wounded in the service of their country. Prior to going on active service, Private Laycock, who i5..27 years of age, made his home with his sister, Mrs. Blackshaw, of 54, Legh-street. On March 3rd, whilst in action, he received a bullet wound in the leg and was conveyed to the base hospital. The wound, however, proved less severe than was at first thought, and Private Laycock is now back in the trenches.

div.head: Six Days and Six Nights in the Trenches.
div.p: Six Days and Six Nights in the Trenches.

Writing to his fiancee in Warrington ,on April 3rd—the letter being received on Wednes- day morning—he says : Thank you for the Parcel and letter I received .last night. • I only came out of the trenches, after, we had had six days and six nights in .them without a break, so you see whit the "Terriers" have to. do. We •-notv expect six days'. rest, but we do not go to the same place evetY time. It is a shame that what used to be beautiful villages have been knocked down by shot- and ..shell. This must have been -a -lovely place' before the war. I have had a letter from home, and am doing my level best under‘he circunuAances. I think it is a shame, and I always say a few words every night, and also when going into the trenches. Try and buck up."

Why He was One of the Lucky Ones. The official notification • of the fact that Private , Laycock had been wounded Was received from the Preston War Station, on March 24th. It stated that he had been wounded in action at Kenimel, on March 3rd, and had returned to duty. Writing on March 18th to hi "dear sister and all at home," he says:—
_ " 1 was one of the lucky ones to go into the trenches straight away and ,do a 24 hours' In another letter, in which he described his injury as "only a scratch," he ,says: "I am
PRIVATE ,J. LAYCOCK Wounded in Action.

div.head: PRIVATE E. INIIITTAKER.
div.p: PRIVATE E. INIIITTAKER.
Shot In The Right Forearp.

Private Edward Whittaker, 88, Lythgoes-lane, writing to his mother, Mrs. M. Whittaker, on the 4th inst., from the Second Western General Hospital, Whitworth-street, Manchester, says in a letter written with his left hand:— . " You would he surprised when you heard

„ that I was in Manchester. I am in the best of health and my arm is improving wonderfully. Excuse writing, but it is the best I can do with my left. hand. I have been shot through my right forearm, the bullet coming out through the elbow. I went under an operation last Thursday in a hospital in France, at a pretty little health resort in the south. It was a dreary train ride, taking us twenty-six hours. Hoping yon are not bothering yourself on my account, and with love to all at home.—Ted.” Writing later, Private Whittaker says he has . . _
been transferred by motor to Moss Bridge ITospital, 'llarwen. Where he will remain for a wec.k or two before coming home for, a long fnrlough. . ..: ,"My arm is getting on fine, so
lon't worry." Private Whittaker, who is 23 years of age, A a warehouseman at Howley Quay. As a boy le attended the National School, Church-street.

div.head: " Pretty Hot."
div.p: " Pretty Hot."

Private Whittaker, writing to a friend, Mr. 3. }Tannin, 66, Leonard-street, before being wounded, says:-,- . "I shall never forget the 'first night's walk to the trenches—bullets flying all round, but now we. take .no notice at ,all. . . . I think the Germans are afraid of attacks at night, as they keep up a rapid fire from dusk to daybreak.. . . On Wednesday night trelioh,digging, we caeglit it pretty hot, having about nine casualties... .
son? May Easter bring its message of hope and consolation in your great sorrow.—Yours sincerely, H. Marshail, chaplain.
ONE 00 THE THREE HUNDRED.

Private Bennett, who like his father, worked in the wheelshop at Dallam, was one of the three hundred Volunteers who joined the Territorials to raise the original battalion to war strength for foreign service. Ile was 21 years of age last January, and he had every qualification of a 'good soldier. His school days were spent in St. Ann's School, and he also went to. the Sunday school belonging to the same parish. He belonged to the Juvenile Forqters. FOND OF SPORT. ,

Private Bennett was very fond of games and sports of all kinds, and the letter he had written home but had not had the opportunity of post- ing chiefly - reflected that fondness. Referring to his cousins (Messrs. W. and P. Blackledge) he sa id _ _ .

Tell Willie and Percy I am hoping to have a few games of bowls this summer With them. How is Henry Holbrook -going on? . . . We are having our turn in the trenches. lam writing this while I am in . Hope you are in the pink, the same as myself. . . . Ask our Willie what about the old Wanderers for the cup?" Priyate Bennett was a member of :the Junior _ _ _ .

Ctins€4vative Club and bowling club, but he was a 'visitor to many of • the -greens of the town. Tho doings of his uncle, Mr. W. Bennett, the Warrington • Conservative Club bowler, he followed with the keenest personal interest. He was an only son, but leaves two sisters in lddition to his father and mother to mourn his loss.

div.head: WOUNDED.
div.p: WOUNDED.
NtIVATE 3. FILLINGHAM.
One Bullet Hits Five Men.

Mrs. FiHingham, lti, Soott-st-reet, received a )oStcard on 'Good Friday intimating that her tusband had been wounded. Alter he had been carried to a temporary hospital he sent Mrs. Tillingham a letter, which she received on Tues- day morning. The letter was written on Good Friday. He said he Would have no fish for dinner, and that he had received lcir parcel. the day before he went into the trenches, which was on March 27th. He was wounded on Saturday morning, March 27th, at 11.30. In the trench they had got two sandbags. Just as they were

home from hospital describing' what had hap-. Pened, and a further letter received on Wed- nesday morning states that his wound was of so comparatively light a nature that it was only necessary„ for him to remain in hospital three days. The wound, he said, had rapidly healed, and, there scarcely remained any trace of it. From the gallant " Terrier's " letter it appears that his company were occupying an old German trench in the Champagne country at the timebe received his injury. lie adds the fact that his company were only 80 yards from the German trenches when he was hit, and says that up to then ,he was wonderfully well. Up to the .time of writing, he says, it had been very cold at nights. He was then-billeted in an old farmhouse, where the conditions were 'much better than some he had experienced, though not so good as those in the hospital. Private Howells has a very large number of friends in W,arrington.who keep him well sup plied with parcels of " goodies " and useful things; and there were, he writes, no fewer than seven ,t4nch parcels awaiting him at the time. of penning MS most recent letter. home. . The gallant Private is a young man of excellent character and is a total abstainer.

He- told her not to worry as he was going on all right. The shock he got was not. so nice. He thought the.top of his head, had gone, but now thought he would be all right in a day or two. It had no finger on and was a foreign one, and had belonged to some soldier who had gone through the wood. lie was going to take care of it a 4 a keepsake. .

On, the Thursday prior to Good Friday, five .f . the Warrington Territorials were getting eady for tea in the trenches when an explosive lullet, probably fired by a sniper, came into heir midst, and more or less wounded the lot
of them.

Private Robert Besley Howells got part of the shot in his cheek-bone. He went to the dress- ing station, where he was attended by Dr. Law, who sent him in the ambulance to the nearest hospital. ' Private H. B. Howells is 20 years of age, and his home is at Oak Vale, Prappenhall. Prior to offering himself for active service he was a, clerk in the goods manager's office at Arpley, L. and N.-W. Railway Station. He stands 6ft. 21n. in height, and is a fine figure of a man. Prior to enlisting in the Territorials in August last, he was Sergeant-Instructor in the Church Lads' 'Brigade connected with St. Clement's Mission :Church. Since leaving the countrY in.Fehrttary he has kept up a regular corresPonaence-With Ins p*nts keeping them well informed as to his doings. His training in this country, he .says, did him a lot of good physically. After he was wounded he wrote

all right now, so don't worry yourselves. The, only thing that I need most while I am over here is something to drink, like cocoa or coffee, and something to eat, for they sell cocoa and sugar and milk mixed up altogether in tins. Private Walter Hardman. 27, Scott-street. almost. oppOsite to Private Fillinghanes, is 30 yeai;s ,of age and an old. Volunteer, who had joined. the Territorials before the outbreak of, the war; He is a native .of Warrington, and was emidoyed Bewsey Forge, Messrs. Parson and Knowles Coal And Iron Co., Ltd. He was famea as a bowler, and was frequently engaged i &matches.

Received Slight Injuries. Private Hardman, whilst in the trenches, received n slight flesh wound in the shoulder. lie .wrote home to his wife informing- her .of what had occurred, and the message was quickly -followed by'an official notification, which was accompanied by the statement that Private,liardman was again on duty. Ile has also a brother-in-law, Private Tom Nicholson, serving with the Territorials, and is also related to Private Fillingham, another of the wounded.

div.p: ?RIVATE tan EDWARD 'WHITE
Stilt In The knee By A Sniper.

Mrs. White, of 36. Battersby-lane, has two soldier sons. Their, father was also a soldier, and had 21 years' service to his credit, rising to the rank of sergeant. He died about 18 months ago. One of the sons, Private George E. White, who is only 22 years of age, worked at Rylands Bros.' before volunteering for active service With the Territorials at the outbreak of war. His mother received a letter from :him on Wednesday morning, addressed from the Scot- tish General Hospital, Glasgow, t and ,dated April 6th. 1915 t— "Dear Mother,—just a few lines to tell you that I am getting on as well as can be ex- pected, hoping you and all at home are in the best of health. I am sorry to- say that a sniper cut my stay in France short. He dotted me one right through the top part of my knee. I thought a horse had kicked me when I got it. It happened as we were going

div.head: PRIVATE G. CHADWICK.
div.p: PRIVATE G. CHADWICK.
Preston Man Who Joined The Warrington `"rerriers.-

Private G. Chadwick, a Territorial, whose home is at • Preston, writes to his sister, .*ho lives at 4, Brick-street, that he has been wounded, but is now back in the firing line. H 6 states that he has been very lucky _so far. A bullet struck his spade before hitting him. 'He ,also went- through the Beer War and was wounded in'the arm and then- acted as signaller. He joined the Territorials at the outbreak of the war.' '

div.head: PRIVATE ;101IN CALLON.
div.p: PRIVATE ;101IN CALLON.

Private j. ,Calloh, 21 years of age, a basket- maker, wiiOSe wife and family reside at 6, Mersey-terrace, was stick in the stomach dur- ing fighting at Ypres On March 13th.. He has sufficiently- recovered from his wound to enable him to be removed to England, to the Ist Eastern General Hospital, at Cambridge. His wife paid him a visit on Saturday. His condition is not now quite, so precarious as it has been for the past three weeks, but the bullet has not been extracted yet. In a letter received on Friday morning by Mrs. Callon, her husband says he feels a little stronger. , • - Private Call4lh had served four years in the Territorials and re-joined immkdiately on the outbreak of the war, volunteiring for active service.

div.head: PROBLEM-MELODRAMA AT THE COURT.
div.p: PROBLEM-MELODRAMA AT THE COURT.

Many a dramatist has essayed to combine the concomitants of the problem play with those of the melodrama, but few have suc- ceeded so well as the author of "The Woman. Who Did Tell," though truth to relate, even when the the/he be so tellingly handled as in this case, complete success is not obtained, for inevitably realism has to be sacrificed to the effects that "get" the gallery, or: broader lines have to be developed to the irritation ana non- comprehending mood of the, people rhose only idea of the theatre is compaSsed within the. limitations of the phrase "place of amuse- ment"

However, "The Woman W4i- Did Tell" is quite an excellent production M its kind, and it has proved just the right sort of fare for hosts of Royal Court patrons this week; The piece is excellently played by a capable ,o-npany toured by _Messrs. Jason and Mont-
gomery. Merry and Bright Revue Next Week.

Next week, at this •popular place of amuse-, merit, will be seen the latest London. craze;- 'All the 'Nice GirlS!" It will be Played by Messrs. Vint and :McKenzie's No. -1 Company,. which is this week taking St. • Helens by storm-. The piece is quite one of the brightest and not laughable revues before the public, and H replete with gorgeous costumes, elaborate scenery and sparkling ,music. With such artistes, as Jack McKenzie, Sid Kearns,' G. West, &c:,‘ to supply the comedy,. Royal Court :Itrons may look forward to a feast of mirth, nile the special numbers rendered by the charming and popular soprano, Miss Viola :Rene,. and Mr. ,Kenneth. Seymour, ensure a musical treat. The talented principals are supported by a full chorus of thirty charming Prench and English beauties, who disport themselves in the very latest Parisienne cos- tumes.

div.head: ‘CRORATIC POT-POtTIRI AT THE HIPPODROME.
div.p: ‘CRORATIC POT-POtTIRI AT THE HIPPODROME.

A specially strong and altogether capital bill of fare obtains at the Hippodrome this week. Naughton and Gold, "originators of all they say and do," cause unlimited laughter with the droll way in which they do all sorts of eccentric absurdities. The Seltini Trio's acro- batic act is not only remarkably clever, but also very amusing; whilst the Martelloni Family of lady acrobats perform with grace Hand apparent ease the most difficult and daring feats. The Five Joy Belles give a captivating ,klanciiio.b revue in numerous styles and costumes :The Bros. St. John appear in fine music, !humour; and dancing. Dalkeith makes tip- Itop comedy with his chalk-picturing, and iHarry- Rogerson gives a gripping uni-duologue in clever fashion. Next Week's Fine Fare.

A sparkling bill has been drawn up for next ;week, and it will be headed by that brilliant stock-whip manipulator, Frank Lindsay, whose .feats .have to be seen to be credited. Agda and Co., in " The Lady of the Future." will pro- vide another strong attraction. and A Fairy Story," a semi-dramatic playlet, will form a third leading feature, many other turns help- ing'to make a sterling two-hours' entertainment.

div.head: ILL-SI'AR PROGRAMME AT THE 'STAR KINEAn.
div.p: ILL-SI'AR PROGRAMME AT THE 'STAR KINEAn.

The programme which is being shown at the Star Kinema this week-end is quite one of the most enjoyable of the many enjoyable ones which the management have provided, being well varied and containing some of the latest and best stuff on release, and thoroughly main- taining the reputation of the management for providing thoroughly enjoyable and high-class entertainments.' For next week two specially fine films have been booked by way of premier attractions—the first, which will be shown on Monday, Tuesday .and Wednesday, being entitled The Vendetta," and the second, which will be shown at the week-end, "The Spoilers."

div.head: GRAND PICTURES AT THE GRAND.
div.p: GRAND PICTURES AT THE GRAND.

Tip-top programmes continue to be the order at the newly re-decorated and extremely com- fortable Grand Electric Theatre, which is enjoying 4: new lease of popularity; The show this • week-end is of the most fascinating description, being well varied and containing something suited to the taste of every living- picture lover. For next week two fine pro- grammes have been secured. That on the first three nights will be headedittly "A Page From Life," a specially attractive film dealing with things as they are, ,whilst the big draw at the week-end will be "The Mill Stream," another very fine subject.

div.head: ahurril
div.p: ahurril
CHRISTIANISING AFRICA.
Missionaries Tell Bold-st. Wesley ans
Of Their Work.

The Eastertide services at the Bold-street Wesleyan Church afforded an opportunity for urging upon large ongregations the claims of foreign Missions. As was briefly reported in our last issue, the Church, on Good Friday, received a visit from a couple of missionaries —the Revs. Simon C. Hall and Alfred S. Sharp —who have had long experience in the mission field in different parts of Africa, the last- named having but recently returned from work in the Transvaal. The two missionaries ad- dressed a largely-attended public meeting in the evening, Mr. Frank Hickman being in the chair. ,
THE CHURCH'S MISSIONARY CONTRI- BUTIONS.

The Rev. 11. Williamson presented the annual report on tile missionary efforts put forth. by the Church, and said that there was no need for them to sing .any psalms of woe in connec- tion therewith; indeed, there was no work in the Church whioh gave them, more hope for the future. The work continued to prosper,. and he trusted that it always • would, but they must have money' and still more money, •if the work was to be carried on as they would like to see it carried on. Referring to the Centenary Fund which the Wesleyans of the country were raising and to the general finances of the Church throughout the country, he said that it was a delightful sign of the times that despite the extra financial strain imposed upon them by the war, their own par- ticular branch of the great Wesleyan Church had been able to make an even higher contri- bution—£3l 18s. 9d., which was some 275. more than in the previous year. The total raised throughout' the Warrington Circuit was £316 12s. 4d., as against £314 • 15s. 9d. the previous year.

div.head: CONFUSION OF TONGUES.
div.p: A CONFUSION OF TONGUES.

The Rev. S. C. Hall then spoke of missionary Work in Africa, which, he reminded his audi- ence, . was the greatest of the Continents, and whose inhabitants spoke no fewer than 843 "languages"; a fact from which they might deduce something of the difficulties Which barred the way of the bodies who sought to spread the Gospel of Christ throughout that vast domain. South Africa, with which he was More particularly acquainted, was a land abounding in wealth and also in ,startling and striking 6ontrqsts; it was a vast tract of coun- try which had•been three times lost and three times re-discovered, and there was no part of the world whiCh had more readily and encour- agingly responded to Missionary work and enterprise. GOOD THE MISSIONARIES HAVE WROUGHT.

The Rev. Alfred S. Sharp spoke of his work hr southern Central Africa, and, as illustrat- ing the immensity of the continent, mentioned that although the previous speaker and he laboured in what was generally spoken of as the same mission field, their spheres of work were actually from 3,000 to 4,000 miles apart. It was thirty-one years since he first went to -Africa as a pioneer missionary, and the good that the missionaries had wrought in the land' was such that there was now no comparison between the country of that day and the country of to-day; in -every direction improve- ment was very obvious even to the most casual eye. The problem of Africa was a great one, but it was being slowly and surely. solved. On Sunday missionary sermons- were preached by the Revs. IL T. Dixon and A. J. Morton.

div.head: LEGH-STREET SUNDAY
div.p: LEGH-STREET SUNDAY
SCHOOL.
Prizes for Forty'-five Diligent Scholars.

The annual tea party and prize distribution in connection with the Legh-street 'Primitive Methodist Sunday School took place on Good Friday and were well attended. After the tea tables had been cleared, Mr. J. Griffiths took the chair and the remainder of the evening was devoted to music. Pianoforte solos were contributed by Miss Harding and Mr. F. Ban- ner, and violin solos by Mr. Harold Woodland. Mr. McDiffen recited, and other recitations, as well as a number of solos, were given by various of the scholars. During an interval Mrs. Mills presented the prizes, and, in doing so addressed a few appropriate, remarks to the young people present, congratulating those who had been successful and encouraging to further effort those who had not won prizes.
Teachers and Old Boys at the Front. The Secretary (3lr,_A. (2resswell) presented
his annual report.
They had on the register,

_ be said, 24 teachers and Officers and 197 scholars / —lO2 - boys:. and 95 girls. Of the total number 45 had this year won prizes, as against 38 last year. The income; for the past year amounted • to J. 82 65., and the expenses to rt 69 19s. 110., sd that they began the present year with a balance of ,212 65., Old. A number of the teachers and old scholars had offered their ser- vices in the great cause of upholding the honour and integrity of our beloved country in the present great struggle, which, they trusted, would soon end in a lasting peace. The names of the teachers and old scholars re- ferred to had. been emblazoned on a Roll of - Honour, which had been hung in the school. The Chairman then briefly addressed the gathering, after which the •programme was • proceeded with.

Allowance. • There is an editor in a little „New York town who has a well developed streak of gentle humour and a fondness for gardening. Not long ago his man of all work left him, and the editor advertised for some one to fill his place. Among the applicants for the position was a man who seemed to know his business thoroughly, but who failed to produce references as to character when requested. Moreover, his eyes were somewhat shifty. You say, you have no references?" the editor asked.

"No; sir, I have not," the man replied in a tone of humble, pride; "but I think, sir, that you will find honesty printed on my face." The owner smiled a little. " Well—er—per- hops," he admitted; "that is, allowing for typographical errors."

div.head: DIED FOR HIS COUNTRY.
div.p: DIED FOR HIS COUNTRY.
litkiev Rifleman's Remains Interred
With Military Honours.

On Sunday week thousands of people assembled in Risley and Croft to witness a military funeral in the graveyard attached to the local Unitarian Chapel. The people had come 'from many miles around, scores on bicycles and motor cycles, others in motor cars. carriages, Cabs and wagonettes, to say nothing of hundreds of pedestrians from Glaze- bury and the surrounding districts. The fallen soldier—Rifleman Harold Houpiton—came of a weii-knos n Risley tamily, AL.L. and Mrs. F. Houghton, the parents, having for a number of years kept the Noggin Inn. Mr. Houghton, the father, like his father before him, was an ironworker, who used to wala daily some five miles to work at the Vulcan Works, Earlestown. Mr. Houghton had a family of eight boys and girls.

div.head: ENLISTED WITH A BROTHER.
div.p: ENLISTED WITH A BROTHER.

After the war broke out, two of the boys, Harold, who was 24 years of age, and Fred, who is• 18 years old, and who were both mechanics, determined to do what they could to help their country, so enlisted seven months ago, in the 2nd Battalion of the Rifle Brigade, and in due course, after receiving training, were drafted away to France together,' and ultimately fought together in the same trench, in the historic battle of Neuve Chapelle. All went well with them until a week ago last Thursday, March 18th, when Rifleman Harold was shot in the lievc! and his skull fractured.' His brother assisted in his removal from nib trench.

div.head: SHOT IN THE HEAD IN A BAYONET CHARGE.
div.p: SHOT IN THE HEAD IN A BAYONET CHARGE.

He received his hurt when taking part in a bayonet charge levelled at the German advance trenches. After being taken to hospittil he was sent to England, arriving in Norwich Military Hospital on Friday night, March 19th. He never complained of pain, and had nothing but praise to utter concerning the hospital arrangements He said that nothing more could be done for him than was actually done It was Apparent, however, that he was dangerously hurt. Since their sons enlisted Mr. and Mrs. Houghton had removed to Rochdale. ;Mrs. Houghton, on hearing of her son's misfortune, wept to the hospital at Norwich to visit him, mitt remained at his bedside until death took place on Wednesday, March 24th.

div.head: WELL-KNOWN LOCAL FOOTBALLER.
div.p: WELL-KNOWN LOCAL FOOTBALLER.

Rifleman Harold Houghton was an Oddfellow. The members of the lodge to which he belonged held' iheir Ineetings at the Noggin Inn. He was also a footballer, and played in the Leigh and I )istrict Sunday Schools League, and more recently in the Warrington and District League. He was also a popular member of the Risley Institute. The body was removed from Norwich on Thursday, and arrived at the house of his eldest brother, Herbert, at Risley, on Friday. Mr. James Henshaw, a local undertaker, carried out the funeral arrangements. The gallant Rifleman was buried with mili- tary honours.

div.head: AN IMPRESSIVE FUNERAL.
div.p: AN IMPRESSIVE FUNERAL.

The military authorities sent a detachment of nine soldiers belonging to the 6th Man- chester Regiment, now stationed at the Leigh Camp, acting a guard over the prisoners of war interned there, and also twelve men and two non-commissioned officers of another regi- ment to make up a firing party. A bugler and a drummer were also in attendance.

The funeral cortege, which formed up shortly after three o'clock, reached the burial ground aboat 4.30, and was headed by the Glazebury Brass Band, who played funeral music en route. Beside the family mourners, the mem- bers of the Oddfellows Lodge to which the deceased belonged, and many old friends followed the remains to the grave. The coffin was met at the chapel by the Rev. J. J. Wright, of Atherton. The service in the chapel began with the singing of the hymn "Oh, God, our help in ages past."

div.head: PASTOR'S PANEGYRIC.
div.p: PASTOR'S PANEGYRIC.

After reading the Unitarian funeral service-- for the deceased and all the members of his family were members of this denomination—the Rev. Wright said that courage and comfort were the two passwords for them that day. Comrades and relatives, to whom the deceased was most dear, had .gathered together to per- form the last offices to one they knew and loved. As a boy, Harold Houghton was a prize-taker in the •Sunday school and a regular attendant at the Chapel. When the_eall came for young men to serve their country he and his brother heard it, and obeyed, and they were fighting together in. the same trench when the first notes of a still higher call reached the ears of him whose loss they, that day, deplored. He had passed from them, but they believed that all was well with him—he had gone to receive the Great Prize, the reward for duty' faithfully - done. Those- who remained behind prized the, honour of having known him; of having been acquainted with one who had made the greatest sacrifice that a man could make for his country. As he lay dying he said to his mother, "I am not afraid!" He had done his duty and he had no fear of the hereafter, and he now lived with God.

CLOSING SCENES AT THE GRAVESIDE. As the coffin was being removed from the chapel to its last resting place, Mr. T. Whittle 'laved the voluntary "For ever with the Lord." Three volleys were fired over the grave, and the buglers sounded "The Last Post," after which the band played "The Penticost." - Some/beautiful floral tributes were placed on the coffin, which was covered with the Union Jack for a pall. The breastplate bore the simple inscription: "Rifleman Harold Hough- ton. aged 24; 2nd Battalion Rifle Brigade." Floral tributes were sent by: The Father, Mother and family, the wreath bearing the in- scription, "He died a hero "; "Sister Jane. Jim and Dick," "His Brother Tom," the Ris- ley Institute Football Club, "His fellow workers," "A few friends at the 'Horse Shoe,' " Mr. and Mrs. Collier and family, "Herbert and Lizzie,". the members of ,the Risley Institute, and the Risley Ladies' Sewing Class.

div.p: Rather Dubious.
"This is an age of steel," said the after- dinner speaker. "Permit me to suggest," interrupted- the chairman courteously, "that for the benefit'of the reporters preSent you spell that last word"
