div.head: wth CURER.
div.p: wth CURER.
LIYMM

Free Church United Service.—The Free Church Council held a united service on Good Friday in the Wesleyan Church. The Rev. J. A. Penaliggon (Congregational minister) con- ducted the service, and spoke on the significancy of Eastertide.
Will Rev. Penaliggon Leave?—The Re. J. A. Penaliggon, of Lymm, has received a call to the Congregational Church at Littlemoor, Glossop. Mr. Penaliggon has not as yet made known his decision:

Primitive Methodist Sermons.—Special ser- vices were conducted in this, church on Easter Sunday by the Rev. R. W. Ferguson.. In the morning the reverend gentleman spoke from Philippians iii. 20, 21, and dealt with theecitizen- ship of the saints and its manifestation. 11 evening subject was: "The ever-abiding pres- - of Christ."

Former Resident Dies at Cambridge.—An old and at one time well-known Lymm inhabitant has passed away in the person of lfr. George Enoch Morgan, who died last week at his home in Cambridge. He was 62 years of age. His father (the late Mr. George Morgan) lived at Cherry Tree Farm, Lymm, and the son speAt his young days in this part of the country. Easter In The Trenches.—Private Percy Clare recently wrote home to Lymm : "We shall be in the trenches on Good Friday and Easter Sunday. We have just had an open-air service —because we shall not have the chance on Good
Friday and Easter Sunday. . . . Don't be downhearted. Jim Taylor has just left here in a motor-van. . . ."

Waterloo Recalled.—ln Mr. C. E. Ardern's shop window is a silver medal attached to a dark red ribband. It is stamped "Waterloo," and was the special memento of that battle be- longing to John Wheeler, of the 13th Regiment Light Dragoons—who also held the Peninsular War medal, bearing the battle names, Toulouse, Nives, Salamanca, Vittoria and Cuidad Rodrigo. He was wounded in the fighting around Badajos, and lies buried in Lymm Churchyard.

Railway Pensioner Dies.—At the Infirmary, after an operation for cancer, the death took place on Sunday afternoon, of Mr. Isaac Worrall. He had been under the care of Dr. Burrowes, and was 69 years of age.—Mr. Worrall was well-known in Lymm, having lived there all his life. He was a signalman at the station, where he had been employed for about fifty years, retiring on a well-earned pension five years ago. He lived near the station, and leaves a .widow to mourn him. On Wednesday afternoon, at the Parish Church, the Rector (Rev. G. B. Thurston) conducted the funeral. Mr. S. Scragg (stationmaster) represented the railway staff, who Ow sent a beautiful floral tribute.

Bad Roads at the Front.—Private S. Linley writing ,before he was wounded to his -wife at Pepper-street: "I am still in the pink.. We get done-up sometimes-- the march to the trenches is heavy; it is not the distance but ths roads. But we soon get all right again after. a. night's rest. It seems strange that each time, just before going to the trenches, I have received a letter from you to cheer me up. ,We have had it lively. The shells were bursting-all round us, right on the side of the trenches. . . . It was really the hottest time we have had. Sunday we were -working nearly all day, trench-digging; it re- minded me of being* in Suffolk again. The weather here seems to be picking up..a hit; we can have good weather it will be better for Ils• • • r

Rev. R. W. Ferguson at Dunham Massey.— A grand miscellaneous concert, on Wednesday evening of last week, was given in the Dunham Massey Primitive Methodist Schoolroom. The Rev. R. W. Ferguson (of Lymm) presided, and gave a brief and appropriate address. The fine programme was sustained by the following: The Misses Edghill, Warham, E. Holt, M. Astall, D. Pennington, G. Pennington and D. Perrin, and Messrs. E. E. Whittaker, C. Boyd, E. Jones, A. Jones, E. Litherland, J. Penning- ton. A. Clark,' R.' Ankers and Ketels, while a Male Glee Party sang several quartets. At the conclusion Mr. Ferguson moved a compre- hensive vote of thanks to all who had taken part in making the gathering such a success. The proceedings concluded with the singing of the National Anthem. Concert for Red, Cross.—A fine concert in aid of the Lymm Red Cross Hospital was given in Statham School on Tuesday evening. The chil- dren greatly charmed the audience with their various songs, recitations and dialogues—as also did Mr. .C. James with his violin solo and comic songs. The Misses Wright, Richardson, Wal- ton, Little, Dalton and Dixon considerably en- hanced the entertainment by their two sketches entitled "Just my luck." and "Wanted, a governess." The Misses Wright gave a very pleasing song entitled "I should like to be a soldier or a sailor," and the duet, "Pretty Polly llopkins" (sung by Miss F. Little and Mr. James) was greeted with loud applause. The Misses C. Norcott, E. Walton and E. Dal- ton efficiently acted as accompanists.—The pro- ceeds of the concert. amounting to £B, has been handed to Mr. Giles Hunt, the Hospital treasurer.

" Very Good Soldiers."—Sergeant Harold Clare's latest letter from the Front reached his mother at Booth's Hill, yesterday:' "I was de- lighted to receive your beautiful Easter card this Morning, and I shall always remember Good Friday and Easter . Sunday of 1915, both being spent in the trenches. This is a lovely mornink, and we are all thinking more than ever—if, that is possible—of our wives and children and parents... . . The Lymm .boys are enjoying the best of health. . . . I hope and trust it will continue, and that I shall not have the unpleasant task of reporting any more deaths. I am looking forward to the time when we shall all be at home again. . . . I- am doing all I can for the safety of all our boys—who, I am pleased to say, have turned out to be very good soldiers. Of course we can't send much news. We came oat of the trenches on Easter Sunday night for four days' rest. Please give my kind regards to all I know. . . ." Wedding of Mr. C. V leather.—A pretty wedding took place on Wednesday, in the Con- gregational Church, the contracting parties being 4Liss Grace Dowlman (daughter of Mr. George Dowlman, of Lincoln) and Mr. Charles Vickerman Leather (second son of Mr. Albert Leather, Booth's Hill Post' Office, 'Lymm). Mr. Percy N. Leather acted as best man, the Rev. J. A. Penaliggon (pastor) officiated. Miss Jessie Simpson was the bridesmaid. The bride was attired in a Saxe blue costume and a white hat and had a bouquet of Sweet Nancy's. She was given away by Mr. JaMeS Hewitt (of •Lymm). The bridesmaid wore a navy blue costume with cream hat.—The bridegroom's father played organ accompaniments to the hymns—The ,wedding breakfast was held in Mrs. Walker's Room, Bootk's Hill, at which several happy speeches weM Made. Among the guests were Mr. and Mrs. Joseph ViCkerman (Bury), Mrs. A. Kay (Bury), Mrs. Dixon (Lymm), Mrs. P. N. Leather, Miss K. N. Leather, and the Rev. and Mrs. J. A. Penaliggon.—Many useful pre- sents were received by the happy couple. Broom Edge Primitive Methodists.—On Good, Friday, in connection with this place of wor- ship,..a: public tea and grand miscellaneous con- cert was given on behalf of the, trust funds. A large 'number sat down to tea, the provisions for which had been given by friends.—The even- ing concert was presided over by the Rev. R. W. Ferguson, who opened with prayer and a short address. The programme, much enjoyed by a' crowded audience, commenced with a pianoforte solo by the Rev.' W. Daw. Miss Marjorie Priestner recited " Nellie, the match girl," and Mr.' Newton sang." Thebest friend is mother" hi. good style. Master Sydney Wright rendered well two songs. Mr. Newton again sang, Mr. Daw pleasing with a second' pianoforte solo. Mr. J.- Perrin recited," The muster roll,h and Miss Lois Priestner " Curfew " most' expres- sively, whilst two capital dialogues (" Playing at school" and "A most obliging customer ") were excellently presented by Miss Marjorie and Master Norman Priestner. Miss M. Priest- ner also recited "How would you •hike to be a baby ?"—which concluded the programme. hearty vote of thanks to all concerned was ex- pressed by the Chairman, and the Doxology and , Benediction brought the proceedings to an end.J

Friends Meet At Front.—Private Arthur Hadden writes:—" Tell Mrs. Kay [of Rush Green, who has three sons serving in the Army] that I was talking to a man in the same [Red Cross] regiment as Tom, and he is at the same place as Harry. He said he knew him, and lie looked very well. I wrote and told Harry what he said. . ."
Killed in Action.

being himself wounded, and which was received on Tuesday evening. Referring to Private Leigh, he 9id : I don't know whether you have heard that he was killed by my side. He was a good lad for doing his duty. He was killed about 4.30 p.m. on April Ist. Four other men were in- jured, but you do not know them? Yesterday word written on the 2nd by Sergeant 11. Clare, reached his mother : I am sorry to tell you that poor 'Peter' Leigh died of wounds received by shrapnel yester- day. We did all that was possible, but he died peacefully soon after he was struck. He is buried in a cemetery in the village, so we all have the satisfaction of knowing where he is.
Private Henry Brooks, writes, saying:—
' Peter' Leigh was hit in the head.
STORY OF HIS LIFE.

Private Leigh, whose age was nearly 20 years, was born at Newfield, and had lived in, Lymm practically all his life—for the last few years at Poole-lane, Statham, where his parents also reside. He was unmarried.

As a boy he attended the Lymm village school; and at the age of 13 became A newsboy for Mr. Pell Araen, afterwards working on Mr. Henry Lloyd's farm at Thelwall. Twelve months later he became a labourer with the Manchester Ship Canal Company, by whom he had been employed at Lymm and Irlam ever since.

With the Territorial Movement he was heart and soul, joining it so far back as six years agO. Of their annual camps he was a regular and enthusiastic member. A fellow Territorial now writes to say how he "fought hard up to the last."
At the Parish Church Private Leigh 'was an occasional attender. lie leaves father, mother, three brothers and two sisters to mourn their loss.
Woundeciin .Action.

himself on April 4th, to his mother, Mrs. Jane Shaw, of Booth's Hill, Lymm. Her it reached on Tuesday morning, saying: I have been wounded and am going on well. I am being sent down.tp the base. I have received your letter. Letter follows at first opportunity. This card only took one day to reach home. • No further particulars are yet to band, and
naturally they are eagerly expected at any moment. .
Private Shaw's duties at the Front are of especial responSibility, as he is a stretcher- bearer, whose part is to convey the wounded from the trenches—in safety.
PRIVATE ARTHUR HADDEN.
Fractures Shoulder By Fall Into "Jack
Johnson" Hole.

An unfortunate accident has befallen Private Arthur Hadden, of 13, Rush Green, whilst serv- ing with the Lymm "Terriers" in the firing line. The news was contained in a postcard message received by Mrs. Armstrong (his sister, with whom he lives) on Sunday morning: You will be wondering why I have not written before, but I have had no time. I am in England now, but I do not know what hospital I shall go to yet. It is not a bullet wound; I fell on my arm.

On Wednesday morning his next card was received,from a, Wrexham Red Cross Hospital: I am getting much better. You have no need to trouble yourself, as I ,will soon be all right. The nurses are very good indeed •to us. You need not come to see me, as I ex- pect they will let me come home when I am better.

From other sources "The Examiner" learns that about ten days ago Private Hadden fell into a large hole made by exploded shells, thereby fracturing his shoulder. This unfortunate Private is in ordinary life a labourer, and was called up at the start of the war with his fellow "Terriers." With them he had been serving at the Front since ,February. He is an orphan, and will be 21 in September. lie is a popular member of the Lymm Lad's Club Football team.
PRIVATE JAMES TAYLOR.
PRIVATE HENRY
PRIVATE -RICHARD SHAW,

div.head: GOOD AND BRAVE SOLDIERS.
div.p: GOOD AND BRAVE SOLDIERS.
Splendid Under Fire ; Attention A
Marked Feature.

• Mr. W. Mullard, of Eagle-brow, Lymm, has beard from Sergeant Clare. This letfer says:— " It gives me great pleasure to write to you, for I know what a keen interest you take in us. Lymm boys. I am very pleased to say we enjoy the best of health. . . . "Our boys have turned out like I knew they would—good and brave soldiers. Their be- haviour under fire is splendid, and their attention to all orders is a marked feature. I am indeed very proud of them, and I know Captain Hartley thinks a lot of them. "We go in the trenches again on Wednesday night, till Sunday night; so we shall be in for Good Friday and Easter Sunday. I know the thoughts of all our good friends will be with us "We all think of you out here, and we remem- ber how kind you were to us—which .gave.us a leal of encouragement whilst training for this work. . . . . "We have to write all our letters on the floor and on our caps. . . . I trust I shall always be able to send you such good news as now."

div.head: TERRITORIAL ROLL OF
div.p: TERRITORIAL ROLL OF
HONOUR.
FOUR CASI N.!,TIES REPORTED.
Further casualties amongst the Lyrara Terri- torials now serving so nobly in the firing line are reported this week as follow :
KILLED IN ACTION. Private Henry Leigh.
WOUNDED IN ACTION. Lance-Corporal Sydney Linley. Private Richard Shaw.
ACCIDENTALLY HURT. Private Arthur Hadden.

Private Percy Clare has had a remarkable escape from being Wounded, Whilst a fine tribute is paid to the heroic conduct of Private James Taylor, who (as fully reported in our last issue) was wounded a week ago,

Private Shaw had -already only narrowly escaped wounding before ,being. hit. General indignation runs riot throughout the district against those—truly described as "wicked "—who persist in circulating abso- lutely ill-founded runionrs, about the, fate ,of men at the Front. Last week it was under- stood ,in several quaiter liat Captain G. W. N; HartleY had.been -killed, and thiS,Week that. 'Private 'Ernest Tradden (of Pepper-street). had shared a similar fate; that Private Richard Shaw had been shot dirough the head; that two, or three men' from Rush Green were wounded, and that Lance-Corporal Linley's arm had been blown off. None of these stories appears to have the slightest truth, and it is justly felt by.Ly.mmites in general that the evil practice of rumour-spi:eadingtinust at any cost be put a stop to without further delay.

div.head: PRIVATE HENRY LEIGH.
div.p: PRIVATE HENRY LEIGH.
Good and Dutiful "Terrier," Who
"Fought Hard to the Last."
The first news of Private Henry Leigh's sad but heroic death was contained in a letter which Lance-Corporal Linley wrote before
Wounded in Action.
LANCE-CORPORAL LINLEY,

div.head: HIS HISTORY.
div.p: HIS HISTORY.

The gallant Lance-Corporal, whose age is 30, lives at Pepper-street; Lymm—with his wife (whom he married eight years ago) and! .little girl and boy.. iltypace times he is an neat for the Pearl Assurance. .ComPan.V. He was not born at Lymm, but has lived there practically all his life, being also educated at the village school, under:Mr. R. Oddie's.head mastership. His mother lives at Btrefford. . With a natural gift and taste for-ministerial .wOrk,...Lartee-:Corporal-Linley has for some time been a popular Wesleyan local preacher; both at Warrington and his own village. This has proved a special blessing in connection with the Lymm Territorials—which he joined 'about 14 years ago. Since February he had been at the Front, having been called up at the outbreak of hostilities. He is, of course, well known in Lymm as the soldiers' preacher away in the war ~zone, and (as announced.. in. "The Ex- aminer" only last week) had just written home for )00 hymn-books. These, we understand, are nor.- oi their way to the Front. .

div.head: CONDUCTING SERVICES.
div.p: CONDUCTING SERVICES.
Lame-Corporal Linley in a • letter written before hq was wounded said:

"We have left • and moved on a few miles to some other trenches. We have lost 'a few men Out of the sth Chesbires and one Lymm lad wounded in the arm (Jim Taylor). I had a bit of an experience the other night with :a party of sick men, and four men to carry a dead man from the trenches, to the village to be buried. It was a moonlight night and We had a lively time. When, we got half-way we came across a wounded man, so we had to lay the dead body clown on the side of the road and pick the wounded one up. • However, we landed through quite safe. We have moved now to another place a bit farther from the firing line, so do not worry about us, as we are getting on quite well. I still feel that our Father is look- ing after, me and' after you all at home. I am. still conducting services with our lads. Last Sunday I had two in different parts of the building, and I am hoping to give one to-night. I went to a service which was held in a room belonging to a. convent, which is also a hospi- tal. The .Church of England chaplain took the first half of the service and the' Wesleyan one. preached."
Yesterday Sergt. Clare's word said the Lance- Corporal will soon be all right again.
Yesterday another Lymm- "Terrier" wrote raying: " We shall miss Syd. Linley, as we used to have such nice meetings when be preached."

div.head: PRIVATE RICHARD SHAW.
div.p: PRIVATE RICHARD SHAW.
Ambulance Man's Modest Report Of Ca.sualty.
. Private Richard Shaw has also been wounde. By a. coincidence, he had only a day or two before had a "very narrow squeak." Sergeant. Clare then wrote home:
Tell Mrs. Shaw that Richard does very good work. He had a near go in the trenches the other day. A bullet went through his oil-sheet, which he had over his shoulder.
The ,news that he had been wounded was con- veyed by himself on an official card, sent by

div.head: Hit I.Viien AVithin Fifteen Yards Of
div.p: Hit I.Viien AVithin Fifteen Yards Of
Trenches.
Sergeant Clare writes to Mr. W. MuHard:—

"Private James Taylor unfortunately was wounded last Friday night. We were going into the trenches, and it was when fifteen yards away he was hit. It is most dangerous going in and out. The trenches we occupy are only forty yards from the Germans, so you will see how very careful we must be. .. . Private Taylor's wound is not serious—just a flesh wound. The bullet has gone through his arm, but not a bone is touched. We hope to hate him back with us soon. Ire is such a bright lad, and we miss him. . . ."

Private James Taylor writes home to New- fiel4l, from the 4th Northern General Hospital, Lincoln: "I hope you .are all 'in the pink,' as it leaves me at present—though wounded in the left shoulder. I can get about all right without assistance. I shall be all right in about a month, and probably at home."

div.head: "MOURNING lIER LITTLE LOT."
div.p: "MOURNING lIER LITTLE LOT."
All The Same Lymm Is Lucky, Says Cheery Soldier.

Yesterday 'Private Henry Brooks wrote to his mother (Mrs. James Taylor, vf 1, West Hyde, Newfield, Lymm): "I am uiell and in good spirits. . . . suppose you have heard from Jim [wounded] by now. He will be in Eng- land. Don't worry about me, mother. God is good and I trust•to Him. . . .

div.head: " Marvellous Escape,"
div.p: " Marvellous Escape,"

"The other day we were shelled in the trenches, and we had about five _wounded. ' Peter ' Leigh was killed, and Sydney% Linley got slightly wounded, having a scar across the back with a piece of shell; It's marvellous how Sergeant Clare, Lieutenant Walker, jack Moston and me escaped—as we were side by side of those who got hit./ . . . We may consider ourselves very fortunate in not having More casualties. . . .

"We have nice little services in the trenches, and the officer enjoys them. . . . "Well, . I know that Lymm will be mourn- ing her little loss already; but take it from me we have been fortunate and blessed, and our prayers have been answered. I feel confident that this job cannot last long. . . I hope everything will go well. . ."

div.head: PRIVATE TAYLOR'S BRAVERY.
div.p: PRIVATE TAYLOR'S BRAVERY.
"Go To That Other Man; He Is Worse
Than Me!"
Private P. Clare, in a letter received early in the week by his mother (Mrs. G. Davies, of Booth's Hill) says:—

"All the Lymm lads are in the best of health, except poor Jim Taylor. He got wounded in the arm, but will soon be ail right again; he might get home with it. "When they went to bandage him 'up he said: 'Go to that other man; he is worse than me!' He is a brave lad. . . CSptain Hart- ley is our captain now, and we are proud of him. He is fine to his men." FtHRACULOUS ESCAPE.

In a later letter, Private Clare says:— , "I am very lucky. .• . When I was in the trenches yesterday I got a tap on the head, .but it was not Much, thank. God; it just scarred my head. I thought I was done for, hilt I am quite all right."

div.head: ONLY .30 YARDS OFF GERMANS.
div.p: ONLY .30 YARDS OFF GERMANS.
mm " Terriers" In Worst Trenches
In British Lines.

Private Joseph Clare writes to his mother at Booth's Hill "I have not been able to write for these last few days, as we have been in the tremhes for four days—in the worst trenches in the British lines, only thirty yards off the Germans; so it has been very nearly a case of shaking hands with them! To get in the trenches we had to crawl 100 yards in mud on our stomachs. "Two got wounded; Jimmy Taylor got shot in the arm. It was awful—bullets just grazing us. Percy [Clare] has been very lucky. A bullet came through a sandbag and caught him on the head. It's a good job it caught the sandbags, or else he would have been a dead 'un. But lam pleased to say he is all right.

div.head: Worst Part About Trenches.
div.p: Worst Part About Trenches.

"The worst part about the trenches is get- ting in and out of them; for we are partly safe when we get in, and don't . give them much scope. For the Allemans ' (as we call them) are such deadly shots they have us in a second. Well, I am still in the pink and doing well; so keep on smiling. . . . I don't mind a Paper .now and again. Its nice to see a bit of Lymm news. . ."

div.head: LANCE-CORPORAL GIBRS
div.p: LANCE-CORPORAL GIBRS
-;peahs Of The Devoutness Of The
British Soldier.
Lance-Corporal Gibbs, Henry-street, Lymm, writing to his wife, thanks Sylvia for her piece of wood, which heowill keep with him for luck, and adds:—
"Percy had a very near escape Testerday. A bullet just grazed his temple. It bled a little. but he is quite a 1 right now. -

"We had five 'killed 'and-three wounded in our half-battalion. They have had four days in the trenches this/ time. I only went for one day. Percy and I have been on our job— range-finding. We -are now in a quiet little village for four days'. rest. It is a very pretty place, with a fine big church, which I hope to .attend to-night. "Do not send any more cigarettes, as we get hundreds here. Mr. Cooke, Lynam, has sent the Lymm boys 150 each. I shall- never forget my 23rd birthday out here, yesterday. The trenches we were in are only 40 yards from the Germans and .we .had to crawl out on our stomachs for about 50 yards. One chap, before he died, while I was holding his head, prayed that God would take him to that Better Land.
"This war makes every man realise what our Saviour is, and every man prays that God will help him. My job is a good one. I do no firing in the trench. so I have every chance to keep. my head down."

div.head: SANKEY.
div.p: SANKEY.

Wedding.—'he wedding of Miss Annie Sut- cliffe, Liverpool-road, Sankey, and Mr. George Davies, Park-view, Bold, was quietly solem- nised at St. Luke's Church, Liverpool-road, Sankey Bridges, the Rev. E. L. Roberts officiating. The bride was dressed in a Saxe blue costume and hat to match. Miss Nellie Sutcliffe (sister of the bride) was bridesmaid, and she wore a deep blue costume and hat .to match. - Mr. Thomas Sutcliffe (father of the bride) gave her away, and Mr. T. Sutcliffe, jun. (brother). acted as bet man. A brother of the bride is at present in the trenches, so it was decided not to invite anyone except the neare‘t rela- tives to a. small reception. There was a largo number of beautiful presents.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

Friends': School Sports.—Splendid weather favoured the largely-attended annual athletic sports held on Monday at the Friends' School. There was an entry of over 100, and 38 events were brought oft. The Headmaster (Mr. W. E. Brown) and staff are to he congratulated upon the high physical standard of the boys and wa,s- served to the visitors in the hall.—The sports were concluded on Tuesday afternoon.

Wesleyan Sunday School.—The. annual tea • and distribution of prizes took place on Good Friday at the Wesleyan Sunday School. A large number pf scholars and friends sat, down to tea: 'after which they were - entertained by some of - the children, who gave a very creditable con- cert, Misses A. Davies and F. Moores and Mr. G. Carman being mainly responsible for their training. Reports from the secretaries and ' treasurer followed. The distribution of the , prizes by Miss- E. Dumbill brought a pleasant , evening to a - " Wedding„—A quiet but pretty. wedding, was solemn ised at the Wesleyan Chapel, Penketb on Saturday, the Contracting parties being Mise Annie HOdgetts;' Widnes, and Mr. Harry Car- man, Doe Green, Penketh. The Rev.. T. 1.1. Dixon officiated. •- The bride wore a Saxe blue velvet . dregs,- trimmed with champagne em- broider y , silk hat, trimmed feather ruff to match, and carried a bouquet of pink carna- tions... Miss Linda Hodgetts (sister of the bride) acted as bridesmaid, and wore a helio- trope costume,. with black hat trimmed with white plume, and carried a bouquet of deep pink tulips. Mr. J. Hodgetts (eldest brother of the bride) gave her away, and Mr. W. Foderb filled the post of best man. The reception wag held at Laurel Bank, the home of the bride- groom's elde,st brother. The presents were numerous, the young , couple being great fav- ourites in Penketh.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Amateur Actors Support C.L.8.--A very inter- esting programme Iva,. presented at the Padgate Church of England schools on Thursday and Friday evenings, when Mr. R. Dickinson, of Fearnhead, produced his original sketch, "The Padgate • Assizes; or, Who Stole the Weather- cock?" The artistes, who were all „local, dis- played exceptional ability, and are to be com- plimented on the excellent manner in which they acted the various parts allotted to them. The principal artistes were: Judge Jeffries, Mr. R. Dickinson; Counsel for Crown, Mr. W: Fryar.; Counsel for defence, Mr. R. Simpson; Usher, Mr. H. Dutton; Prisoner, Mr. A. Proffitt; Prisoner's Mother, Miss Hilda Antro- bus; 'Weathercock, Mr. G. .Monks. The play was preceded by a short sketch entitled "The Bosun's Mate,'; a farce, which was very well acted* by Mr. F. Dickinson, Mr. H. Dutton, and Miss Ida Haddock, and was greeted with much applause. The schoolroom was well filled on both occasions, the proceeds being in aid of the Church Lads' Brigade, Mr: R. Dickinson being the organiser and captain of the Padgate branch, which has now about 90 members, and is doing good work in the village.

div.head: Nerve Collapse
div.p: Nerve Collapse
Anwmia and Indigestion Cured by Dr. Cassell's Tablets, the All-British Rem,

div.head: SONGS OF SORROW.
div.p: SONGS OF SORROW.
How Poetry Mourns the Deaths of Warriors and of Nations. THE TRIUMPH OF RIGHT.
Yes, they return—but who return? The many or the few ? Clothed with a name, in vain the same, Face after face is new. . Let none forget THE OTHERS, marching With steps we feel no more. .

"Poets are the trumpets which sing to battle," cries Shelley; and poets are they .who mourn the fallen. In a time such as the pres- ent—when the head of a strong nation is bowed in bitter and unfeigned sorrow at the loss of noble sons, and when the world de- plores that mighty empires Must for their sin perish in the dust—a tracing of the influ- ences, be they lasting or short-lived, exerted by such emotions over the philosophy of the outstanding bards of that country cannot but prove of peculiar interest and enlightenment. As, however, we turn our attention to those in our own nation, it would not be desirable for us to investigate as to the general trend of such influences, nor do we intend to do so. Diverse as are the sentiments expressed in our great English war-songs of sorrow, one is inclined to imagine them largely representa-, tive of those moods which are so familiar to the poetic temperament. 'Moreover, such -a task would prove no trivial one. We examine the poems then, only individually. Naturally, we first have the simple, sad acceptance of the (apparently) inevitable. Note its quiet dignity: lie is dead, the beautiful youth, The heart of honour, the soul of truth: He, the life and light of us all, Whose voice was blithe as a bugle-call. The imprisoned knight dwells upon the slay- ing of his companion: They bound my blood-stained hands together, They bound his corpse to nod by my side: Then on we rode, in the bright March weather, With clash of cymbals did we ride. We ride no more, no more together; My prison-bars are thick and strong, I take no heed of ally weather, The sweet Saints grant I live not long. On the first anguish of the loss there shines no ray of hope: We'll hear nae mair lilting at our ewe-milking; Women and bairns are heartless and wae; Sighing and moaning on ilka green loaning— - The Flowers of the Forest are a' wecle away. Though one at least there is who yet stands secure on the foundations of an indomitable faith: All is over and done: Render thanks to the Giver, England, for thy son. Let the hell be toll'd. Render thanks to the Giver, And render him to the mould. But to others there come. doubly thoughts of the -foeman.. Surely this is the cry of Bel- gium: A waefu' da; it was to me! For there I lost my father dear, My father dear, and brethren three. Their winding-sheet the bluidy clay, Their graves are growing green to see: And by them lies the dearest lad That ever blest a woman's ee! Now wae to thee, thou cruel lord, • A bluidy man 1 trow thou be; For mony a heart thou hast made sair That. iie'er did w rang to thine or thee. Scott makes the woman assume that the war- rior loathes the fight: Soldier, rest! thy warfare o'er,' Sleep the sleep that knows no breaking; Dream of battled fields no more, Days of danger, nights of waking. which perhaps is not so: Oh, never more, my comrades, Shall we see that falcon eye Redden with its inward lightning, As the hour of fight drew nigh! Never shall we hear the voice that, Clearer than the trumpet's-call, Bade us fight for Sing and Country, • Bade us win .the field, Air fall! THE SOLDIER'S GRAVE. "Or fall!" That carries back our mind to the soldier's grave. From the poetic stand- point the field of battle is perhaps the most desirable resting-place for the slain warrior. It seems picturesque; it is glorious: Few and short were the prayers we said, And we spoke not a word of sorrow; But we steadfastly gazed on the face that was dead, And we bitterly thought of the morrow. . . We thought, as we hollowed his narrow bed, And smoothed down his lonely pillow, That the foe and the stranger would tread o'er his head, t And we far away on the billow! Lightly they'll talk of the spirit that's gone, And o'er his cold ashes upbraid -But little he'll reek, if they let him sleep on in the grate where a Briton has laid him. . Slowly and sadly we laid him down From the field of his fame, fresh and gory; We carved not a line, and we raised not a stone, But we left him alone with his glory. Another lays his fallen comrade beneath the turf with simpler thought: And I closed our hero's eyelids, And I left him to his rest. And yet—is the warrior content to die on the field? Comfort thyself: what comfort is in me? I have lived my life. . moans the dying Arthur to his solitary so"- rower. To him there is little glory in the soldier's death on the field; the lust of battle is not the real compelling force. He is no hankerer after life, either, but to him the earthly cause seems lost and he deems him- self almost unworthy to die: I perish by this people which I made. And Tennyson would lay his hero elsewhere: Where shall we lay the man whom we deplore? Here, in streaming London's central roar. Let the sound of those he wrought for And the feet of those he fought for Echo round his, bones for evermore. Nay! Is the battid-Pld picturesque? They say it was a shocking sight After the field was won; For 'many thousand bodies there Lay rotting in the sun: But things like that, you know, must be After a famous victory. We pass over any question as to the prob- ability of so philosophic an abandonment to Fate. And sic a weary buryin'

I'm sure ye never saw. There can be no doubt that the description itself is true. The battlefifld is a scene of indescribable horror. And there lay the steed -with his nostrils all Isl,ide, But through them there rolled not the breath of his pride; And the foam of his gasping lay white on the turf, And cold as the spray on the rock-beating surf. And there lay the rider distorted and pale With the dew on his brow, and the rust on his mail; And the tents were all silent, the banners alone, The lances uplifted, the trumpets unblown. . Again: There Confusion, Terror's child, Conflict fierce, and Ruin wild, Agony, that pants for breath, Despair and honourable Death. • Of if there be any glory it soon becomes lost in this horror: Last noon beheld them full of lusty life, Last eve in I3eauty's circle proudly gay,

The midnight brought the signal-sound of The morn the marshalling in arms—the day Battle's magnificently stern array! The thunder-clouds close o'er it, which when rent The earth is cover'd thick with other clay, Which her own clay shall cover,. heap'd and pent, Rider and horse—friend, foe—in one red burial blent! And Bad becomes Worse: But redder yet that light shall glow On Linden's hills of blood-stained snow, And bloodier, yet shall be the flow Of Iser, rolling rapidly. • until at last Few, few shall part where many meet! The snow shall be their winding-sheet, And every turf beneath their feet Shall be a soldier's sepulchre. THOUGHTS OF THE DEAD. Wherever the soldier be laid, however, he will die doubting not that with the passing of the years his country will realise his worth in laying down his life for its sake: When he who -adores thee has left but the name Of his fault and his sorrows behind, . Oh! say wilt thou- weep, when they darken the fame Of a life that for thee was resign'd! Ye, Weep, and however my foes may condemn Thy tears shall efface their decree; . . Oh! blest are the lovers and friends who shall live The days of thy glory to see; But the next dearest blessing that Heaven can give Is the pride of thus dying for thee. Thus he can die calmly. How sleep the brave, who sink to rest By all their country's wishes blest! When Spring, with dewy fingers cold, ' Returns to deck their hallow'd mould. She there shall find a sweeter sod , . Than Fancy's feet have ever trod By fairy hands their knell is rung, By forms unseen .their dirge is sung: There honour comes, a pilgrim gray, To bless the turf that wraps their clay; And Freedom shall awhile repair To dwell a weeping hermit there. . That is a beautiful sentiment for the " rela- tives of deceased," but perhaps a somewhat insufficient—we do not say small—recomPense for the loss .of nearest and dearest. By the way, who can but marvel at the blind egotism of the monarch, who, undoubting,. could be told Mighty victor, mighty lord" Low on his funeral Couch he lies! No pitying heart, no eye, afford A tear to grace his obsequies. , Somewhere there is sorrow—often in the camp of victory. In honour a soldier .departs, and to him Humanity will pay its trubute : 0 civic muse, to such a name, To sueli a name for ages long, To such a name l'reserve a broad approach of fame, And ever-ringing avenues of song. PASSING OF AN EMPIRE. Here the sorrow is submerged in hero-wor- ship, and, coming from the lips of one himself great and noble, it is stirring! Even if the life has been laid down in a cause born to die, yet
. . What if she had seen those glories fade Those -titles vanish, and that strength decay,— Yet shall sonic tribute of regret be paid_
When her long life bath rea-eh'd it; final day: Men are we, and must grieve when even the
shade Of that which once was great is passed away. Even so it will be with the triumphant nations:
But ah, an inextinguishable sense Haunts him that he has not made what he
should; , • • That he has still, though old, to recommence Since he has not yet found the word God tvould. And Empire after Empire, at their height
- Of sway, have felt this- boding sense come on :• Have felt their huge frames not constructed
right, And droop'd, and slowly died upon their throne. —which, though very different from Shake- speare's treatment of the same subject, still tells us:
Time doth transfix the flourish set on youth, And delves the parallels in beauty's brcav ; . . And nothing stands but for his scythe to mow. FEAR NOT THE TYRANTS. _

It is all very sad, but it has proved true. Shelley knows that the evil .nations will die a more violent death: • Fear not the tyrants will rule for ever, Or the priests of the evil faith. They stand on the brink of that raging river Whose waves they have tainted with death. It is fed from the depth of a thousand dells; Around them it 'foams and rages and swells; And their swords and their sceptres I floating
see, Like wrecks on the surge of eternity.
Byron also believed in the triumph of right: And the widows of Ashur are loud in their wail, And the idols are broke in the temple of Baal; And the Might of the Gentile, unsmote by the

sword, Hath melted like snow in the glance of the Lord. And Cowper: Ruffians, pitiless as proud, Heaven awards the vengeance due; Empire is on us bestow'd, Shame and ruin wait for you! But our Empire will have been bought at the cost of many broken hearts: Tradition, legend, tune and song, Shall many an age that wail prolong: Still from the sire the son shall hear Of the stern strife and carnage drear. That will be in the day when the Kaiser, like Napoleon, has said: - -
Farewell to the Land where the gloom of my glory Arose and o'ershadow'd the earth with her name— She abandons pie now—but the page of her

, story, The brightest or blackest, is filled with•my fame. ( I hAve warr'd with a world which va.nquikbed me only 'When the Tneteor of conquest allured me too far; I have coped with the nations which dread me thus lonely, The last single captive to millions in war. Farewell to thee, . ! when thy diadem crown'd me, I made thee the gem and the wonder 'of earth; But thy weakness decrees I shall leave as I found thee, pecay'd in thy glory, and sunk in thy worth. And ,o us Wordsworth will cry from the grave: Another year! another deadly blow! Another mightytempire overthrown! _ .

And We are left, or shall be left. alone; 'rue last that dare to struggle with the Foe. • 'Tis well! from this day 'forward we shall know That in ourselves our ,safety must be sought; That by our own right hands it must be wrought; That we must stand unpropped, or be laid low. 0 dastard whom such foretaste cloth not cheer! We shall exult, if they who rule the land Be men who hold its many blessings dear, Wise, upright, valiant; not a servile band Who are to judge of danger when they fear, And honour which they do not understand.
Not Bad News. " Beware!" whispered the fortune teller; "your bitterest enemy will shortly cross your path " " Horray!" cried the man, 'delighted, `-‘ my new motor car won't do a thing to him,"

div.head: UNITED EUROPE. Philornaths' Lively Discussion On Its Possibility. NATIONALITIES.
div.p: UNITED EUROPE. Philornaths' Lively Discussion On Its Possibility. NATIONALITIES.

, A highly-animated discussion took place at the Church House, Market Gate, on Wednesday evening—when a grand team debate attracted a very fair number of Warrington Philomaths to the last ordinary meeting of their session. The question for discussion was: "Is a United States of Europe Possible?" •The members of the society council took the affirmative side, the other members' ~ "team opposing; heartily-applauded speeches on each side, were given alternately. Mr. James Ball (ex-presi- dent) occupied the chair. . r•

div.head: COUNCIL OF NATIONS.
div.p: COUNCIL OF NATIONS.

Mr. N. Nield (president) opened the discus- sion on behalf of the council. Could the States of Europe be bound together ,by a practical scheme based essentially on peaceful methods? In outlining such a plan he did so with full cognisance of its many difficulties. It was not to be expected that the definite steps would be either perfect or laNting; and of all likely opposition, that of the Englishman would be the strongest.

The Chief object was the abolition of that greatest of all curses war—which would be worth the utmost sacrifice. Each State Would be granted a complete autonomy in accordance with the customs, traditions and ideals of. its race. Of all States a co-ordinate whole would be produced by means of a States Council corn- posed of equal representatives from each unit State (say three, giving a total of sixty). The council would deal with international affairs as they affected the interests of the United States. including the defence of the realm, it would be solely responsible, and would -levy necessary taxes equally on all States , pro rata of the population. As arbitrator' in national disputes it would. be backed by _public opinion: The great obstacle would be general disarma- ment-in the presence of suspicion and jealousy: For the defence of the Bmpire a' standing army of not more than a million should be main- tained, but. forehad still a useful purpose in man's affairs. As our interests were so deeply merged with those, of other nations, let us adopt those sound axioms of union and co- operation.

div.head: HUMAN NATURE.
div.p: HUMAN NATURE.

Mr. C. S. Woods introduced the negative Point of -view. They must look at this question not from the top of a New York sky-scraper, but from their own Market Gate. (Laughter). The brotherhood of man was an excellent idea, but the chief Objection, was that it was absolutelY contrary to human nature. At the outbreak of this war, for instance, it was said all in the country must join together against the com- mon enemy, and yet during the last season it was all the 'parties could do not •to fly at each other's throat, Whilst industrial strife had only been disposed of by - semi-martial methods. That was consolidation during our greatest crisis! After the' war, human nature would tend still more towards severance. Germany's enmity to us would.be greater. • In precedents, they had the United States of America (joined together, although it was to their own interests, only after a most bloody war) - and the German Empire. The scheme would break down because Ger- many would have to come into the United States of Europe. Her idea in the past • had been development and a place in the • sun, ,but no nation would be inclined to offer her territory, and therefore until sho got such an outlet her interests would be against those of the other nations. And if the Slates were united by force they would Come to grief at the outset. . •

Mr. Jas. Walsh said all Christian peoples were compelled to realise on what shifting sand European civilisation had been erected. • The. history of man was not simply the conquest of eternal power, and _their ideal was well pos- sible of accomplishment as. compared with already vast revolntionary changes. The old tendencies of hiunaw nature were incompatible with the death-dealing. inventions which the inhuman logic of science had produced. Antago- nistic; groups lire;tdy foreshadowed a closer union.

div.head: WOULD MAJORITIES RULE?
div.p: WOULD MAJORITIES RULE?

Mr. 11. Sherburn could not reconcile himself to the States' equal representation in Council when taxation fell per .head .on their popula- tions. They were expecting ti e principle of democracy. Again,'. Some countries had Jorge colonies. Would they be repreSentee America must also he considered: the European States would combine. at the expense of outside nations Would. the decisions of the Council be arrived at by majorities? And how would they be enforced in face of opposition? The success of the ..United States of Europe would be the death-knell of nationality; yet it would have to admit every cult and creed. Mr.' A. H. Eathbone pointed Out that men had combined from time to time to overcome difficulties, and the.canibination,now suggested was only a logical sequence. The admitted difficulties (such as reaction and stagnation), .their relative importance,. showed the mak- ing of sacrifices to overcome them well worth while. Of the advantages, commerce Other than in national competition would be chief. The even division over .areas of population and food supply could, also bp introduced; the revival of agriculture would stimulate all other indusL tries. The achievement of less -armaments would guarantee au ininAliate l'eduction in the cost of living. • Weights, measures and language might also be standardised.' Mr. F. Chadwick reminded the meeting that they were•debating not the advantages, ha the possibility of a United Europe. The conditions needed to bold lieoples together were national interests, common sentiments and language, customs and forms of government. None of these obtained in Europe. , Commercial ties were very insecure, and might be ignored when

national ,queAtions came to be dealt with. The war,, moreover, would have a definite bearing on the commercial, relationships. of all cont..; tries. There' was no commtnity. of .national or commercial.. interests, and the United States formed would be of Greater Britain. .

div.head: IS UNION NECESSARY?
div.p: IS UNION NECESSARY?

Mr. E. (1. Burgess asked not if the union was -possible, but if it was necessary. It was Only ''natural evolution; the day would come when continents would band themselVes to- gether. • Colonies could be included in the 'Union—in which, should -a large nation attempt to exploit a small one, the ,others would im- mediately-come to the latter's assistance., The Allies' success would make democratic nation- ality predominant. ,111 r. Tickell said that alliances and enteetes had, to some extent resulted in the war, but the. United States of Europe would be an amal- gamation of them. - The colonies could not•be thrust aside as suggested; they. would never agree to become vassals of States such as the Balkans. The suggested Union would be the death of the mighty. British Empire, and our inclusion was therefore impossible.

div.head: INTER-MARRIAGE
div.p: INTER-MARRIAGE

Mr. IL H. Taylor opined that a United Europe - meant -inter-marriage and inter- mixture amongst the States—which was pos- sible. It had always gone :on, and. should continue no .more or less with the organisatiOn of the States; • a nation. could always maintain its individuality. Competition was necessary to progression, but ,it would be fairer; " chief cause of emigration was the inability to obtain 'a decent hiring • in One's own country. If each were better governed, emigration from good stock would only 'take _place when the country had enough and to Spare. Ni. Robinson, said a most important draw- back was the ,Army and Navy—which - would .liave to 1)e. " pooled" were the States united. Then Great Britain would not be where She was to-day. Great Britain might _retain her Fleet and guarantee European trade all the 'world over, whilst the other nations provided an Army to guarantee British trade on the Continent. •

Mr. D. J. Dunn -maintained that second only to political institutions stood religion. The Union was possible because in tile fiekl of morality there was no real difference between the teachings of. all, religions. The ameliora- tive loss, of. .force could only be brought about by religious, influence. .

div.head: LEADERS REPLY.
div.p: LEADERS REPLY.

• . Mr. Woods, replying, said the Council had practically ignored the 'all-important . Army and Navy, whilst a 'statement made to the effect that it wOuld be better for us to Join with countries near our shored rather than with colonies far away showed a. loss of the sense of huMour—it was so absurd the colonies would be the first tiv object. They did not say the whole was not a beautiful scheme, but it was unworkable. A United -States of England would be better. . • . . _ _

Mr. .Nield• replied for the "affirmatives." Construction was much more difficult than destruction, and their ,scheme,,had .many magni- ficent points. They. would give the colonies to their inhabitants—the only passible course. The Union would not kill nationality, which could not be stamped out. He would remind them that in Peace-times they had, (apart from military preparations) filmast a United States of Europe, although with artifipiar barriers. Of .course, in giving each State equal represen- tation they were following their own govern- ment. • _ _
A .vote was .then. taken, The affirmative side having eight supporters, and the negative five.
CHAIRMAN'S VIEWS.

• The Chairman, having declared the vote, said the council's object WIIS !lased upon the demo- cratic principle lie (lid not think a United States would •help national individuality—the idea of which would be lost as soon as a small nation became part of one •large - scheme. In- dividuality was the most precious and vital thing in human life, and each nation sbculd have the opportunity to develop and foster its own life. The union policy would not only break down the artificial barriers, but later the natural barriers also; literature aml tradition would become lost. In ,a great race such as that of the Slays, many separate types, out- looks and traditions were preserved: in Ger- many, however, the single Prussian typo had kecome predominant. Again,,,.onr colonies' sense of attachment to us would .be gone, and our Empire would inevitably break tip into separate States. He did not think they were prepared to sacrifice the Empire even for so wonderful an ideal as the brotherhood of man. (Loud applause,)
THE CALL.

The Call rings loud and true To all, men sound and tit, Your country's 'call to you! • How shall you answer it? When' others do and dare Across the narrow sea, Can your own heart-declare, "They have no need of me?"

Listen once morel The Call , Beats in the throbbing drum, Bidding.not.one, but all, . Of Britain's manhood Come! Because our comrade .went, Freely and othing loth, Shall all his toil be spent , To keep you here' in sloth?

What use to shut your ears? . Your country claims her debt, And in the coming years. YouT heart shall judge you yet! Think of that future day And °hoe tho nobler Plan; That You may truly say, "At least I played the man!"

div.head: TAXATION OF BICYCLES.
div.p: TAXATION OF BICYCLES.

It is quite possible that some future Chau- cellor of the Exeliequer may resort to the taxa- tion of bicycles a.S.: a means of .raising, revenue' in time of difficulty. /The proposal has a cer- tain amount of logic in,its favour, but there its virtue ends. It is, of course, true that all 'other forms of pleasure vehicles are taxed, and if the same impartiality of treatment were extended', to the. bicycle .the. Government would doubtless gain very considerably in the matter of revenue. On the other hand, the bicycle is in an entirely different position from the carriage or motor car. The days when a cycle was a luxury have gone. Nowadays hundreds of thousands of people use their mounts for the purpose of going to and from their work, to say nothing of, the probably greater number of tradesmen's Car- riers. Under the existing law, carts; &c. used for business• purposes with the name Of the owner painted- thereon are exempt from taxa- tion. But in the case of the.cycle such a differ- entiation would be impossible, since very few machines are used solely for commercial pur- poses. The tax-free bicycle is now an accepted factor in everyday life, and any departure from the present system would probably be disastrous to the one who introduced it. Regarded from the, point of view of wear and tea', not the slightest case can be made out fbr the taxation of the pedal machine.

div.head: CYCLE ACCIDENTS.
div.p: CYCLE ACCIDENTS.

Some official reports and a good many Mem- bers of the general public are all too ready to attribute to the cyclist an exaggerated. respon- sibility for tho prevalence of street accidents in 1)3t% town and country, although it is in the former where the problem is most pressing. To give one example. Should a stretch of road be defective and a bad spill result the cyclist is generally blamed. A careless pedestrian step- ping from the pavement without due regard for approaching traffic is knocked down by a, cyclist, who apparently is again responsible, There is no further elaboration. Our present system of statistics seems to be defective in that it fails to give really satisfactory distinctions, with the result that the cyclist is usually blamed for every accident he happens to figure in at all. Accidents on the road which come under the notice of the police should be descibed min- utely, and placed under a suitable healing so as to differentiate between the various causes. In- cidentally. I 'should very much like to see a return giving accidents, by, and to cyclists, with an emphasis on the latter. Considering the small amount of space the cyclist takes up in comparison with motor 'buses, to say noth- ing of horse-drawn vehicles, it is decidedly un- fair for such a number of complaints tti be laid at his 'door..

div.head: CONE ADJUSTMENT.
div.p: CONE ADJUSTMENT.

• in cycling, as. in most , other pastimes, it is, the little ilvings Which matter. For example, there is nothing more destructive to smooth running than faulty 'cone adjustment or a few defective.bearings. Of course; a really .bad ease soon becomes obvious by its melancholy squeak, hut there is no need to wait for the audible stage.. If a bicycle has been in use for several seasons the bearings require a...thorough over- haul. Unscrew the various parts, -taking great care that law pt the elusive balls escape. Then each oneoan be wiped and examined. Bearings aro quite inexpensive, so any 'doubtful ones should 'be rejected without hezl,itation. and re- placed. Many amateur mechatkies find it /10 easy matter to restore the halls to their right- ful Places, but • if the hall races are well smeared with vaseline all difficulty vanishes. In -.,•rewing up the cones it is most desirable to avoid either •under or .over screwing. Both re- sult. in damage by unnecessary friction, and both can .be easily avoided by holding the cones in, position until the nuts are tightened.

div.head: STOPPING FOR A SENTRY.
div.p: STOPPING FOR A SENTRY.

At, Swansea Police Court a week or two ago a chauffeur was fined A:10 or two months' im- prisonment for not Stopping his car when called upon to do so by aientry. This is in. contraven- tion of regulation .53 'of the Defence of the Realm Act, 1914. The offence happened a little before midnight. The sentence was a just one, for the fir# duty of all drivers is to obey- the special regulations in force to-day. - There have been instancesin which a driver failing to pull up when challenged has been' shot. In certain dis- tricts 'especially one cannot he too careful to stop the moment one is told to do so, since the safety of the nation depends upon the proper carrying out of the special orders. For myself, I err on the safe side-1 have no wish to experi- ence the emotion of being fired on. Keep a strict look-out for sentries, and come to rest as cluiekly as possible after being called upon to stop. -

div.head: CARRYING SPARE WHEELS.
div.p: CARRYING SPARE WHEELS.

A few days ago I saw in a contemporary an excellent 'suggestion for the disposal of the spare wheel. 'ln effect it is that the upholstery of the back seat should be mounted Sufficiently far from the body panel so that the space be- tween could be utilised for the accommodation of the spare wheel. The upper portion of the upholstery could be hinged so as. to form a lid. This is about one of the best suggestions I have come across. It would prove a most convenient and practical *ay of carrying the spare wheel. That somO' 'such' accommodation is needed is certain. As it is now the spare wheel is ex- posed to the effects of rain and sun, both of which are bad for the rubber. „Again, to carry the wheel on the running board is unsightly—it takes away from the uniform appearance of the car. Lastly, it gives an increased weight to the off side, a. side which in any case is called upon to bear more weight than the near sido. It is 'a good suggestion, and I, for one, should like to see it adopted.

The Return of the Petticoat.

The petticoat is an essentially feminine gar- ment,,and its return adds a charm to this year's spring and summer outfits. It is capable of many varieties, and full advantage of this characteristic has been taken by manufacturers. The more useful garments are of soft satin in comparatively dark shades, finished at the hem with two or three closely-kilted frills. For afternoon wear, something smarter is required, and taffetas and glace silks of the softest tex- ture are used, matching the gowns in colour with which they are worn, and trimmed with delicious little ruffles and ruches; or these materials have accordion-pleated frills and fripperies of alr kinds and descriptions. Crepe de chene, trimmed with lace, is largely used for very beautiful underskirts in the most delicate shades. Some of these have a tiny pocket bn the left side, just big enough to hold a lace hand- kerchief. A specially attractive model opened at the side, showing the most fascinating little lace flounces. Hand-embroidered muslin petti- coats are much to the fore, as are also white petticoats of very fine cambric trimmed with hand or other embroidery.

The Striped Blouse. It is not often that a particular pattern in fabrics of all kinds is selected for the fashion- ing of shirts, blouses and neckwear. The striped blouse and shirt is just now the most striking development of that evergreen garment, and promises to remain in evidence for some time yet, although it has already had a con- siderable vogue. The stripes are broad, and equal in width, one is generally white, the other neutral or pale in shade. The light browns and greys are very effective, and biscuit, fawn and ecru are preferable to the more vivid mauves, pinks and sky blues. The pouch effect at the waist is noticeable in many of the newest designs. In simple white muslin or lawn shirts and blouses, hand embroidery plays a con- spicuous part, and the Irish hand-worked voile blouses are particularly handsome. They are fastened with crochet buttons and have collars and cuffs of voile edged with a narrow crochet lace. The dainty little garments are to be bought for a few shillings. Veilings are still in great request for blouses of a smarter descrip- tion, but simplicity is a characteristic of this season's models of all kinds.

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
Useful Information in Popular Language.

Boiling a Ham. • Improperly cooked pork is always dangerous because of the presence of a parasite or worm that occurs in the flesh of swine. The U.S. Federal Department ot Agriculture has fre- quently issued warnings to housewives that thorough cooking is necessary as the only safe- guard. Its recommendations may be boiled down to these rules: A, Iolb, ham should be boiled for three hours if placed in boiling water; if placed in cold water which requires one liour to come to a boil the ham should cook two hours and a half after toiling begins. The eighteen- minute-a-pound allowance should be followed in summer as well as in'winter if the meat is taken from cold storage and cooking is begun before it has had time to reach the ordinary house tem- perature.

Baby's Bath. This should be given every day softer the first week or so. The morning is the best time, as it begins to form a healthy habit which can be kept up with advantage throughout life. At night a sponge all over is enough. A bath should never be given directly after food, but the child should have its bottle immediately after the completion of its dressing. 'she food should be prepared beforehand, so that it only needs warming. The temperature must always be taken with a thermometer and never be tested simply by the hand. If there is no ther- mometer the nurse's elbow will fairly accurately gauge the heat of the water. During the first month this should never be below 100 deg. F. At the end of the second month it may be low- ered to 98 deg. F., and later, at the age of seven months, to 90 (leg. A cold bath should never be given to a child. Children have little animal heat, and cannot afford to lose it in this way. The fingers and toes often turn blue, and the circulation is not restored for some hours after immersion. The face and head should be care- fully washed and dried while the body is warmly wrapped in a towel. The child is then quickly soaped all over and put into the water. The first few baths should not last longer than two or three minutes, though later they may be pro- longed from three to five minutes. The child is then quickly lifted out of the water, placed in a warm Turkish towel, and Covered all over.

Drying should be done by dabbing, never by rubbing, or the skin is apt to be chafed, and this leads to red and sore patches. After a careful and thorough qrying the body should be pow- dered all over, incept the face, especially in all the crevices and folds of the skin and joints. No powder should ever be put on to a wet skin; it only cakes and does harm. Windows should be closed and all draughts avoided during the bath and dressing of baby.—Celina Fox, M.D.
the cream and turn it slowly round and round. This is the way old-fashioned folk—who have not got a churn—still made butter in Devonshire.

Tommy would run to the dairy door and peep in; and when he saw Granny settled at her work he would slip fit' and begin to toss a bit of bread in the air and catch it again. "Take care, Tommy!" Granny would cry in a, warning voice. "That ball of yours will be doing some mischief presently." And even as She spoke down it would fall into the tub of cream.
"Oh, you careless child 1" Granny would then cry, fishing out the bread—with its rich coating of cream. "Run away this minute, and do not come hindering me at my work."

Tommy would obey with a grin, and gobble up his bread-and-cream with great satisfaction as soon as he was out of sight. It was rather naughty, was it not? But I think Granny was not quite so much deceived as she pretended to be. She knew a bit of fresh cream was nice and wholesome for the boy; and if he liked to play a little game to get it—why, per- haps Granny enjoyed a pretending game as much as he (lid!

Mother tiaid she spoiled Tommy, but he was a good boy on the whole, and loved both his mother and his granny very dearly. He would not have grieved them by doing anything that was really forbidden, but lw could not help seeing that they were more amused than vexed at his trick, and he kept on playing it until he went away to school and learned more manly ways of having fun.

div.head: WAR ANP NEW SCHOOLS. Proposal To Hold Up Building Operations.
div.p: WAR ANP NEW SCHOOLS. Proposal To Hold Up Building Operations.

The question of "holding up" the building of a new school in consequence of the war, was debated at the last meeting of the War- rington Education Committee which was pre- sided over by Councillor H. Roberts, newly 're- elected chairman of that body for the ensuing twelve-month.

The discussion arose out of a minute pre- sented by the Sites and Buildings Sub-com- mittee, to the following effect: "The archi- tects and the director NV .re instructed to approach the contractor for the erection of the Parr-street Council School with a view to the temporary cessation of further building opera- tions, and to request the contractor to furnish the comntittee with his proposals in the matter." _

Mr. R. T. Fairclough, the eiairman of the sub-committee concerned, moved the adoption of the minute and, in doing so, said it was passed in pursuance of a recommendation which had come down from London urging that no further expenditure than that which was absolutely necessary should be incurred in these times of war.

div.head: "A STANDING DISGRACE TO THE TOWN.-
div.p: "A STANDING DISGRACE TO THE TOWN.-

Mr. Plinston desired to know a little more about the committee's proposal. Whilst agreeing that if was true that powers of borrow- ing money for the purpose of erecting additional schools, or anything of that nature, were to be stopped, he could not help thinking that the old School of Industry in Smith-street, which it was intended to replace, could not be more ill. adapted to the purpose. for which it was in- tended. In the case of other smools on which it had been proposed to spend money, the problem had simply been one of extra accommo- dation, or something of that sort; but in this case it was a matter of a building to take the place of one that was entirely unfitted for educational purposes; one that was a standing disgrace to the town of Warrington BY ORDER OF THE TREASURY.

The Director of Education (Mr. J. Moore Murray) said that the position was that the Treasury had issued an order that, unless a loan had been raised since March 12th, all work was to be stopped, subject to their re-consideration and decision as to whether the work should go on or not; they were going to decide as to the necessity of all public work before allowing it to go on. It was a Very difficult matter and, a very complicated one, because it did not concern one contract alone, ana the resolution of the Sites and Buildings Sub-committee was in the nature of a pre- liminary to se cl what the exact 'position was, and whether they could state a good case to the Local Government Board to allow them to go on. Apart from the question of the building as such, there was the question of employment. If those works were stopped it might necessitate some, at least,- of the workmen being kept by
:he town. BUILDING OF SCHOOLS A SECONDARY CONSI DEBAT, ON..

Councillor Pemberton said he would supp6rt the minute, because, he thought, that under the circumstances, the Government, in the present extraordinary Circumstances. were the hest judges. Some members did not appear to understand the position; indeed, the want of understanding of a great many people in this country was appalling. The building of schools was a secondary consideration altogether to the tremendous issues at stake.

Mr. Upson said he would like to know whether the Board of Education had been in- formed as to the action of the Local 'llovern- meat Board. The Board of Education had imposed fines on the committee because they had not provided school accommodation, and now another department stepped in and said, in effect, "You must not provide this additional accommodation." If this proposed new building was not proceeded with, how did the committee stand in regard to the matter of fines?

div.head: NO MORE FINES UNTIL AFTER THE . WAR.
div.p: NO MORE FINES UNTIL AFTER THE . WAR.

The Director replied that he did not think the Board of Education would refund the fines already paid, but, in regard to the future, they would put on no more fines of. a like nature until after the War.
The Chairman said that the Sites and Build-

ings Sub-committee were simply carrying out what amounted to an instruction from the Local Government Board, in approaching the contractor to see on what terms, if any, the contractor would be prepared to suspend his present contract. They woulct then report to the Education Committee, who could consider the whole position with a view to making such representations as they might think desirable. They all appreciated very keenly indeed, the extraordinary position in which they were placed by present circumstances, and it would not be either prudent or businesslike to pre- sent to the authorities above any part of their case by itself. They must present a whole and complete case to the Board of Education and then await their decision, and that was a matter, of course, which would have first to be discussed and settled by the committee, as a whole, before any representations were made. The committee's minutes were then adopted.

div.head: HELP FOR THE WOMEN.
div.p: HELP FOR THE WOMEN.

The woman at home, deep in housekeeping duties and the cares of motherhood, needs an occasional help to better tier health. The demands upon a mother's strength are many and severe; her own health trials and her chil- dren's welfare exact heavy tolls, while hurried meals, broken rest and much indoor living tend to weaken her constitution. No wonder that the woman at home is often indisposed through weakness, sick headache, backache and nervous troubles; indeed, many have grown to accept these visitations at fre- quent intervals as "motherhood's lot." But many and varied as her health troubles are, the cause is simple and the cure near at hand When well, it is the woman's good blood that keeps her well; when ill, she must make her blood rich to renew her health; and the nursing mother—more than any „,other wohian in the world—needs rich blood and plenty of it. div.head: WAR AND WORKERS.
div.p: WAR AND WORKERS.
Rural District Council Vote Their Men A Good Bonus,

The Warrington Rural District Council, at their monthly meeting on Wednesday, decided to grant a war bonus to all their employes earn- ing less than 30s. per week, the employes having petitioned for a temporary rise in view of the greatly increased cost of living. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell proposed that a bonus of 2s. per week be voted the men, irrespective of whether they were married or single, Mr. a. Mather dennitred that it did Pot cost: a single man so much to keep himself as it cost a married man to keep a wife and family. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell replied that single men frequently had 'a mother to keep. The reverend gentleman's proposition found no seconder, but, instead, Mr. Packhonse pro- posed that a bonus of 3s. per week be granted, during the period of the war, to all married employes earning less than 30s, per week, ams one of Is. kl. ,to all single employes receiving similar waged. M ;Weil that he was giving the lower paid among his own men Is, a week extra during the war. Mr. J. Ball opined that, it was very easy to clap in a rise during the war, but they might find it difficult to take it .off when peace times came again.

The - Vice-Chairman (Mr. P. Longton) seconded Mr. Backhouse's proosal, which was eventually carried unanimously, it being further decided that the ' bonus should be retrospective, as from the Arst pay day in IKarch,

div.head: WOMAN'S WORLD.
div.p: WOMAN'S WORLD.

interesting employment was, until about twenty yoars ago, almost entirely in the hands of French women, who were highly skilled in the art, but since then more ,attention has been given to lace-mending by homeworkers in this country. At present the market is by no means overcrowded, although there may be less to do on account of the war. It is work suited to the refined woman of gentle birth, as it can be done at home, but training is an essential to success.

Germans Wear English Waterproofs. The German women, from the Empress down- wards, are said to hate the English even more than do the men. But they have no objection to wear British-made goods when they can get them. A noted London maker of waterproofs both for men and wometi, had a well-stocked branch at Lille, and when the Germans took possession of that town they raided the shop. The German officers gladly availed themselves of the opportunity of providing themselves gratuitously with rainproof coats of world-wide celebrity. Their wives and other feminine be- longings as eagerly divided their share of the spoils, with the result that on a wet day the Germans and their women folk relatives and visitors in Lille, sally forth clad in waterproofs of British manufacture. A Million New Dresses

A visit to the West-end shops of London would lead to the conclusion that the demand for new clothes of all descriptions is quite normal. It has been computed that at least a million new costumes and gowns will be bought in London alone this spring, and these will all be modelled on the new lines, or suggest the new silhouette, if they do not embody it. The eye will therefore soon be quite accustomed to the new outline. Tailors start their modes in the spring, and French designers, in spite of the war, have been quite as active as usual. Military styles are very pronounced in Paris. In London this influence is perceptible chiefly in details, such as the cut of certain coats, the use of silk braid in close horizontal formation, on basques, and on the tops of skirts, and in the flatness that characterises the region of the hips. Capes, many of a military type, will be worn all the summer, made of all kinds of light fabrics, such as shantung, alpacas, the latter more especially, in cream shades, and all descriptions of dust-coat fabrics.

div.head: CHAT and GOSSIP.
div.p: CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MARJORIE.

The Royal Family. The King and Queen, who early set an example to the nation in agreeing to banish all alcoholic beverage from the Royal Hojisehold, look well and bright, whenever they appear in public. They are as busy as ever, and there is no doubt that their example has been, and will continue to be an inspiration to all classes, whilst Queen Alexandra and Princess Victoria are equally tireless in aiding good works of all kinds. Queen Mary is most tactful in express- ing her sympathy with those of her friends who have been bereaved of beloved relatives by the war, forced upon Europe by the eldest grand- son of Queen Victoria. Ea tprprising Glasgow. Several women tram-conductors have been appointed by the Glasgow Corporation, whose male employes, to the number of one thousand, have joined the forces. It has been found very difficult to maintain the services' even when the remaining men worked seven days a week— hence the innovation.. The women appointed have been chosen fro& the clerical staff, and have been provided with a neat uniform con- sisting of a blue coat and skirt, with yellow facings, and a distinctive cap. Should the experiment continue to give satisfaction, more women will be employed. They work the same number of hours per week as the men, and it is satisfactory to be able to state that in this in- stance they receive the same pay..

Women.

Lace is one of the most fascinating items of a woman's dress, and the mending, restoring and washing of it may be recommended as a remunerative feminine occupation. The girl or woman who decides to take up this wokk must posses ,goods eyesight, patience, and artistic instinct, and some knowledge of drawing. This

div.head: HOME NOTES.
div.p: HOME NOTES.
Profitable Recipes and Useful Suguestions.
No stale pieces of bread should be wasted. By sprinkling these with a little milk and heat- ing for five or ten minutes in a quick oven they acquire the flavour and tazality of biscuits.

Dripping Pudding. Rub 2oz. of dripping and a pinch of salt into half a pound of flour. Add one teaspoonful of baking powder. Mix into a paste with milk or water. Steam (or boil in a floured cloth) for two hours. Serve with treacle. To Cook Peas, Beans, or Lentils.

They must be soaked overnight and will then take about two hours boiling. No salt must be added till they are cooked, or they will not get soft. As they contain no fat, some fat bacon or dripping, or a suet pudding, should form part of the meal.

Plain Suet Pudding. Half a pound of suet, threequarters of a pound of flour. A little salt and cold water. The pudding is much improved if 12oz. of flour and 3oz. or stale bread-crumbs are used instead of all flour. Shred the suet finely, mix it with the flour and salt, and enough water to form a stiff paste. Tie it in a floured cloth, and place it in• boiling water. Boil quickly for an hour and a quarter. If you have currants stir them in. • Baked Plaice.

Well wash a large fresh plaice, well scraping away the black skin near the head. Dry the fish well, and rub it over with a little flour mixed with pepper and salt. Put a generous lump of dripping or butter in a baking-sheet. When quite boiling hot dip the.fish in on both sides, with a good covering of finely-chopped parsley, onions, chervil, a little lenion peel, and just a few gratings ,of nutmeg. Bake the fish in a good hot oven for three-quarters of an hour, basting it frequently. Put it carefully on to a hot dish, pour the sauce .from the pan over the fish, and serve with a dish of nicely- mashed potatoes.

Blanquette of Chicken. To make any chicken left .over into a blan- quette, cut it into small pieces after removing the skin. Put three tablespoonfuls of butter in a frying-pan, stir in a tablespoonful of flour:, and then a tablespoonful of the stock in which the chicken was cooked; Add salt and white pepper to season the gravy, and finally a cupful of rich milk or of half cream and half milk. Put in the pieces of chicken. Add the yolks of two eggs beaten with a little of the hot gravy. Dish the chicken in a pyramidal form, and pour the hot sauce over and around it, and arrange a border of rice around the whole.

Every -day a Japanese woman of the poorer classes has to wash rice for the needs of her family. her sleeves are fastened up out of her way by means of a long band, which is kept for the purpose, and always used when any work is being done. The comb. stuck at the side of her head is for use as well as for orna- ment, being taken for a dressing-comb when required. By a Woman Hater. Cold cash covers a multitude of freckles. A pound box of candy will win a girl quicker than a 300-line poem. The man who trusts to luck and women is apt to get the short end of it. The society belle isn't satisfied until she is given an engagement ring. A wise man never tells a girl that she is pretty in the presence of her rival. Wives should remember that they married for worse as well as for better and act accord- ingly.

Heart Disease. A gentleman riding in a railroad train was impressed with two passengers, one a pretty, delicate-appearing young lady and the other a plain-faced maid. While the mistress was at dinner the gentleman remarked to the maid in a tone of great sympathy: "Your young lady seems very ill." "Yet, sir; she suffers sadly." "Consumption, I should fear?" "No, sir; I am sorry to say it is of the heart." "Dear me! Aneurism?" "Oh, no, sir! It is only a lieutenant in the navy."
Unkindness. If we will remember unkindnesses it is well to begin with own own. Those we have received are not usually one-sided, and the bitter words

whose memory stings were seldom entirely with- out provocation. This, at least, is true: If, on examining our animosities and resentments, we find ourselves wholly blameless, it will at once become easy to forgive. The person hardest to pardon is the one whom we have wronged, and the breach most difficult to heal is the ont where we are unwilling to face the consciousness that half the guilt was our own.—" Great Thoughts." •
