EVERYONE HAS WORK TO DO.

Far away in the Pacific Ocean, where the great waves dash against the coral reefs, a coral polyp lived in a little home beneath the blue waters. A sad life it was for the little creature just now, for it was filled with grief at its small part in the world. "Of what use am I?" it would cry mourn- fully. "What work do I do? Should Ibe missed if I were gone? Would my place be empty?" "My dear," was the advice of a wise old polyp who lived hard by, "you are too young to understand these things; attend to what is before you, and do not waste time in repinings." But the little one, although he listened duti- fully and tried to comfort himself with this counsel, soon felt the old unsatisfied feelings return.

" Ah, if I could but know that I am not quite idle and useless in the world! But what can a little weak thing like me do?" But the waves rolled on and the sea-weeds waved their graceful fronds, and the polyp found no answer to comfort him. But one day, as he was making his sad complaint, a little fish with shining scales came swimming by. "Little polyp," said he, "why are you un- happy? It is because you are so small that you cannot understand great things; but I will tell you what I know and what others have told me to comfort you. Up,above the water, in the air as it is called, there are solid lands built up -tvtirelv by such little things as you—islands .where man can live and make a home. -Is this nothing? Do you not see that, though small yourselves, yau are parts of a great whole?" Then the fish swam away through the blue water; and, as the last shimmer of green and silver vanished, the polyp gave a sigh of con- tent and settled down peacefully in its little home, to clo its quiet work.

Own Bottles.

A fourteen-year-old boy was brought before, the Borough magistrates, sitting as a Child- ren's Court on Saturday, charged with stealing two bottles, valued at 25., the property of the landlady of the Feathers Hotel, Bridge-street. The Chief Constable told the Bench that for some months -past bottles had been missed from the yard at the rear of. the Feathers Hotel. Arrangements were made to keep a watch, and at about 9.45 the previous Saturday night the boy was seen to enter the yard and take two bottles.. He was caught and he then admitted that he hail two other bottles a week or so before. He said that his idea was to take the bottles round to the liar in front of the hotel and get a penny on each of them. After his capture the boy was kept at the Police Station all night. The police sent up to his house for the father. He was not at home at first and when he did arrive he was in a beastly drunken ati4e. With his father behaving like that, it was not to be ,wondered at that the boy should do as he had done. The father told the Bench that he could not make out why the boy should want to steal. the bottles, as he had a good home and plenty of money. As to himself, he could not have been so very drunk, because he landed home all right and he had never been in trouble. The Chief Constable said that whilst the boy had never previously been convicted, he had, nevertheless, been brought down to the Police Station charged with stealing a couple of pies. The Bench imposed a fine of 10s.

BENCH PASS MAXIMUM SENTENCE.

A young man named John Grounds, whose address was given as 261, Winwick-road, was before the Warrington Borough Bench on Sat- urday, charged with stealing scrap iron, leather, copper, and No. 1 cloth. The scrap iron—to the weight of 191 b. and of the value of £1 Bs. 9d.—he took from. Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' Dallam Forge, the. leather—to the weight of 53.11). and of the value, of ,t4— from Hutchings, Ltd., and the copper and the No. 1 cloth-41b. of the former and live yards of the latter, and of the total value of 19s. 6d.— from the St. Helens Cable Company. He was further charged with assaulting P.O Clarke in Dallam-lane on Friday, March 26th.

div.head: How He Was Caught.
div.p: How He Was Caught.

Mr. T. S. Steel prosecuted and said that at 3.15 on the afternoon of Friday, March 26th, P.C. Clarke was near the Dallam-lane crossings when he saw • the prisoner coining along with a brown paper parcel on his shoulder. The constable stopped hint and asked him what he had got. He replied: " Only some light scrap I picked out of the rubbish heap at Longford." The constable, however, was doubtful and he took hold of the man by the collar with one hand, whilst with the other he attempted to open the parcel. Whilst he was doing this the prisoner struck him a violent blow on the jaw, which caused the constable to loose his hold. The prisoner then ran away. On examin- ation the parcel—a box wrapped in brown paper—which the prisoner had been carrying, was found to contain scrap iron on the top and a large quantity of brass underneath. The constable knew tile prisoner and he went down to 204, Winwick-road, and, on searching the house, found tin( other stuff referred to in the charges, as well as some glue which the pri- soner subsequently admitted having stolen. from Messrs. Richmond's works at Grappen- hall.

div.head: Very Dangerous Man
div.p: A Very Dangerous Man

Prisoner, added the speaker, was a very dangerous man.. He went round from works to works obtaining employment, and having got a job he only, stayed in it a few days. Having got a job, of course, he had the run of the works, and he utilised his time to see what he could steal. He had repeatedly stolen fellow- workers' meals. He worked at Hutching's for about .a fortnight, at the St. Helens Cable Co.'s works for two days, and at Messrs. Guest Bros. for about a week. He was discharged from the employment of the Cable Co: because he was found asleep, and whilst at Messrs. Guest a watch and a man's waistcoat were missed. The watch and the waistcoat were found hidden at the top of the warehouse, and the prisoner was evidently waiting for an opportunity of taking them away without being seen. Wheu taxed with, the theft the prisoner admitted it, but the owner did not care to prosecute and the prisoner was merely discharged from his work.

div.head: Asleep in a Furnace Shed When Arrested.
div.p: Asleep in a Furnace Shed When Arrested.

- . When arrested prisoner was found asleep in a furnace shed at Messrs. Monks, Hall and Company's works. He gave his name as Brown, and said that he came, from Earlestown, but when he was told that his name was Grounds he admitted it. In reply to the first charge he said : "I did steal it, but did not think the weight was as much as you say." To the second charge, he made answer "Yes, I did," and to the fourth- "That's right," but he would not admit the assault on the constable, saying, "I struggled to get lawßy from him." Mr. Steel added that it seemed as if the man could not keep his hands. from picking and stealing; if a thing was ,lying about loose lie must have his hands on it, and if it was not loose he very soon made it loose. (Laughter.) -As the prisoner admitted the thefts, only evidence as to the assault, which he denied, was called.

div.head: " ANGEL " CABMAN. Assaulted By Drunken Man Whilst Sitting On Box.
div.p: THE " ANGEL " CABMAN. Assaulted By Drunken Man Whilst Sitting On Box.

Andrew McLoughlin, labourer, of no settled abode, was charged at Monday's Court with having been drunk and disorderly in Crown- street, on Saturday; with assaulting George Douthwaite, cabman; and with doing damage to the extent of 4s. 6d. to his whip.—lle ad- mitted the, first charge, but denied the others.

div.head: Deed Described
div.p: Deed Described

George Donthwaite, of 56,• Academy-street, and employed by Mr. Edward Connor, said that at 8.15 on Saturday evening he was on the box of his call in Crown-street when pri- soner suddenly 'wiled across the street, got hold of the horse by the reins, and "nearly threw it down." Be. next soiled him by the legs and tried to pull 'him off. Finding he could not move him, however, lie took hold of the whip, struck at him with it, and broke it. An assistant came from the cab stand and they helped a constable to take McLoughlin into custody. On the way to the Police Sta- tion prisoner was very violent and used very had language. P.C. Ford said that, having received a com- plaint, he went and found "NlcLoughlin stand- ing by the wall. The man said he had done nothing and could prove it. lie was very drunk, and became violent—using filthy lan- guage. Prisoner's Protest.
Prisoner: I wasn't that very drunk when I came in here.

The- Chief Constable: This man was in 6101 a beastly, filthy condition of drunkenness when he .came in that I. ordered hi-in to be put in the cells. Ile was quite incapable of under- 4anding anything that was taking place.—The Chief Constable added that the. Man was a perfeet pest. Since 1907 he had 'appeared be- fore- the Court twelve times—mostly for drunk and disorderly behaviour, and drunkenness. He came from Golborne, but belonged to the West of Ireland. That was where he ought to be. He treated like that a man who was sitting on his cab doing, nothing.

div.head: What Was Not Prisoner's Fault.
div.p: What Was Not Prisoner's Fault.
Prisoner: I don't think so! Cabmen is not all angels. (Laughter.) ' The Chief Constable: I know; but be was an angel on this occasion. Prisoner: I haven't been up since Christmas.
Mr. Nicholls: It hasn't been your fault ! McLoughlin was fined 21s. or a month. He also had to pay 4s. 6d. for damage done to the cabby's irhip.

Warrington's second holiday engagement was With the Rochdale Hornets and it ended in defeat by 6 points to nil. The match was I Played at Rochdale on Saturday and was wit- Xessed by a goodly-sized crowd, who took advantage of the last opportunity that will- be vouchsafed- to °them this season of seeing their favourites play at home, .. all , the outstanding lixtures,On the Hornets' card' being Of the. away _variety. The defeat of Warrington 'enabled the Rochdale men to complete a record un-, Daralleled in the history' of their club, inas-. Aluch as it enables them, to boast that they have not been beaten at home, this season. The achievement of this record was something on which the Hornets had set their hearts, and it, has to.be confessed that Warrington were never, 4 serious menace to their ambition. With the exception of Jolley, who played a capital game, t,he backs were a very moderate lot. • Beaten -1-111 the forwards, Young rarely got the •bail among his backs, and what few chances came their way were not ' made the most of: :

VISITORS OUTCLASSED ALL. THE TIME. At no time did Warrington shape like a inning'team, and they were rather fortunate 11 having been beaten by so small a margin, for the score of 6-0 by no means represented t,he real superiority of the Rochdale men as oisclosed on the day's play. The Wilderspeol lads Were forced on the defensive in the first 41% minutes, and it was rarely that .they were out of their own half. Certain it is that they never had a good chance of scoring. Harassed nearly, all the while, they Yet put up a good 4efonee in the first half, and when the interval was called the score sheet was of virgin white- ness, a fact for which Jolley was mainly re- He played a dashing game and urought off more than one daring save. More- over, he was quite übiquitous, and but for his sterling work it would have been a very dif- ferent tale that the scorer had to tell.

HOME TEAM'S STREAKS OF BAD LUCK. Warrington as was their play in the first half, 7arrington showed even • more disappointing I°llll in the second moiety, whilst on the other 'land the Hornets imparted even more clash ,and vigour into. their play, though they were rustantly .running up against streaks of bad 21ch- Time and again they got within a pace two of the line, only to .find something or uther go wrong—either the player slipped 'and tueas ured his length on the greensward. or he `',l4ol)Ped the leather at the critical moment. !t'uMetimes, of course, Jolley and his coadjutors vel'e responsible for "the slip 'twixt the cu ;tad the lip," so to speak, but in quite a um- ofn- (4)" instances Warrington's escape was more ~110 to good luck than to judgment. Another slice .ef- luck Warrington, for it was subsequently dis- sered that the referee had accidentally sig- '4l, led half-time five inintites., too. early. That ;44 only one of the instances in which the - ws fought on the losing side.

In the second half the early stages were noticeable for. a. great •effort by :Young, who, defeating all opposition, passed across to Brad- shaw, who scored a grand try, which Jolley failed to augment. •Batley warmed to the game and Grandidge scored a penalty goal for them. A combined raid, which was ill-judged by the Warrington defence, • ended in Lockwood scor- ing their first try, Grandidge failing badly at goal. In a long passage of even play War- rington maintained the upper hand and Cox scored a fourth try, which Jolley, again failed to angment. •, The final 'score read :---War- rington, 1 goal 4 tries (11. points); Batley, 1 goal try (5 points). THE PLAY.

_ Batley suffered by a re-shuffling of their team at the last moment, and Warrington were strengthened by the inclusion_ of ''Bombardier Chesters. The home. tot showed an all-round superiority. It was clearly jolley's day out, however, and his efforts at the aggressive come near to his scoring tries on three occasions. As a set-off he missed all his chances to score goals except the first, although the positions were mostly 'easy ones. Tranter did not give of his best and, he ,made, Very,bad%use of passes galore. The Other threeqUarters did remark- ably well, Bradshaw giving . many exhibitions of his old-time speed and judgment. Laws and -Young did yeoman service at half-back. The forwards were.a:Solid body of .triers, and, as, the .score showed, Cox was -there when he was wanted. The visitors played .a consistent and attrac- tive game, but they found Warrington just too good, for them. - .

div.head: AA-ARRINGTON AGAIN UNLUCKY. llan Collar The Points In The Last Home Match.
div.p: AA-ARRINGTON AGAIN UNLUCKY. llan Collar The Points In The Last Home Match.

Warrington experienced something like their usual hick, _which is bad luck, in their last home Match of the season, which was played at Wilderspool on - Tuesday evening, in the presence of getting on for 3,000 spectators, Wigan being their. opponents. The Meeting of the teams had stood postponed owing to the Strike indulged in by the Wigan • player S: in January last. The Warrington team was at full strength, but it was noticed that Charles Seeling and Seddon were missing from the Wigan ranks, the conelusion to be drawn being that they were resting . in preparation for Wigan's big cup-tie semi-final with Hudders-. field this afternoon.

div.head: HOME TEAM'S HARD LINES
div.p: HOME TEAM'S HARD LINES

Throughout the game bad luck dogged the Warrington men. They played the more at- tractive football, they were the more .enter- prising, and they did the bulk of the attack- ing, and yet the points were not for them. The first score fell to Warrington, Cox showing ,a fine turn of speed and getting over for a good try, which Jolley failed to convert. The scorer was not, troubled again during the first half, and they crossed over three points to the good, Wigan's score-sheet being blank. Judged on their 'play, Warrington should have .had a more 'commanding lead at this juncture, but their luck was "(lead out," for with Chesters hurt, . and Brookes largely incapacitated, they were to all intents and purposes reduced to an eleven-men side.. But, still, they struggled on gamely, and though they were frequently to be found attacking, they only managed to add a penalty goal, per. Jolley, to their score, whilst Wigan 'responded with two goals and - three tries, the, game therefore ending :—Wigan, 13 points; Warrington, 5 points.

div.head: PHAIE FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: PHAIE FOR WARRINGTON.
The Home Forwards Dominated The
Come.

, "Observer," of the "Daily Dispatch," ,has some fine things to say of the display made by Warrington, which we reproduce As the opinion. of an impartial outside critic.. To begin with, he says that four matches in five days had left Wizan leg weary .and that they were for- tunate ru win. As to being leg weary, we may, say that Warrington, too, had filled 'engage- ments through the. holidays. Wigan, says the critic, were indeed leg weary and had they been defeated it would have been ..no more than :.they' deserved. . They were from start to -finish the inferior -side, .and it was remarkable how Warrington missed scoring on at least five occasions.

div.head: Splendid Forwards.
div.p: Splendid Forwards.

The home forwards were indeed in aggressive mood, and besides holding the advantage in the scrummages they,.,controlle4 the hall splen- didly. in .the. loose, Wigan .:seemed content to keep them at'hay. Still, they could not:pre- vent them dribbling the ball over, their line On 'seven occasions, and on each it beat Ahem for pace and rolled dead. It was extremely hard luck, and the team would have got no more than they deserved had they held a lead of at least a dozen points at the interval. As it was, their only advantage was a try, and with a couple of players crocked in the second half, Wigan went ahead and won by 13 points to five.

div.head: Advice fcr Spectators.
div.p: Advice fcr Spectators.

While one sympathises with the Warrington supporters at their disappointment, it cannot be said that they enhanced their reputation, as sportsmen. It is bad, policy .to barrack a referee,. even if :they • his decisions are bad. Personally, I thought that Mr. May con- trolled the game exceedingly. well, and there was not a single fault in any of the decisions he gave. Some of the Warrington spectators would do well to study the rules a „little more,. and besides getting to know what, constitutes a knock-on, also what is offside play. They were also at fault in their idea of what constitutes a legitimate tackle, and also :ob- struction. partisanship serves no useful pur- pose,:and when a referee is doing his duty he is entitled to be treated with respect. .

div.head: About the Players.
div.p: About the Players.

Without doubt the Warrington forwards were the dominating factor, aid they kept up a won- derful pace from start totnish. There was not a weak man among the six, though Chesters, Cox and W. Cunliffe stood out Prominently with rare scrummaging, delithtful work in the loose, and deadly tackling. - Dainteth and Young got through a tremendous amount of work at half- back, while Laws and Brookes were the pick ,of, the threequarters. Jolley, at full-back, gave a polished display, and was well ahead of Price, who, however, it is only fair to say, was in an. unaccustomed position, and has not played foot- ball for some considerable time. Bth Curwen 1-a Jenkins were weak in the, three-quarter line, and there was such slackness that Hayward w:l4 brought from the forwards as an extra throc-quarter. Thomas was the better of the half-backs, while .Francis, Cold- rick and Richards did best among the forwards. It was, however, a display unworthy of Wigan, though there is4some excuse in the light of the great Cup-tie with Huddersfield on Saturday.

div.head: S;i. Helens To Wet Rochdale At Wilderspool.
div.p: S;i. Helens To Wet Rochdale At Wilderspool.

It is expected that-there will be a big crowd at Wilderspool this afternoon, when St. Helens and Rochdale Hornets appear in the semi-final of the Northern Union Cup. The Committee and Honorary Secretary (Mr. T. P. Bradshaw) have made every arrangement both for the comfort of the spectators and the convenience of the players. A special train is running from Rochdale, and we bear that every vehicle has been requisitioned to bring St. Helens admirers to the scene of the fray. All will pay, including soldiers and sailors, by order of the Northern Union. THE TEEMS
will be selected from the following :
St. Helens.

Full-back.-11. Roberts. Threequarter-backs.—T. Barton, J. Flanagan, 0. Stirrup, T. White and H. Oreenall. .;Hall-backs.—M..Creevey and F. Trenwith. • Forwards.--:41.. Heaton, S. Daniels, W. Jack- son, W. Myers, G. Farrimond, J. Durkin, J. Shalleross, and J. A. Fisher.

div.head: Rochdale Hornets.
div.p: Rochdale Hornets.

Full-back.—M. English. Threequarter-backs.—C. Mole, J. Corsi, G. A. Prudence (captaio and J. W. Fairhurst. Bralf-backs.—R. Schofield and E. W. Jones. Forwards.—C. Ashton, J. Fitzsimmons, V. B. Slade, S. Carter, W. Ashworth, J. Bowers .and S. D. Webb. _ _
The appointed officials are :—Referee, Mr. 'F. Renton (ifunslet) ; toAch-judges, Messrs. J. Dutton (Warrington) ankl T. Kiley (Leigh).
WIGAN v. WARRINGTON.

Wigan are engaged, to-day in the other semi- final of the 'cup, against Huddersfield, and, so are unable to receive .Warrington for the .Ye- turn match at Wigan. The local lads will, however, play at Wigan on Monday evening, kick-off at 5.30.

div.head: WARRINGTiIi Only a Trifling Increase in the
div.p: WARRINGTiIi Only a Trifling Increase in the
County Precept. ADDITION TO THE UNION.

The laSt meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians for the financial year 1914-15, was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning, when Mr. A. J. Jolley (chairman) presided over a small attendance of members. TOYS FOR THE KIDDIES.

It was reported that a big gift of toys for the children in the Cottage Homes had been received from Lady Greenall. Mrs. Hall and Mr. Shaw had also sent Presents of books, and on Good Friday Mr. E. L. Bent forwarded hot cross buns for. the youngsters, whilst Messrs. Greening's employes had given a large consign- ment of Easter eggs. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: The Guardians do .not come in for any of the eggs, do they? A. Member: No eggs for them, except rotten ones at election times. (Laughter.) • It was decided to send letters of thanks to the, gift-givers. . THE BOARD'S PRIVILEGE. '

The Clerk (Mr. A. -Bottowley) reported:shat the amount required under the county 'precept' this half-year was £14,264 3s. , That .was more than in the Corresponding half of last year; but was only an increase of about £2B over last half-year's call..

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: There is something' like a 10 per cent. increase over the cerrespond- ing period of last year. The Clerk: The amount required in the corre- sponding period of last year was-t 13,399 is. 3d.,. and last half-year it was 04,236 gs. sd. In answer to a member, the Clerk said that the Guardians had nothing to do with their precept except pay it. (Laughter.) The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: That is the bitter part of it. We have to pay and say nothing. Mr. Shaw: It's the Englishman's privilege. :(Renewed laughter.) The Clerk reported the receipt of a letter from the Local Government Board with regard to the borrowing of money by local authorities at the present juncture, and the importance of

_ restrictions in that direction owing to the war. The Board, Mr. Bottomley added, would have to borrow money for furnishing the new block, which is to .he used as a temporary -hospital for sick and -wounded soldiers.. Seeing the purpose ,for which the building was going to be first 'utilised. he thought the ,Board would be able to' get the loan all right. The Clerk reported that a communication had been received to the effect that the destitute aliens.being maintained by the Board would be paid for by the Government and not out of the local- rates; the Guardians having to render their account quarterly. At the moment, the Clerk added. there was a destitute German boy in the Workhouse, as well as a destitute Belgian refugee, whilst on the out-relief list was the English wife of an interned German. THANKS FOR SERVICES WELL GIVEN. Mr. Billinge proposed a vote of thanks to the .Chairman, the Vice-chairman (Mr. W. Furness), the Clerk and all the ;other' officials' of: the Union for their services during the past year. Under their superintendence and advice, he said, -the Board had been well guided and. the -niembers,.whilst tendering them hearty thanks, anticipated .from them' the•Sa-nie .services in 'the future. (Hear,' hear, and laughter.) The Rev. A. M. Mitchell, in sec.:Aiding, re- marked that the Board had been fortunate having such a. good Chairman. ,• He candidly confessed that when Mr. Jolley was appointed he did not anticpate such good_ results as they had actually oh," and. laughter):-7 -butlie was sure they were all very gratified. 'with ..the outcome -of his year in :the chair. (Hear, hear.). During the whole twelve- -month:they:had only had one little tinge 'of dis- cord. . The Chairman had been most kind and considerate to him personally, and he would like to acknowledge that kindness and consideration with genuine thanks. The Vice-chairman, too, was admirably suited to his position,. because he knew how to hold his tongue. (Laughter.) The Clerk had tried, and tried with success, to treat them all with courtesy and consideration, as, indeed, had all the officials., (Hear, hear.) Messrs. W.''C..Brooks, Flanagan and others having .associated themselves with-the proposal, it was carried With acclamation.

The Chairman, in acknowledging the 'com- pliment, paid a tribute to the V41.111e, of the ser- vices rendered.by the offieials, and went 4m to thank the- members for the geniilneness of their expression of thanks and good-will, and for the good feeling that had pervaded their meetings during the past year. He had done his little best to work in a harmonious manner, and on the whole he thought he had succeeded, though on occasions a slightly jarring note might have been .heard. just as .the .finest musical instrn- ment ocoasionally emitted one. lie had honestly epdeavoured to do all that was in his power to ensure. efficient and smooth working, and be was Pleased to feel that lie had on the whole enjoyed the confidence of his colleagues. (Hear, bear.) , The clerk. speakiiw.on,bebalf of the officials, •said that it was a pleasure to him and to them to know that their serviCes were appreciated.

Something Like an Interview. Mark Twain says his first and only interview with Horace Greeley was when he sought work as •a reporter at the " Tribune " office in New York. By mistake he opened the door to Greeley'S room, when the great writer looked up angrily at the+ visitor and exclaimed: "What in h- do you want here?" Mark rushed to the street•fearful of being arrested for dis- turbing the trend of thought of the famous editor.

div.head: T)-(E STARKEY CUP.
div.p: T)-(E STARKEY CUP.
Orford White Star Qualify For The Final.

div.head: DISQUALIFIED ON PROTEST.
div.p: DISQUALIFIED ON PROTEST.
Notes by " Linesman."

For Good Friday a, fixture had been arranged between Earlestown Mission and the War- rington Central Club. The officials of the latter must have overlooked the fact that on that day the train service is the same as on Sundays. When the players met at the station they were disappointed to learn that they were too late for trains that morning. They then procured a conveyance and arrived at the Mission head- qUarters rather late; and were again dis- appointed as the greater portion of the Mission players had gone away. To add further to their misfortunes it was raining so hard that, n all probability the game would have been cancelled.

On Saturday the Walton team should have made their initial appearance in the League in opposition to the Elmwood Congregationalists, but owing to the late notice the latter received they were unable to get a team together to play the match. •

The Elmwood 'Congregational Recreation Club having -recently- obtained the tenancy of the King and Queen Football Ground, they gave permission. to the Warrington and District League Committee to play the first of the semi- final ties for the Starkey Cup Competition on Easter Monday morning. , There was a good crowd and a keen and enjoyable game was wit- nessed between the Orford White. Star. and the Longford United clubs. Owing to various reasons the White Star had great difficulty in raising a team, which caused a. delay in start- ing. • The game was contested in a very keen and robust style, the .United 'players having weight in their favour. The White Star exhibited more science, .and at the call of time the .White -Star were victorious- by the only goal:of 'the matA. The monthly meeting. of the Warrington and District League was held on Thursday night .the Lion Hotel, Mr. J. Wright presiding. _ _

, • Arising out. Of the .seini-final tie in the "Starkey" Cup Competition was a. protest from Longford 'United: against Orford White Star being awarded the match, on the ground that they wilfully played two ineligible men. The protest was upheld and Longford awarded the tie.
The other semi-final tie between Paddington and Walton was postponed to the 17th nil account of the semi-final tie for the Northern Rugby Union Cup on the Wilderspool ground.

were easily given back. Then the visitors took up the running and attacked the home goal, Roughsedge making several clearances. Play was again transferred to the visitors' goal, Holt clearing easily and the home forwards did not take advantage of several good openings. Following mid-field play the visitors gained ft corner-kick, which was well placed, and Abel heading through, scored the visitors' first goal at the end of thirty minutes' play. From another attack on the home goal Roughsedge cleared well and Asher Oft gaining the ball quickly returned between the uprights. Half- time: Balfour-road, 2; Preston Brook, 0. On resuming the home team went off with a dash but Holt cleared easily, and end-te-end play followed, and for some time the game was not very interesting. In the last fifteen minutes the visitors gained the upper hand and had all their own way, and further goals were added by Peacock •(3), Abel, G. Saunders and Clukas. At ,the call of time the result was: Balfour-road Old Boys, 8; Preston Brook, 0.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.

FAIRFIELD UNITED v. ST. BARNABAS'. These teams met in the first of their League fixtures on Saturday, on the Padgate-lane ground, which was in a very heavy condition. owing to the teavy rains. Both teams were strongly represented owing to the inclusion of players belonging to 'the Great Sankey Club. There was a good crowd of spectators present 'When the fol/owing:,plaieis lined up:— FairVeld•United: Roberts; Bebbington and Gleave, •Ditehfield and Paine; Wood- house, Hunter, Millward, Poulter and Taylor. St. Barnabas': Davenport; E. Glover and E. Long; O'Neill, Challinor and Robinson; Jeffer- son, Midge, Banner, Vernon and Lemons. 'Referee, J.. T. , The home team wori the toss and set the visitors to 'play 'against the wind,' After even mid-field play .Challinor. set his:forwards going and a strong attack was Made on the home goal ' and one .of the defenders handled. A penalty- kick beinc, awarded, Davenport was entrusted with the 'kick, which he placed wide of the uprights: This was considered, a very lucky escape fOr the home team, who replied with a determined, onslaught ~,on the visitors' goal. Ditchfield shot strongly and Davenport brought off a splendid save, falling full length across the goal-mouth-in the effort. Both teams played strenuous football. A .fine drive by. Long enabled his forwartl-; to gain possession, and by

good combination the leather was transferred towards the home goal and Vernon opened the score frOm short range. The United retaliated strchigl7 and fiercely Attacked their opponents' goal and were successful in scoring twice in quick succession by Millward and Poulter. Half-time: Fairfield -United, 2; St. Bernabas', The second portion opened strongly in favour of the heme players and owing to their eager- ness some good 'openings were spoiled by off- side infringement. The visitors appeared un- able to do much again:4 the home defelce and they adapted themselves to' spoiling 'methods. For a While these- were successful, but' at length Millward got through .rain for the United and gave his side a two goals lead. From the centre-kick the visitors improved somewhat and made several dangerous raids on the home citadel, but Bebbington and Kelly defended well and at the end of twenty five minutes' play Lemons reduced the arrears with a splendid effort. From now till- the close of play the, home' team had the best, of the ex= changes:, and the visitors were. not allowed much SCOP, but the visitors' defence played well; and no further goals were 4gistered. 'Result: Fairfield United, 3 goals;' St. Barna- bas', 2 goals. GRAPPENHALL V. ORFORD WiIIITE STAR. At Grappenhall. Grappenhall: Burrows; sWilson and T. Ford; Foam Rathbone and H. Parr; Starkey, Shake- shaft, Thomas, Owen and Oakes. White Star: Millar;- Pilling and Evans; Gif- ford,. 'F. Parr and Connor; Barlow, 'O'Day,' Medellin, Stubbs and liankinson. .The home team won the toss, and Meaehin set the ball roiling. Stubbs was quickly' in the home quarters,. where Ford relieved, and Parr (Orford) gaining possession worked the ball back again and 'passed to Stubbs. The latter Was thus enabled to' .open the score after five minutes' play. From -the centre-kick Thomas and Owen became dangerous, when Gifford, relieved well, and Rathbone securing, Ire,. judiciously passed to Owen. The latter worked A.:grand opening for Oakes,. who made' the scores equal' with a good shot. The visi- tors now became more aggressive, but Meachin got offside. The visitors still pressed and 'Bur- rows did splendid Work .in goal. Hankinson centring well, Stubbs received in, an offside position. From the free-kick the home ten'in gained possession and 11. Parr gave them the lead. Shortly after Stubbs again equalised. Half-time: Two goals each. . The 'second portion opened briskly and the home forwards were well supported by 11. Parr and Rathbone, and Millar wit 4 called, upon several times. Hankinson broke away and forced a fruitless corner, and Evans, who was playing a grand game for the visitors at fnlh back, tel his forwards in fine style, and Bar- low ,centring, a free kick was, given against 'Meachin for a foul on Burrows. Good play by Owen (rave Shakeshaft a clear opening, which he faired to accept. o•Day gave the visitors the lead after beating the home backs, and directly after Meachin added a further goal. Evans and Pilling played a fine game for the visitors, and Burrews, in the home goal, saved the borne team from a heavy defeat. ',Result: Orford White Star,' 4 goals; Grappenhall, .2 goals.

div.head: CHESTER AND I:( \CORN LEAGUE.
div.p: CHESTER AND I:( \CORN LEAGUE.
PRESTON BROOK v. BALFOUR-ROAD OLD BOYS.

On Saturday, on the ground of the former. Each team had only ten players:— Preston Brook: Roughsedge: Antrobus and Jones; Whitlow Johnson and Hind; W. Jones, Webb, Littler and Roughsedge. . Balfour-road: Halt; Lightfoot and Leach; .G. Saunders, Jim Saunders • and, RawlinSon; Asheroft,,ClUkas, Abel. and PeacoclL • The home team won the toss and played with the slope and wind in their favour. The open- ing exchanges were very tame, and the home forwards advanced to their opponents' end, but

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCHES.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCHES.

STOCKTON HEATH v. PADGATE UNITED. The above teams met on Saturday on the West-avenue ground. The home club was not strongly represented, five of their usual players being absent. The opening exchanges were evenly contested, and then each side attacked, but were unable to break down the defence. Play settled in midfield for a while. Then the home team asserted themselves and after several shots had been repulsed by the visiting defence, Barlow opened the score for the Heathens with a splendid long drive. Prom now to the interval the game was very even, but neither side scored.

In the second portion the Heathens had the greater share in attack, but they were met by stubborn defenders, and failed to pierce their defence. The visitors were only dangerous on few occasions, and failed to make the best of their chances. Result: Sthekton'lleath, 1 goal; Padgate 'United, 0. FRODSHAM v. GREAT SANKEY.

At Frodsham on Easter Monday, before a good number of spectators. Both teams were fully represented, and a keen game was expected. The game opened very, fast and Was keenly contested, both teams giving a good exhibition of the passing code. The respective defences played well. Gradually the visitors began to show their superiority and forced the home team on the defensive. The first goal was brought about by good work by Ponlter, who transferred very favourably to Banner, and the latter making a grand centre, Midge had not much difficulty in heading past the home goal- keeper. From the centre-kick the home team made strong efforts to break down the visitors' d*nce, but were eventually driven back to their own half and their defence yielded a penalty kick. Forster took the kiek.but hit.the upright. Whitfield met the ball on the rebound, and scored the second goal. Soon after the interval arrived with the score: Great Sankey; 2 goals; Frodsham; 0. The genie restarted in spirited fashion. The visitors' forwards ' combining well .from mid- field, poulter Scored the third goal after' five minutes' play, and a few minutes later Banner added the fourth point. From, the centre- kick both teams attacked in -Nen ..but the defences prevailed until Illidge broke.away and passed on to Forster,' and the latter transferred back again for Illidge_to score the fifth goal. Following these successes the visitors appeared to slacken a little and the homesters availed themselves of the opening. Savage centring splendidly, Millington handled and Hughes im- proved upon the resulting penalty. The home centre-forward scored a second point with a shot which completely beat Brindle, the final' score being Great Sankey, 5 goals; Frodsham, 2 goals
RUNCORN GUARDIANS.
Three Resignations And An Appointment.
The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held on Tue6day afternoon at the Dutton Workhouse. Mr. C. E. Linaker, jun., presided, and there was a small attendance of members.

div.head: "STARKEY P A )IIPETITION.
div.p: "STARKEY P A )IIPETITION.
Semi-Final Tie. ORFORD WHITE STAR V. LONGFORD UNITED.

The 'semi-final tie for the above competition between these two clubs was played on Easter Monday, on the King and ' Queen- ground, in grand weather and before. a -good croQ of spectators. • 'The clubs were represented by the following players:— White Star: • Miller; Pilling and Millward; Gifford, West and Gregory;' Barlow, - Smith, Meachin, Stubbs- and Hankinson.

Longford: Sturgess; Holden and Mason; Bennett, • IFe.:lrnley and Stevens; Hands,' Eccle- ston, Sherratt, Shelmardine and Hughes, Referee, 31 r. B. Howell. Longford won the toss and played uphill. There was a strong wind blowing across the field. .Meachin set the ball rolling and the United .quarters were quiekly visited. -Holden -relieved with a big punt and play was 'trans- ferred to the opposite end, and Pilling was penalised for "hands." Stevens took the kick, but placed wide. Play was kept near_ the -Longford 'goal, and ..Stubbs Sent over the bar and then Millward cleared. a dangerous centre from Hankinson. Both teams now settled down. and-some•keen and 'hard 'play Was wit- nessed, and the game was very fast. The defenders on both sides tackled well, with Pilling mast prominent. From .a throw-in the United became dangerous And gained a couple- 'of Corner-kicks in quick succession;. but failed to improve on them The _danger being re- lieved, a short visit was made to the opposite end, where, Holden relieved With a splendid drive. Eccleston raced away along the touch and centred. Hughes' final .effort was wide of the goal. From the goal-kick. the White Star •forwards Combined well. together and set up a strong attack on the United 'goal, where Stur- gess saved finely, but was penalised for after- wards pulling a player down. Stubbs took the kick- and drove the ball straight, at Sturgess, who _cleared, much to_ the delight :of the United supporters. 'Play was transferred to ..the.oppo-' sife end and several keen attacks were repulsed by Pilling and Millvi-ard. Qradually the United were forced back to 'their 'own quarters, where iTolden again mis,kicked and let in Stubbs and -Hankinson. From a centre from the latter Sinith had an open goal to shoot at, but failed to take advantage of the opening. This gave relief to the. United defence and some hard play was witnessed in mid-field until, by a good pass from Pilling, the Star forward line was again in the ascendancy, and a good movement ended by Stubbs beating, Sturgess With . a good .cross-shot after forty minutes' play, The .United gained -another •corner-kid;, 'which the Star defence got, away,• and the in- terval being called the score was: White Star, 1 goal: Longford United, nil. •_

. On the resumption the wind bad beconie stronger and more behind the 'players and the game .started very keenly, the United making the first advances, but, meeting strong opposi- tion from Pilling, Millward and Hughes, they ended the Attack by sending over the bar. Off- side against Barlow gave the United relief for a.moment, as from another raid by the Stars Trankinson centred from an awkward position, and Smith was too late to intercept. From the goal-kick 'the United forwards made strenuous efforts; to break down the Stars' de- fence, but Miller was not seriously troubled. and gradually the players slackened down and play was chiefly in the IThited's half. Owing to big kicking the game was not as interesting as it had been, and whenever shots reached the goal Sturgcss .was equal to the calls- ,made upon him. For the Longford team StUrgeSs. excelled in goal and saved his side frolii a heavy 'defeat. Stevens, Eccleston and liands also (lid well. For the White Star Pilling and Millward at full-back defended in splendid style. West was a hard worker at centre-half, and • Hankinson. Barlow and Stubbs did well in the forward line, Result: Orford White Star, 1 goal; Longford United, nil.

div.head: NINE GUINEAS FOR MANCHESTER INFIRMARY.
div.p: NINE GUINEAS FOR MANCHESTER INFIRMARY.

The 'correspondence read by, the Clerk (Mr. Ilough) included a letter containing the sanc- tion of the Local Government Board to the granting of a subscription by the Guardians of nine guineas to the Manchester Royal Infir- mary.

div.head: THREE RESIGNATIONS.
div.p: THREE RESIGNATIONS.
A letter was read from Mr. A. Houghton, resigning his position as organist at the Work- house.
A second letter wiA% from the Rev. L. J. T. Darwall, vicar of Walton, and in it he re- signed the chaplaincy of the Workhouse.
A further letter was also read from Mr. Cor- nelius 1)odd, resigning his position as care- taker of the Smallpox Hospital at Moore.
NO NEED TO BEG.

From the North-Western Vagrancy com- mittee came a communication stating that all tramps or destitute wayfarers can obtain food and lodgings for the night on application at the Poor Law Institution, or to the Relieving Officer, as the, case May be, in each Union. There could be no bona-fide excuse for., beg- ging.-- In a further letter it was ,sliggested that the way-tickets system should be put into operation forthwith, but that the distribution of meal tickets should be delayed until after April 9th. MEDICAL RELIEF NO BAR TO OLD-AGE

div.head: PENSIONS.
div.p: PENSIONS.

A circular letter from the Local Government Board respecting- the disqualification for old- age pensions of persons who were in receipt of out-relief was read. It pointed out that if only medical relief was given the recipient would not be disqualified from receiving the pension.

div.head: CHAPLAIN-CUM-ORGANIST.
div.p: CHAPLAIN-CUM-ORGANIST.

At the last meeting of the Board the Rev. W. L. Johnstone, vicar of • Sutton Weaver, was appointed Workhouse _Chaplain in place of Mr. Darwell, resigned. Mr. Johnstone now wrote 'accepting the position, and also intimating that he would carry out the duties of oiganist well, without any remuneration as organist; The office of chaplain carries with it a stipend. of 00 per annum. On the motion of Mr.. Morris, the thanks of .the Guardians were accorded to Mr. Johnstone for consenting to couple the posts of .chaplain and organist. • AN EXPLANATION.

. Dr. Maxwell wrote under date April Ist, re complaint to the effect that he had declined to attend a sick pauper. After hearing the letter detailing the - circumstances - of the case the Guardians agreed that the .exPlanation was a satisfactory one.
The business of the Board was completed in about 25 minutes.

div.head: ABSENTEES AND DESERTERS.
div.p: ABSENTEES AND DESERTERS.
UNSANCTIONED HOLIDAY.

Rifleman Joseph Whitfield appeared at Mon- day's Police Court for having been an absentee from the sth Rifle Brigade since March 16th. He wa,s handed over to an escort. GUNNERS'. UNAUTHORISED RESPITE.

. At Tuesday's Police Court, Gunners 'bun Burgess and Herbert Unsworth (the latter of 30, Brighton-street), respectively .of the 16th and 17th Heavy Batteries Royal Garrison Artillery, were said to have admitted being absentees from their base in the South since April lst.—They were handed to the escort. DISCARDED UNIFORM.

Private Thomas Sandon was brought before Monday's Court for having been a desertEti from the 3rd Battalion King's Liverpool Regiment since March 24th.—He said "it was right."—lt was stated that he was found in plain clothes, having discarded his uniform in Liverpool.—He was handed to an escort. "GOING TO STATION!"

Private Thomas -Hennessey appeared at Tuesday's Police Court for being an absentee from the South Lancashires (stationed in Lan- cashire) since Saturday.—He could produce no pass, said a -constable, when stopped in Scot- land-road.—Hennessy : All the same, I was going to the station when .he stped me!—He was handed to an escort. ABSENTEES' ADMISSIONS.

Drivers John William Richards and Robert Boyle were brought before Tuesday's Court for being absent since March 13th from the filth Brigade Royal Field Artillery (stationed in the South).—A constable stated that he visited 3, Speneer's-yard, where he saw one °Utile men, who admitted being an absentee; whilst the other made a similar confession when brought in by another constable.--Both men were ordered to return with an escort.

WHAT INEBRIATED ABSENTEE pip. Private John Brown, or Quinn, was clarged at Monday's Police Court With being absent from the 2nd Lancashire Fusiliers.—lie denied the offence.--A constable said that shortly after half-past eleven he was called to a disturbance at ,- 22, Old-road. Prisoner, apparently the sole cause for the trouble, was under the influence of drink. Re had no pass, and was .Stated to have said ha did not intend to go back.—The absentee—having told how he forwarded his pass ,to • the regimental- pay- master so that he,-should forfeit pay during his week's extension—was handed over to an escort.

div.head: Should Tho' Be Made Notifiable?
div.p: Should Tho' Be Made Notifiable?
RURAL COUNCIL SAYS "NO."

The Warrington Rural District Councillors at their monthly meeting in Bewsey Chambers, Warrington, on Wednesday afternoon, deliber- ated as to whether or not measles and German measles should be added to the list of infectious diseased which are made compulsorily noti- fiable.

Mr. G. Mather: German measles, indeed! We are having none, of them. We must stop importations from the enemy. (Laughter.) The Chairman (Mr. W. Furness) : The Medical Officer will make an attack on the German measles! (Renewed laughter.) The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: Yes, we want to kill the German measles, as well as beat the Ger- mans! (More laughter.) The Medical Officer (Dr. Sephton) said that hitherto measles and German measles had not been notifiable, and had they been so during _ .

the last six months or so it would have cost the Council hundreds of pounds for notifications. When the proposal to make the diseases com- pulsorily notifiable was first brought forward some six months ago, many authorities took up the matter and made notification of the two varieties of measles compulsory, and now they were anxious to retract, and he would not advise ,the Council to put the two diseases named on their list. The Council decided to take the doctor's advice.

div.head: BURTONWOOD ROAD MATTERS.
div.p: BURTONWOOD ROAD MATTERS.

At the same meeting the Rev. A. M. Mitchell said that at the annual meeting of the parish- ioners of Thittonwood a number of those pres- ent had a. great deal to say about the state of• the roads, 'which Was---horrible in the extreme. He pointed out to them' the view of the Rural District Council, which was that it would be rather a Mistaken policy, Until the Sankey bridge was really completed, to proceed with the work of repairing the roads leading to the bridge, because, in all pr6bability,. the repairs would have to be done a second time, and that, therefore, ,it would savour rather of a ease of throwing good money after' bad. Since the parish meeting he had had sundry complaints made to him as to the road that led up to Bold- lane , from Collins Green. He had it on, very good authority that the materia4 which had been put down was only about an inch and a third thick, and the feeling was that that was not enough, and that if roads were, to be re- made the work ought to be done in a thoroughly businesslike way,, So that .they would last not merely for a few :months or a year or .two, but more or less permanently. The Chairman Said he thought himself that it would be best to put off the matter of the re- making of this and other roads until Sankey bridge was absolutely finished.. Whatever work the Council did on their roads was done as well as it was possible to. do it, and he thought the Surveyor would bear 'him out that, when the time .came, they would not be found lacking so far as `good work and substantial work was con- cern&l in Burton Wood and district.
IF THE COUNTY COUNCIL DO NOT GIVE SATISFACTION -

The Surveyor (Mr. Newcombe) reported that further representations had been made to the County Council with reference to the damage done to the Burtonwood roads in consequence of the diversion of traffic owing to the work pro- ceefling at Sankey Bridges, and failing some satisfactory offer from the County Council he suggested that representation be made to the Local Government Board for arbitration in the matter.

div.head: THANKS WHERE THANKS IS DUE.
div.p: THANKS WHERE THANKS IS DUE.

After eight months of war Germany was still fighting, for the most part outside her own land, and the terrible casualty lists showed why more men Were essential in this fight for our own existence. He believed the appeal would not be made in vain to the young men of Warrington' to come forward to prevent War- rhigton women and children suffering what the Belgian women and children had endured. ,The first battalian were fighting in the trenches, undergoing fatigues in the midst of dangers, and perfnrming deeds of which any town might be proud
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. APRIL 10, 1915.

div.head: NEW TERRITORIAL BATTALION
div.p: NEW TERRITORIAL BATTALION
,Satini,actory ria3p.m3e to Appeal
for Recruits.

As we announced in "The Examiner" last week a third battalion of Warrington Terri- torials is in the course of formation. Captain Townroe, who is the head of the recruiting staff that has the task in hand of raising 600 men, is meeting with the.. success his energy deserve. The men must be nineteen years of age at least, sft. lin. in height, and if no taller than that '34in. round the chest. Taller men may be 33in. chest measurement.

This third line depot will be merged with the Second 4th Battalion South Lancashire Regi- ment, that is, they will be sent on enlistment to .be trained along with the Reserve Battalion, which is of considerable strength both in officers and men. It is felt that all that is neccs- sary to ensure the success of the effort to raise this additional local battalion is that the em-
ployers should co-operate loyally, maieng it easy for men who are not engaged upon war work to join, coupled with the willingness of young .men fit and free to do their duty.

div.head: ENTHUSIASM AT THE THEATRES.
div.p: ENTHUSIASM AT THE THEATRES.
Captain Townroe and his staff visited, the oval Court Theatre, the Picturedrome, and :he Park Picture Palace on Saturday, and the lippodrome, Star Kinema House, the Picture-

droine, the Picture 'House and the Park Picture Palace.- on Easter Monday. The Captain's appeal for recruits to assist in putting an end to German .pretensions were received with great •enthusiasm. If that enthusiasm is translated in a practicitl •manner, our third Battalion of Territorials should soon become an accomplished •fact.
TO FIGHT FOR OUR WOMEN AND CHILDREN.

div.head: Baby Nailed to a Door.
div.p: Baby Nailed to a Door.

They, and thousands like them, were protect- ing Warrington women and children from the awful sufferings of war. It was hard to realise what war meant, but he would give one ex- ample which be had heard from an officer of the South' Lancashire Regiment. The officer was going along a road in Belgium when he noticed what he thought was a curious knocker on a doer. On making a closer examination he was horrified to find it was the body of a baby which had been nailed alive to the door. Our women and children must be protected- against such horrors ever happening in this country. We must have faith in Lord Kitchener, and when he gave Orders that another Warrington battalion was needed, surely the eligible young men, who could be seen in the town in great numbers, _would come forward.

"Come to the Drill Hall any evening," added Captain Townroe: "We will give you a warm welcome; if passed .by .the doctor, you ,will be sent .straight to Tunbridge Wells, and .you will be loyally taking your part in defeating Ger- man militarism utterly, and in .bringing this war th 'a victorious conclusion, and ensuring a lasting „peace."

div.head: TUNBRIDGE WELLS.
div.p: TUNBRIDGE WELLS.

Tunbridge Wells is a.n ideal town in beautiful Kent and comfortable houses, including several mansions. have been placed at the disposal of the Tet•ritorials.. The food is good 'and ample, and daring recent weeks has been augmented by a portion of the Canadian cheese that has been sent as a gift- from the Dominion to the Mother Country. As an example of the in- terest taken by the, residents in the men it may be recorded that one gentleman--a

retired colonel—bas given a standing invitation for ten " Terriers " to take tea with him every Sunday The hand of the regiment, -which played at the Pantiles, a fashionable resort; on Easter Monday, does much to cement this friendly feeling. • The feather beds and comforts of .Blackpool may be absent, but the real war atmosphere with the , areoplanes, bi-planes Much in evidence, more titan makes good that deficiency. There is a splendid chance of promotion on the raising of a new battalion, non-Com- missioned officers being in great demand.

div.head: BANK HOLIDAY SPORTS.
div.p: BANK HOLIDAY SPORTS.
" Terriers' " Marathon Racing
And Football.

The brigade of which the 2ndrith Lancashire Regiment form a part, spent Easter Monday in a .pleasant and profitable manner. In the morning there was a great "Marathon" race open to a team from each battalion. The Course was A distance of 71 miles. The roads were in excellent condition and the weather, though threatening, was fine. A stiff climb of about a mile was encountered •through Cfroombridge, and it speaks well for the vitality of the competitoxs that out of 78 starters no fewer than 73 finished the course.

_ hornet-Hately after this event, there was an inter-battalion marching competition, open to N nibiors and WO men from each battalion. The distance- to be covered in this event was about four miles. and was won by the Liverpool Scottish, who beat the 4th South Laneashires bv two -ininntes. The stamina of the men was well tested in this race. and the fact that not a simile Man " fell out " of our local lads speaks highly of the benefit. of their training.

div.head: Warrington Football Matches
div.p: Warrington Football Matches

In the afternoon, inter-company football matches were held in connection with the War- rington battalion.. In the preliminary round "A" Company won from "B" Company by the odd goal in three: while ."C" Company settled the aspirations of " D" Company by three goals to. one. In the final, "A " corn- pany, after a hard, gruelling game ran Out .winners by two goals to nil. The band of the battalion discoursed sweet music on the historic Pantiles in the morning and 'afternoon. tinder the leadership of Band- Sergeant Sadler.
"Fit" for Anything.,

The Battalion have had a very hard training. and.are 'becoming ON hard as nails. and. getting "fit " to uphold the glerions honour of our First Battalion now taking their full share in upsetting the calculations of the Kaiser. . The other dav the Battalion took nart in a. sham fight. We were very prond to be associ- ated with a portion of the Canadian contingent, including part of Stratheona's. Horse. on this oecasion. The health of the men is very good, and there is very little crime in the Battalion.

The total receipts for 1913, he pointed out, were .058: 18s. 7d., as against, £724.135.' 7d. for 1914.: He thought that was very satisfactory when they considered the war and all the calls that were being made upon :the generosity of, people nowadays; :indeed the fact that there was an increase instead of a decrease was some- thing they might congratulate themselves upon. Rector Suggests Some Improvements. _ . •
He would very much like to have electric
lighting throughout the church, in addition to the gas; it would brighten up the fine old edifice so very _Also he would like the pews

Their present kneelers rather encouraged peoPle to sit on the seats and just lean forward, which did not seem to him properly to realise ,the idea of worship. lie thought something more might be done to the churchyard. it had been suggested that they should lay the tombstones fiat, but, added to the fact that he did not think that would be .feasible, he very -much preferred to see the old tombstones' standing; though hes thought the present grass might he dug up and the soil sown again and alders and privet planted wherever it was possible. •Again, he thanked them for the encouragement and help they had given him. lie could not but. feel how very short his time was .getting. lie. Could not bear the church when he first came, but now he never felt that any other church was quite like their dear old Parish Church. 'THANKS AND SYMPATHY.

At the church, under the chairmanship of the Vicar. (the Rev. James Davies) the St. Ann's vestry meeting was held on Tuesday evening. Mr. Davies said, they could not in some ;respects compare themselves with other parishes, but they were certainly a very united, peaceful and happy congregation, and their work in the parish was carried on in a Christianliko spirit: OFFICERS RE-APPOINTED.

"I have very great pleasure in nominating' Mr. T. IL Corbett to act, as before, as church- warden," concluded the Vicar. Mr. Corbett accepted, saying he hoped their happy relations would continue. St. Peter's Church vestry meeting was lield on Wednesday evening. The &W. B. Percival (vicar) presided, and amongst those present were the Rev. .111. Martin (citrate), Mr. T. S. Steel ( vicar's warden) and Mr. Reddish (the people's .warden). -

Mr. Reddish submitted the- churchwardens' accounts, from which it appeared that the total income was ce.177 ss. Gid. and the ex- penses .t 67 us. div.head: Wardens Re•appointed.
div.p: The Wardens Re•appointed.

The -Vicar, rising to appoint his officers, said lie would like to compliment the churchwar- dens on the balance sheet. The balance was not quite so large as in the previous year, but the ,expenses had been rather heavier and more money had been devoted to objects other than church expenses. The people were at 'present having calls upon them in various directions, but he considered the church ac- counts Very satisfactory. He was pleased to say that Mr. Steel had kindly consented to act again as Vicar's warden, and he had very much pleasure in appointing him. On the proposition of Mr. James Taylor, seconded by Mr. G. E. Greaves, and supported by Mr. W. H. Dickens, Mr. Reddish was re- ap Pointed people's warden. .

Complimentary. references were made to the admirable manner in which Mr. Reddish had fulfilled the office, it being said that the con- gregation would be pleased to see him in office again. He had been most regular in his attendance at the services and attended to his duties most satisfactorily. '
Mr. Iteddisll, in repl , thanked the officers and congregation for the support he had re- ceived during the past year, and for the assist- ance rendered • by his co-churchwarden, Mr. Steel.
Two Hundred Men from the .Parish Serving the Country.

Mr. Steel also thanked the Vicar for again appointing him, and pointed out . that the chu'rch, Owing to the 'War:was passing through a most cri',:ical time. The services were not quite,so.well attended as before the war, but it should be noted that Aomething like 200 men out of the parish had been called to serve their King and country, and that ninny of them were members of the congregation, and also of the Bible-class. He believed that many men, who, prior' to the war, had not been in the habit of attending a place of worship, would be so impressed as a result of the experiences they were having in the war,' that not only many of them, but also their families, • would afterwards connect themselves with some place of worship. •

div.head: Election of Church Officers.
div.p: Election of Church Officers.

Mr. J. Swinton was appointed vicar's warden and Mr. John Povey people's warden. The sidesmen ,eleeted were: Messrs.- Cross, Monks, Brownbell, Siincox, Brandreth and White. Messrs. White: Sinicox and Woods were appointed auditoN.
Vicar's Review of the Year's Work.
The Vicar observed that during the year they

had lost Mr. Spencer, one ,of their sidesmen, and a man whose heart Was in the work. Whilst rejoicing. in his promotion, they regretted his absence from their midst. As regards the dis- trict, the proportion of Churehpeople remained the same, being about two-thirds of the popula- tion They, the Churchpeople of Orford, were all of. one family and were all friends. Refer- ring to the church. workers, the Vica L. said that he must thank them for their kindness to him: kindness which made the work of the parson very much easier. The Bible Class had become almost extinct, the reason being that so many of their. Bible Class 'lads .were away at the Front and elsewhere. They had lost one of them by death, vix.: Corporal George Higham. They had now only seven members left. There were now the names of 112 soldiers and sailors on the prayer list. Not all of them were the names of members of Orford parish, but all had relatives or friends in the place._ He was in correspondence with 101 out of that number. The vicarage was now provided and they would make no further appeal. They should now go ahead for all they were worth with the oigan . _
fund. Orford, the Vicar mentioned in (-'un- elusion, had now just about 1,000 inhabitants.

The vestry meeting connected with St. James' Church and St. lii)da's Mission, was held on Thursday night in the St. James' School. The Vicar the Rev. It B. Firth) presided, and said he had very much pleasure in nominating Mr. Acton, who had consented to be re-eleled, as his warden, Mr. Acton appointed Mr. Stansfield as ,his sidesma n.
Mr. W. Eolcersley was again chosen people's warden, .and be appointed Mr. 13. Hall as his sidesman.
300 Serving With The Colours.

The Vicar said they came on to the meeting of the congregation, the vestry being over. In every parish in England some reference would be made to the war. It would have been Very unbecoming if they had not in their parish Sent out a very large contingent. At the least they had got nearly 300 names on the roll of honour, and he had reason to believe that more men would be asked for before long to join the colours. Ono way in which they could assist the Government was by united prayer for the soldiers and sailors of the country. One was rather grieved that the people as a whole had not respaided as they ought to have done.

div.head: To Work For.
div.p: To Work For.
There were two things they had to work for. One was a new organ, which they got in Decem- ber, and the other was the new Mission build- ing. in which, in a few weeks„ they hoped to bold services.
The voting for the sidesmen resulted in the following being elected,: Messrs. F. A.stley, 11.

Woodward, J. Fargber, p. Hodge, M. George. IL Warburton, 4. Eckersley and A. Todd. , Mr. Acton and Mr. titansfield were appointed lay representatives. The accounts submitted by Mr. Acton showed that the income had been £199 19s. 7d.. includ- ing £lO6 4s. Rd. general offertory-and £B2 Ss. PM. special offertory. There was also a £lO grant from a sale of Work. The year began with a balance in hand of ,V,l 12s. 11d., and ended with a deficit balance of 9s. id.

HINTS AND INTERESTING FACTS AND CHAT FOR AMATEURS. food for any laying hen, however good it may be when used in the fattening pen. 1 An early feed, as early as possible, should then be the rule, and later in the day some green stuff, such as cabbage leaves, cauliflower leaves, and such like, that are not wanted, should be thrown into the run. A good supply of green food is an absolute necessity to all laying stock, and especially to those in confine- ment. The evening meal should consist. of oats in preference to other grains. It is excellent for all poultry, because it is not too fattening, though at the same time it is nourishing and sustaining. Wheat is good, undoubtedly, but its price is against its general use, and it is rather heavier than oats; for instance, a hand- ful of wheat is considerably more in bulk than a handful of oats. As a change, though, wheat is most excellent, and will be thoroughly appreciated by the birds. The grain should be fed in the scratching. shed or even in dry weather on the manure bedding. There is no harm in this, and it will give plenty of scratching exercise, which is good for the circulation of the blood in cold weather.

Private Stanley Daniels, whose home is at 11, St. Peter's-place, and who was wounded at the same time as PrivateiGeorge White, is now in the Second Northern General Hospital, Leeds. . Writing to his mother to, acquaint her of the fact, the gallant Private says:— Just a line to let you know I am wounded. At present I am at a base hospital. Shot In The Side, But Progressing Private Richard George Done, whose parents reside at 54, Fox-street, Sankey Green, ia 21 years of age, and before going to the war was employed as a labourer at Monks, Hall Co. LANCE-CORPORAL LINLEY. Not Downhearted Despite " Nasty Knock In Back." Lance-Corporal Sydney Linley was slightly wounded on Thursday night of last week, and on 9.pril 2nd sent a printed field postcard home to say I have been admitted into hospital slightly wounded, and am going on well, and hope to be discharged soon. I! am being sent down to the base. Letter follows at first oppor- tunity. The "letter followed" on Tuesday night, written on April 4th, from the Base Hospital in France. It was curious that it should arrive on Mrs. Linley's birthday. He says: I have had a bit of a nasty knock in the middle of the back. The skin has been broken a little, and it has made it sore. But I shall soon be all right again. I expect to sail to-day for England, so expect soon to ! be having a look at you all. Do not be ! down-hearted, for the wound might have been worse. Arrival in England. Writing on board ship to his wife, Lance- Corporal Linley adds:— -• " We are just about to arrive at Southamp- ton. I am doing 'champion.'.• They are look- ing after us well. Could not do more for mi." Writing to his wife from Bristol Infirmary, Lance-Corporal Linley says : " I have arrived safely after a grand sail across. When we got to Bristol, we had a great welcome, refreshments on the station and great crowds in the streets. This is a .nice hospital, and I shad! soon be myself again."
